News.title: Horror as deer impales itself on church fence sparking high street closure as cops say animal died from serious injuries
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

DEER TRAGEDY Horror as deer impales itself on church fence sparking high street closure as cops say animal died from serious injuries







Next

A DEER was left dying in agony after impaling itself on a church fence in front of horrified locals.

The badly injured animal was found suffering on the fence surrounding Christ Church in Walshaw, near Bolton.

Cops rushed to the scene as the horror unfolded, with the High Street shut while the stricken deer was dealt with.

Images showed several marked and unmarked police cars blocking the road.





The tragedy left witnesses deeply upset as the animal endured serious injuries.

One person described the scene as “so sad”, while another called it “very upsetting”, reports Bolton News.

Many said euthanasia would have been “the right thing to do” to end the poor animal’s suffering.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed the deer had been seriously injured after impaling itself.



A spokesperson said: “We were called to reports that a deer had impaled itself and it was badly injured.

“The deer has been removed, and the officers arranged for street cleansing to take place, which has now been completed.”

The force later confirmed the deer had died from its injuries.

However, cops did not confirm reports from witnesses that armed officers had euthanised the animal.



Reports of the incident and the resulting road closure began circulating on social media earlier this morning.

The exact circumstances of how the deer came to impale itself on the church fence have not been confirmed by emergency services.

The High Street was left disrupted as officers dealt with the aftermath.

Street cleansing was arranged by police after the animal was removed.

The road has since been cleared following the grim ordeal.

News.title: Kratom killed my healthy 22-year-old son after he used it as a swap for coffee – parents need to know warning signs
News.content:
Next

A GRIEVING mom has warned of the dangers of kratom – nicknamed gas station heroin – after it was found at the scenes of two Ole Miss students’ deaths.

Susan Eppard lost her son Matthew Eller, 22, in 2021 after he became hooked on the substance, which is often taken for energy and focus but can produce opioid-like effects.



She said her “perfectly healthy” son became emaciated and increasingly isolated himself from friends and family before suffering a violent seizure and dying on the kitchen floor of his home.

“Justice for my son Matthew will be when kratom is banned across the entire United States,” Susan told The U.S. Sun.



Her warning comes after Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were found dead in separate incidents on Monday.

Hamilton, a freshman from Colorado, was found unresponsive inside Stewart Hall on the University of Mississippi campus, while Strang, a junior from Georgia, was found dead at an off-campus home in Oxford.

Autopsies have been carried out and officials are fast-tracking toxicology reports to determine how the students died and whether kratom played a role.

Packaged kratom was found in both investigations, but the deaths are not thought to be linked to each other and there is no confirmed connection to the substance.

Lafayette County Metro Narcotics has since urged the Ole Miss community to avoid kratom “out of an abundance of caution.”

For Susan, the deaths immediately brought back memories of losing Matthew almost five years ago.



“It’s heartbreaking every time another person dies from kratom,” she said.

“Knowing what these families are going to have to go through, their brothers and sisters and their moms and dads, everybody.

“It’s heart-wrenching.”

Susan believes Matthew — from Cartersville, Georgia, — had been taking kratom for around two years before his death, although she said he hid the extent of his use from her.

She first discovered empty packets and initially struggled to find information online warning of serious risks.



Susan said Matthew believed it was a safe swap for coffee.

“He thought it was like a coffee alternative. Safe for energy,” she said.

But she said his use eventually became all-consuming.

“All I know was he was spending all of his money on it,” she said.

“He couldn’t pay his car payment, lost his car, couldn’t pay his phone.



“He had been living with me and I didn’t charge him any money, but he just still had no money, even for food or anything.”

Matthew was working full-time, but Susan said he was eventually spending “thousands of dollars” on kratom.

The worried mother also watched her once outgoing and athletic son dramatically change.

“He became quite emaciated. Very, very skinny,” she said.



What is kratom? Kratom is a tropical tree native to South-East Asia whose leaves contain two main psychoactive ingredients: mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. Consumption of the leaves can produce stimulant effects at low doses and sedative effects at higher doses, according to the US Drug Enforcement Administration. It can also cause psychological and physical dependence. High doses have been linked to seizures, liver damage, difficulty breathing and death, while other reported effects include nausea, vomiting, sweating, insomnia, weight loss and hallucinations. The kratom trade is estimated to be worth around $1.5billion, with at least 2,000 fatal kratom-related overdoses recorded in the US since 2021, according to figures previously reported by the Tampa Bay Times. The FDA has not approved kratom for medical use, while the substance is banned in several US states.

“He was always, you know, like the center of attention. Everybody joined around him when he’d walk in a room, just lighting up every room.

“And he became very reclusive. He started staying away from all his friends and family.

“He loved his grandmother so much and he wouldn’t answer her phone calls.”



She recalled asking her son if he was taking drugs because she could not understand where his money was going.

“He said, ‘No mom, I’m not on drugs. You can test me,'” she recalled.

“And he didn’t act like he was on drugs other than when he would sleep.

“He would sleep like he was in a coma.

“I had to buy a sonic alarm clock to wake him up for work.



“I had no idea you could die from it [kratom]. I don’t think he thought he could have died from it.”

Susan said Matthew had apparently attempted to stop using kratom but continued hiding it from his girlfriend.

“I don’t know really if he ever could have got off of it,” she said.

“I think his death was the only thing that was going to free him from this garbage drug.”

Matthew was playing cards with his girlfriend at his home when tragedy struck.



“He just went into a violent seizure and collapsed on the floor and went into cardiac arrest, and they were never able to resuscitate him,” Susan said.

“He died at home on his kitchen floor,” she added through tears.

Susan was around 25 minutes away when she learned what had happened and rushed to the hospital.

“When I got there, they were like, ‘Sorry, but he didn’t make it,'” she said.

“They made me wait outside for quite a while before I could go in, and he was just laying there covered with a sheet and still intubated.



“He was just so cold and dark and gray and stiff.”

Susan said Matthew had never previously suffered a seizure or suffered illness after taking the substance.

She said his toxicology and autopsy results subsequently attributed his death to the toxic effects of mitragynine, an alkaloid found in kratom.

“They didn’t find any other prescription drugs and/or street drugs or alcohol in his system,” Susan said.

“His autopsy showed he had no underlying health conditions. And he was a perfectly healthy 22-year-old young man.”



Since Matthew’s death, Susan has devoted herself to campaigning against kratom and said she regularly contacts lawmakers, testifies and attends government meetings.

“It’s a full-time nonpaying job for me to get kratom banned throughout the whole United States, and I’m not going to stop until that happens,” she said.

She also issued a stark warning to students who might consider using kratom to help them stay awake or focused while studying.

“Don’t use this,” Susan said.

“It’s very dangerous. It’s highly addictive once you get on it.



“How are you going to get off of it even if you wanted to?”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

To watch Susan’s full interview about her son Matthew, visit The U.S. Sun’s YouTube Channel.

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration) at 1-800-662-HELP (4357)

News.title: Brits should stockpile money, water and tinned food in case of attack or disaster, Defence Secretary warns
News.content:
Next

BRITS should have a stockpile of cash, bottled water and tinned food at home in case of disaster or war, the Defence Secretary has warned.

Wes Streeting said the UK is at greater risk of being crippled by fires, floods and attacks from our enemies – including cyber warfare.

He said Britain needs a “whole society approach” to beef up our resilience – although he said the public should be “alert not alarmed” about threats.



Speaking to The Sun on Sunday on the eve of the Labour Party conference, he said: “It’s not a big ask, it’s just a simple ask of people.



“Do they have what they need indoors, should they lose access to their online banking for a period? Should they have a power cut?

“If there was a risk of wildfire, if there was a risk of flooding, sometimes it feels like even in communities that experience those sorts of events periodically, we’re not as prepared as we should be.”

He added: “It’s having some cash at home, having a supply of bottled water indoors, having some tinned goods that you can access if your electric goes and you’re not able to cook on the hob or in the microwave.



“These are basic things, and of course, you know, a lot of people just have that in their cupboard naturally.”

Britain faces risks from enemy states and terror groups – but also from more extreme weather like flooding and wildfires, he said.

Mr Streeting said “individual citizens” should think about “how to be prepared for acts of nature, or acts of terrorism, or indeed in extreme acts of war.



“That can only be a good thing for national resilience.

“I want people. We’ve got to get the balance right. I want people to be alert, not alarmed.

“There is always a risk when you have these conversations that people overreact or think, well why is this important now?

“But resilience is always important for a country.”

The government has released a list of emergency supplies they say every home should have in case disaster strikes.



This includes a first aid kit, batteries, a torch and a wind up radio.

News.title: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warns Britain faces “a greater risk of war than at any point in my lifetime”
News.content:
Next

DEFENCE Secretary Wes Streeting has warned that Britain faces “a greater risk of war than at any point in my lifetime” and Vladimir Putin is enemy number one.

He said the UK must invest in our Armed Forces now – otherwise we could lose a war in just five years time.



Speaking to The Sun on Sunday on the eve of the Labour Party conference, Britain’s new Defence Secretary said our enemies are waiting for us to show signs of weakness.

Mr Streeting, 43, said: “Without a shadow of a doubt, the biggest threat facing Britain is Russia and President Putin.



“We’ve got war in our continent. We’ve got a Russian President who has imperialist ambitions, who is constantly testing Britain’s defences, NATO defences, and testing the strength of our alliances.

“And so, the sobering reality is that we face a greater risk of war than we’ve done at any point in my lifetime.

“And against that backdrop, that is why we have decided to deliver the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the Cold War.

“Because while I can sit here confidently today telling you that I have what I need – and we have what we need – to keep this country safe, were we to stand still I wouldn’t be able to say the same thing with confidence in five years’ time.”

A failure to invest in the Armed Forces now would leave Britain so weak that Russia – or another rogue state – could launch a war against us, he warned.



The Defence Secretary said: “Strength builds deterrence, and deterrence makes it far less likely that we will end up in a place we don’t want to be – which is at war with Russia or indeed anyone else.”

Mr Streeting issued the stark warning amid an ongoing row over defence spending.

Earlier this year, John Healey quit as Defence Secretary with a blistering attack on then PM Keir Starmer’s failure to find the cash to keep Britain safe.

The astonishing bust-up contributed to Sir Keir’s downfall and the decision by Labour MPs to install Andy Burnham in No10.

Mr Healey is now the Chancellor in charge of finding the cash.



He is expected to announce an extra £5 billion for defence at next month’s Budget, but has delayed announcing a plan to spend 3.5 per cent of GDP (national income) on defence by 2035 until next year.

We currently spend just 2.6 per cent.

Military experts have warned that delay makes Britain weaker and our enemies stronger.

The Army has already been told to stop “non essential” training exercises to save cash.

But Mr Streeting insists he is confident Mr Healey will find the money needed.



“Do I have confidence in John Healey to give me and the Ministry of Defence what we need to keep our country safe? A hundred per cent”, he said.

“And he’s already said he’s going to give more to defence in this Budget. He’s already indicated that there’ll be more to come at next year’s Spending Review, and that’s a good place to be.”

But finding money for defence means tax rises or cuts to other departments.

When Sir Keir tried to trim just £6bn from the bloated benefits budget he was hit by a massive Labour rebellion and had to ditch the plan.



Britain’s welfare bill has ballooned to £330bn, with about half the cash going on non pensioner handouts.

Asked directly if a Labour government is actually willing to cut other budgets to fund defence, Mr Streeting said: “There are obvious choices and trade-offs to be faced across government, and that is that is the fiendish job that the Chancellor has.

“And we’ve got to back him up on that.”

He added: “On welfare, we’ve got to bring the welfare bill down. Andy Burnham’s been clear about that.”

I am speaking to Mr Streeting in a room in Horse Guards, the famous military headquarters in Whitehall overlooking Horse Guards Parade.



He is preparing to give his first party conference speech as Defence Secretary after a rollercoaster few months.

Wes began the year as Health Secretary and one of the most famous faces of Starmer’s frontbench.

But he sensationally quit his job in May – accusing Sir Keir of losing the confidence of the public and party and calling for a leadership contest.

His bombshell resignation helped send the Starmer regime into a death spiral.

Wes had declared he would run for leader, but in the end backed the coronation of Mr Burnham as PM.



So does he still harbour leadership ambitions?

Laughing, he said: “That ship has sailed hasn’t it?”

“I know my party well enough that the person who went first and called for change would not be the person that Labour members would choose to be their leader”, Mr Streeting said.

“I did what I did and said what I said because I genuinely believed it was the right thing to do.

“My number one priority was making sure that the Labour Party was able to govern well and win the next general election, and I felt that needed a change in leadership.”



Mr Streeting has not spoken to Sir Keir since his resignation but says he “wishes him well”.

And he is now full of praise for his one-time rival Mr Burnham, who he says is “giving people some hope back”.

The polls suggest he is right – there is a “Burnham Bounce” for Labour.

Although this is small and pollsters predict Labour would lose their majority and be forced to govern via ‘rainbow coalition’ with the Lib Dems, Greens and others.

Despite this, Westminster is awash with rumours that Team Burnham could call an early election in order to seek a mandate for more radical change.



But Mr Streeting laughs off talk of an early election.

“Number 10 has been really clear that there isn’t going to be an early election, so everyone needs to chill out”, he says, “We’ve got a lot of work to do.”

For Mr Streeting, that work means making sure Britain is fighting fit and ready for war should the day come.

It is a heavy burden – and there are reminders of it all over the room we are in.



In one corner, a marble bust of Wellington stares down at us.

Perhaps Britain’s greatest military leader, Wellington defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo and brought an end to tyranny and war in Europe.

Next door has the actual desk where Neville Chamberlain sat with Adolf Hitler to negotiate the infamous 1938 Munich Agreement.

Chamberlain returned to Britain declaring to have secured “Peace in Our Time”.

The Nazis continued their march on Europe, World War Two broke out a year later, and Chamberlain went down in history as Britain’s most loathed PM.



They are two starkly contrasting reminders of the burden every Defence Secretary carries.

Will they help Britain stand up to tyrants? Or fail the test of history?

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Streeting says this Labour government will take the hard decisions needed to keep Britain safe.

Time will tell if that is true or not.

Chagos Deal off without Trump backing, Defence Ces says THE CHAGOS deal will not go ahead until Donald Trump approves it, Wes Streeting says. The Defence Secretary said the plan is not dead – and a deal is needed to protect the Diego Garcia military base. But he said there is no way the deal can go ahead without the US President’s approval and so the UK is going back to the drawing boards. He told The Sun on Sunday: “In order for the Chagos deal to get over the line, it needs the support of the President of the United States of America, and I think we ought to have been clearer about that sooner. “President Trump, I think, has been crystal clear, and therefore we have to rework the deal.” The UK’s original plan was to hand the islands over to Mauritius and lease the military base back at a cost o[f £100 million a year. But Mr Trump has branded the deal “terrible” and the Tories and Reform UK also oppose it. Mr Streeting insisted some kind of deal does still need to be done to protect the long term future of the Diego Garcia base – warning the legal risk is too big to ignore. He said: “Five prime ministers now – Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer, and Andy Burnham – five very different characters, very different politics-have all looked at the risk and judged that a diplomatic track is far better than taking that risk.”

News.title: MP pleads with Andy Burnham to axe ‘cruel’ tourist tax that will hit parents visiting sick children
News.content:
EMERGENCY PLEA MP pleads with Andy Burnham to axe ‘cruel’ tourist tax that will hit parents visiting sick children







Next

A SENIOR MP has pleaded with Andy Burnham to scrap his “cruel” tourist tax that will hammer parents visiting their sick children in hospital.

Alicia Kearns said Labour’s levy on hotels, B&Bs and holiday lets will impose “hardship” on families who need to stay close to loved ones undergoing treatment.



She spoke out for the first time about her daughter who underwent urgent neurosurgery at just four months old in 2021.

Her daughter has a rare condition called unicoronal craniosynostosis where the skull closes over too early leaving no room for her brain to grow.



Ms Kearns was allowed to stay overnight with her baby in Great Ormond Street Hospital after her three-hour surgery. Doctors removed parts of her skull and reshaped her face.



Alicia’s husband slept in a hotel nearby and they all stayed there a second night to be close to the hospital in case anything went wrong.

“I completely understand poor parents who spend months of their lives living outside GOSH, having to take Airbnbs or whatever they can,” the shadow national security minister said.

“I’m very lucky it was only two nights and I’m very lucky that we could afford that.”

Ms Kearns’ daughter had to wear a helmet for 18 months to force her skull and cheek bones to grow the correct way. It had to be refitted every two to four weeks.



The mother-of-three added: “If you are from Cornwall or Belfast travelling all the way to London every two to four weeks – it’s just not fair on families.

“There are so many unseen costs financially – let alone emotionally – that it is immoral to now impose a cost like this.

“It’s very cruel. It’s an additional hardship on those who are already suffering.

The Tory MP said her daughter, now five years old, is doing “amazingly” well.

But added: “Unless the Prime Minister changes course, he will be inflicting cruelty on people in some of their darkest moments and their scariest moments of their lives. Surely he can do better than this.”



Labour is handing powers to council leaders and mayors to impose unlimited taxes on tourists for overnight stays.

Trade body UKHospitality has warned it could add £100 to a family holiday.

Mayor of London Sadiq Khan said the levy in the capital will be capped at 5 per cent of the cost of accommodation.

Ms Kearns called for the whole tax to be scrapped: “You can’t tax yourself to prosperity or to economic growth. That’s something Labour just doesn’t fundamentally understand.”

And warned it will hammer the hospitality industry in her rural constituency of Rutland and Melton where people usually visit for just one or two nights.



“It will cause massive problems for areas like mine,” she added. “People will think ‘let’s just go for a day trip instead of staying overnight’.

Leading children’s charities also intervened in today’s Sun on Sunday, calling on the Government to make an exemption for those seeking medical treatment.

Louise Parkes, Chief Executive of GOSH Charity, says: “A hotel levy risks placing yet another financial burden on families already facing the unimaginable pressure of having a seriously ill child, this is deeply unfair.

“Families travelling from across the UK for potentially life-saving treatment for their child are not tourists, they must not face an additional tax simply to stay close to their child while they receive vital treatment.

“We are calling on the government to ensure families travelling for their child’s care are protected from any additional costs.”



Maya Parkin, Senior Public Affairs and Policy Officer at Bliss charity for babies born premature or sick, said parents can spend weeks or “even months” travelling to and from hospital or staying nearby so they can be partners in their baby’s care. “During this time, many families face significant additional costs, including accommodation, travel, food and lost income from time away from work. “Parents and carers staying close to a hospital because their premature or sick baby is receiving treatment are not tourists, and they should not be treated as such. “Any future legislation introducing an Overnight Visitor Levy must include a clear and explicit exemption for parents and carers staying in accommodation near a hospital where their baby is receiving care. “No family should face additional financial pressure simply because they need to be close to their baby during what is often one of the most stressful and traumatic periods of their lives.” Nathan Grant, Director of Operations at The Sick Children’s Trust charity, said most families have financial concerns before staying in their free Homes from Home for those with a seriously ill child in hospital. He added: “For those we cannot support in our ‘Homes from Home’, the prospect of an additional Overnight Visitor Levy on an already costly hotel room only serves to increase those pressures, both emotionally and financially. “Anything that can be done to make life a little easier for families facing what are often the most difficult moments of their lives would be welcomed by all of us here at The Sick Children’s Trust.” Sonia Malik, Associate Director of Policy at Young Lives vs Cancer, said a cancer diagnosis comes with a “significant” financial burden. She said: “We would welcome consideration from government and local leaders of steps to reduce the financial impact on young cancer patients and their families, including possible exemptions for those staying away from home for medical treatment, so they are not faced with further extra costs at an already difficult time.”

Jeremy Clarkson has also spoken out against the tax warning it will put “even more pressure” on the nation’s businesses.

Migrant hotels will be exempt because they are classed as “temporary accommodation”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Ministry for Local Government spokesperson said: “We’ve always said it will be for local leaders to decide whether to introduce the levy.

“It would apply to short-term, commercially let overnight accommodation and we expect local leaders to factor the needs of medical visitors into their decision-making process, as they decide whether a levy is right for their community and how it should be applied.”

News.title: Labour’s cruel tourist tax will hurt families with poorly children like mine
News.content:
Next

Nothing prepares you for being told your newborn baby needs neurosurgery.

My daughter was just four months old when surgeons at Great Ormond Street operated on her, and it was one of the scariest weeks of my life.

After the surgery she needed to wear a helmet for two years, with a refitting every month.



At the hospital and again at the clinic, I met mums and dads who had driven from Cornwall and flown from Belfast, over and over, because unsurprisingly there aren’t many clinics for children needing specialist helmets.



Most couldn’t get home the same day, so they slept in a hotel or B&B nearby, because getting your child the care they need, is our priority as parents.

Many were juggling other treatments too, so this was one journey among many.

By handing mayors the power to slap an uncapped “tourism tax” on every overnight stay, the Government has decided to tax those parents for that overnight bed.

Shamefully, Labour Ministers didn’t even pause to think about the people who never wanted to travel at all.

The dad sleeping in a hotel by the neonatal unit, the wife in an Airbnb while her husband recovers from a heart transplant, the son keeping vigil beside his mum in a coma, or the family making the same trip every few weeks for their child’s cancer treatment.

These aren’t holidays, they are the worst days of people’s lives. Many of these parents have already taken unpaid leave, cut their hours or given up work to be at their child’s side. And now this Government plans to hand them a bill for it.

I’ve been there twice. First my daughter’s neurosurgery, and then again last year, as a third-time mum needing a hotel stay during treatment for a pulmonary embolism, a blood clot on my lungs.



Weeks ago in Parliament I did what MPs should do – I spoke up for these families and asked ministers to promise that nobody staying away from home for medical treatment will pay this tax. I was promised an answer, and shamefully I’m still waiting.

Leaving it to each Mayor isn’t good enough, it’ll just create a postcode lottery for families at their lowest ebb.

Are Ministers so out of touch, and desperate to tax anything and everything they can, that they can’t just give this commitment not to make people’s lives even harder?

Of course it isn’t only sick families who’ll pay. Families already stretching to afford a week away will be squeezed again as their holiday becomes even more expensive.

In Rutland and Stamford, our hospitality industry relies on short stays, so it’s likely we would be hit with some of the 33,000 jobs losses UKHospitality warns a 5 per cent levy will cause.



It’s not surprising the Treasury admits it never even worked out the damage this tax would have on hospitality, between the economic impact and the emotional toll on families receiving medical treatment, clearly barely any thought went into it.

Ministers needs to scrap this tax, and if they won’t, then at the very least they can exempt medical stays.

Government is meant to lighten people’s load, not treat us as cash-cows to exploit for nights spent at our wits’ end.

News.title: Another woman found dead in South African city as 10 deaths in two months sparks fears of serial killer
News.content:
Next

ANOTHER woman has been found dead in South Africa fuelling fears that a serial killer is on the loose.

The victim is the tenth to be recovered near Johannesburg in just two months, terrifying residents in the country’s largest city.



Cops made the grim discovery in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, early on Saturday.

The semi-naked body was found close to a cemetery in the Tembisa township, police said.



The victim has not yet been identified, but police said she appeared to have been stoned to death.

“We can only confirm the discovery of the body”, the South African Police Service said in a statement.

The nine other victims have been aged between 20 and 38, according to cops.

Several were found naked or partially clothed and left in open areas near main roads.



Police said the first five bodies were discovered in or near the town of Kempton Park on the outskirts of Johannesburg.

The others were found in separate locations between 15 and 21 miles away.

Police say the killings may have taken place in different locations to where the bodies were found.

The first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.

Police have said the ninth killing may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter.



Two women, aged 31 and 38, were arrested in connection with that death and charged on September 21.

Provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Tommy Mthombeni said investigators could not rule out the possibility that some of the other cases were linked.

One of the other victims was identified as Elizabeth Tsontso Moselakgomo, 38, who vanished while out jogging.



She was reported missing after her eight-year-old daughter alerted family members that she had not returned from her daily afternoon jog.

Another body was found naked and in an advanced stage of decomposition, authorities said.

The youngest victim has been identified as a 20-year-old woman.

Cops have offered a 400,000 rand (£22,000) reward for information leading to the arrest of the killer or killers.

And the Democratic Alliance, South Africa’s second-largest political party, has put up a further US$31,000 (£29,000).



Fred Kekana, the Gauteng provincial commissioner, urged people to avoid jumping to premature conclusions.

He said: “Investigators are considering all possibilities, including the possibility of multiple suspects or separate perpetrators.

“Police are comparing the evidence, timelines, locations, victim profiles and circumstances of each case before reaching conclusions.”



The killings have highlighted the high rates of femicide and violent crime in South Africa and sparked a renewed outcry over the safety of women.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Between April and July this year, the country recorded 5,427 homicides, which is an average of about 45 per day, according to crime statistics.

Femicide rates in South Africa are among the highest in the world, according to the United Nations‘ agency for gender equality.

News.title: Inside warped trafficking ring where ‘pre-ordered’ babies are ‘reserved in womb’ & sold to unsuspecting couples
News.content:
Next

STILL kicking inside the womb, some of Asia’s most vulnerable babies are being lined up, presented in a catalogue and “pre-ordered” by strangers – before they have even taken their first breath.

Expectant mothers crippled by poverty or terrified by the stigma of an unwanted pregnancy are lured in by traffickers who offer to pay for hospital bills, arrange the birth and shoulder the costs they cannot afford.





Deals can begin months before delivery, with investigators uncovering cases in which unborn children are effectively “pre-ordered”.

Buyers are then waiting in the wings for the moment they enter the world, with Indonesia’s child trafficking commissioner Ai Maryati telling The Sun: “Babies who are still in the womb are being chosen for trafficking before they are born.”

Newborns are being swept from the delivery room into an elaborate trafficking machine where midwives, forged birth certificates, bogus foundations and social media accounts have all allegedly been used to transform babies into commodities.

And once the paperwork is rewritten, the traces of where a child really came from can begin to disappear with it.

The murky trade stretches far beyond Indonesia, with babies allegedly bought and sold through illegal adoption networks across the world – including cases involving British nationals.

A British national was arrested at one of Nepals’ International Airports in 2019, after allegedly obtaining a one-month-old baby through an illegal adoption deal.

The infant was allegedly handed over by Bal Krishna Dangol, the then-director of children’s organisation Bal Mandir, in exchange for Rs400,000 (£3,148.41.)

Nepalese authorities arrested Dangol and investigated the alleged illegal transfer as part of a wider probe into suspected child trafficking and unlawful overseas adoptions.





Smith and Dangol were charged with human trafficking after cops accused him of helping her obtain the newborn and fraudulent documents falsely naming her as the child’s mother.”

Andy Ardian, of child protection organisation ECPAT Indonesia, said traffickers deliberately exploit pregnancies in which women feel they have nowhere else to turn.

He told The Sun: “These cases happen when there is an unwanted pregnancy so mothers will ask for help, but these people end up exploiting their baby.

“They will help the mother give birth but then take the baby and sell it across the world.”

Arun Dohle, who has long been involved with child protection and adoption issues, said: “Often unmarried or poor mothers get targeted.

“I’ve seen a case where a poor mother was targeted and someone asked her ‘give us one of your children and we will fix your roof for free.’”

He said some parents deliberately sell their babies for cash knowing full well the way the trade operates.

In Depok, West Java, cops busted a ring trawling Facebook for parents prepared to sell their babies.



A mum who was identified by cops only as SU, 24, allegedly handed over her newborn for Rp10million (£440), while another parent, identified as DA, 27, allegedly struck the same deal.

The babies were then allegedly shuttled to Bali and flipped for up to Rp45million (£2,000) – more than four times the amount.

Perhaps the darkest allegation was that some of those children had been earmarked while their mothers were still pregnant.

I Made Aryadana, the leader of Bali Luih Children’s Foundation which ran the trafficking ring is now serving a six-year prison sentence.

The mothers flogging their babies were charged with human trafficking and child protection.

But some mothers are not always clued up.

One sprawling operation saw 19 people convicted over the trafficking of 34 babies through a network stretching from Indonesia to Singapore.

The racket, masterminded by 70-year-old Lie Siu Luan, preyed on vulnerable families across West Java between 2023 and 2025, dangling cash and the promise of a swift adoption in front of parents struggling to cope.

Newborns were hidden away in safe houses and cared for by hired nannies as the gang set about manufacturing them new identities, falsifying birth certificates and other official documents.

The deception even extended to recruiting bogus mums and dads to masquerade as the babies’ real parents, helping pave their passage out of Indonesia and into Singapore.



Investigators in the Indonesian and Singaporean case believe at least 12 of the trafficked babies have already been taken to Singapore.

Lie was handed the toughest punishment, jailed for seven years for orchestrating the operation, while the remaining 18 defendants – including recruiters, carers and document fixers – received sentences ranging from three to six years.

Andy said investigators had also struggled to trace alleged members of networks once the trail crossed Indonesia’s borders, saying of one Singapore connection: “We cannot find the offender in Singapore.”

The high commissioner of child trafficking has also confirmed to The Sun that they are still on the hunt for the Indonesian babies who were trafficked to Singapore.

Andy says traffickers can also exploit contacts inside hospitals, allegedly working with midwives who use offers of money to persuade vulnerable mothers to hand over their newborns.

He said: “Traffickers will kidnap the children – often through having ties with the midwives – and bring the children to the customer.”

In July, the Yogyakarta High Court sentenced midwife Jemitri Eka Lestari, 44, to seven years in prison, while fellow midwife Dunuk Mudjiasri, 77, received two years for supporting the operation.

Police said the pair were arrested in December following an investigation into the sale of at least 66 babies dating back to 2015.



Investigators said the women helped with deliveries before birth records were falsified so that adopters could appear on paper as the babies’ biological parents.

Andy said: “There’s no documents being signed in this process and the child’s identity is completely erased.

“They created lots of fake identities for the children.”

Sometimes, a woman will be so financially desperate, they ask the midwife themselves if they can take the baby away in return for a free delivery.

Maria Yohanista, who runs a pregnancy clinic with a friend in Indonesia, said she has encountered mothers so financially desperate that they have asked whether somebody else could take their child in return for covering the cost of giving birth.

She said: “Women who give birth will frequently tell the midwife they can’t afford the baby.

“They ask the midwife for a free delivery in return to keep the baby.”

A straightforward delivery in an Indonesian hospital can cost around Rp5million to Rp15million (£220 to £660).



The sums are particularly stark against Indonesia’s poverty line, which stood at just Rp669,235 (£30) per person per month in March 2026.

The average Indonesian employee earned around Rp3.39million (£150) a month in May, but women targeted by traffickers can be far more financially vulnerable, including those without secure salaried work.

Mimi Vu, a child trafficking activist told The Sun: “This is a trade and a business. The most targeted are young poor and less educated women who are single.”

Mimi said after the vulnerable mums realise they can’t afford to take their babies home, they are forced to leave the newborn with the nurse.

She added: “The doctors or nurses in the hospital are making a lot of money out of the business.

“Hospitals will often have a system set up where they operate with middlemen.”

She said: “[Agencies] will strike up a backroom deal with nurses, hospitals, and orphanages to facilitate procurement of the baby.”

One of Indonesia’s most extraordinary cases centred on a 32-year-old social media figure who cultivated an image as a guardian angel for women facing unwanted pregnancies.

Suhendra Abdul Halim became known as the “father of a million children”, winning praise online after presenting himself as a man devoted to helping vulnerable pregnant women and taking unwanted children into his care.

His apparent benevolence spread across social media, where his growing profile helped attract more women to him.



Andy, who worked on this case, said: “He was promoting his business pretending to help women pay for their birth on Instagram.

“Because he was viral, people on social media were complimenting his work in helping women.

“Lots of women began asking him if he could help them too.”

Even Indonesian celebrities reportedly promoted his account, apparently believing they were directing struggling mothers towards a charitable lifeline.

But police would later found the wholesome image concealed an illegal baby-selling operation.

Andy said: “He was using social media to recruit women.

“The man would then sell the babies for 15 million rupiah (£632.20)”

“So he would help the mother who is in difficulty but then sell the baby on Instagram.”



Adoption in Indonesia is meant to be free of charge. All orphanages should be registered and accredited with the Indonesian Ministry of Social Affairs.

Arun Dohle said: “The parents who adopt the babies know exactly what they are doing.

“Adoption should not have a price tag on it. They are buying these babies and therefore participating in trafficking.”

The baby trafficking social media guru had a rented house where pregnant women and newborn babies were being kept together.

Police found ten pregnant women living there when the property was uncovered, five of whom had already given birth.

According to Andy, babies were kept at the house while waiting to be taken away.

The scheme began to crack when a health worker noticed an anomaly hidden in the paperwork.

Women arriving to give birth came from outside the Bogor area, yet the same address kept appearing on their records.

More strangely still, so did the same supposed father, Suhendra.

The repetition aroused suspicion and eventually helped expose an operation police said was masquerading as charity.



Bogor Police Chief Iman Imanuddin said: “The culprit offered to help the pregnant women. After the children were born, [he would take them in but] they would eventually be given up for adoption. But the adoption process was illegal.”

Police said Suhendra had falsified documents connected to his Father of A Million Children Foundation and demanded IDR15million – roughly £700 – from people wanting to adopt a baby.

Imanuddin said: “If somebody wanted to adopt one of his children, they would have to pay IDR15 million (£630) to the culprit. The culprit used the Father of a Million Children Foundation as a front.”

He was eventually jailed for four years.

The Bogor case offered a disturbing glimpse into a trade that has surfaced repeatedly across the sprawling archipelago and other parts of the continent.

In July, The Sun exposed a human trafficking racket in India mistakenly contacted an anti-trafficking charity – asking if they wanted to buy a baby.

Using this as an opportunity to act as decoy customers, the organisation, Against Child Trafficking (ACT) started to answer messages posed as a desperate couple unable to bear children.

The child trafficking ring, having moved the conversation to another channel, sent over several pictures of naked newborns and asked the “couple” to choose from their catalogue.

Director of ACT, Arun Dohle, told The Sun: “One day a guy wrote on our own Facebook page and offered us a baby.

“We faked to be a couple who couldn’t have a baby. We pretended to be unsure to not give away our cover.



“It was a really simple process. Then they sent us tons of pictures of babies. It was a horror.

“They started to demand payment like a scammer and in the end we were not sure if they would provide the product.”

After the charity teamed up with cops and planned a sting operation, the gang was paid Rs 20,000 (£155) via UPI as token money and promised Rs 5.8 lakh (£4,500) at a location where they would make the exchange.

That’s when cops swooped in and arrested five men who had arrived for the deal.

The cases expose an underground trade capable of wrapping itself of charity, adoption and rescue while exploiting women at perhaps their most vulnerable.

And at the centre of it all is a baby who has no idea that, while still cocooned inside its mother’s womb, strangers may already be discussing its future.

A Meta spokesperson told The Sun: “The exploitation of children is a horrific crime and we work aggressively to fight it on and off our platforms.

“We respond to valid law enforcement requests, which aid in the arrest and prosecution of these criminals, and report accounts of suspected traffickers to NCMEC.

“Predators will always try to adapt to evade detection, which is why our expert teams are constantly tracking evolving trends and sharing signals of violating behavior across the industry.”

News.title: Paedo swimming instructor jailed after police found more than 120 indecent images on his phone
News.content:
Paedo swimming instructor jailed after police found more than 120 indecent images on his phone

Nathan Berry, 38, was found to have sexually abused two vulnerable children while working at the Penarth Leisure Centre, near Cardiff in south Wales following his arrest this year

View 2 Images Nathan Berry had more than 120 indecent images on his phone (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

A sick paedophile swimming teacher who preyed on vulnerable, non-verbal children has been jailed after he was convicted of sexual assault and possessing more than 120 indecent images.

‌



Nathan Berry "betrayed the trust" of children and their parents "in the most dreadful way", police said, while working at the Penarth Leisure Centre, near Cardiff in south Wales. The 38-year-old man was working at the leisure centre when he was arrested and his mobile phone seized in March this year.

‌



South Wales Police detectives investigating the teacher discovered more than 120 indecent images of children on his device, alongside evidence that he had sexually assaulted a child.

‌



Record number of internet perverts hoarding child abuse images dodge jail sentences READ MORE :

Man used AI to undress images of children and was bailed to flat near playground READ MORE :

View 2 Images Berry worked at Penarth Leisure Centre

Police said his victims were non-verbal children, whom the court heard Berry had targeted due to their vulnerabilities. Parents identified whether their children were victims from the photos on his device, police added. South Wales Police said: "Berry was arrested in March 2026, and his mobile phone was seized.

"Images of children were found on his phone, and he provided the children's names. Officers visited the children's parents who identified their children, who are non-verbal, from the photographs.

‌



"While Berry was on remand, his phone was further examined, and evidence was found relating to the offence of sexual touching." He admitted his wrongdoing and was jailed for more than five years. Berry pleaded guilty at court and was convicted of eight offences - four counts of taking indecent photographs, two counts of making indecent images, one count of possession of prohibited images, and one sexual assault of a child under 13.

He was jailed for five years and four months at Cardiff Crown Court and handed an extended licence period of eight years.

To further protect the victims and others, Berry is also subject of a Restraining Order and Sexual Harm Prevention Order (SHPO). As part of the SHPO he is banned from having any unsupervised contact or communication of any kind with any child under the age of 16.

‌



Officer in the case, DC Julie Lewis, from South Wales Police, said: "Nathan Berry betrayed the trust of these children and their parents in the most dreadful way.

"We hope the outcome at court goes some way in helping them to rebuild their ability to trust and feel safe again. This investigation demonstrates our commitment to safeguarding vulnerable people." Berry was sentenced on August 4.

But police said they delayed publicising the case so the victims' families "were given time to process the legal proceedings and everything that had taken place."

Article continues below

The force added: "We never underestimate how difficult it is for survivors of sexual abuse to speak out and report. But we hope cases like this one provide reassurance that victims will be listened to, treated with dignity and respect, and will be supported throughout the judicial process."

News.title: Newly-wed mum stranded in Portuguese hospital after having stroke during her sleep
News.content:
Newly-wed mum stranded in Portuguese hospital after having stroke during her sleep

Shereen Lafferty, 37, woke up during her holiday in Faro unable to speak and with her right side "paralysed," her devastated family have said

View 2 Images Shereen, 37, is in a hospital in Faro after having a stroke (Image: Supplied/Daily Record)

A newly-wed 37-year-old British woman has been left stranded in a Portuguese hospital after she had a stroke in her sleep while on a weekend break with her husband.

‌



Shereen Lafferty, 37, woke up during her holiday in Faro on Sunday September 20 unable to speak and with her right side "paralysed", her devastated sister-in-law has said.

‌



The Glasgow mum-of-one, who married husband Robert in March, spent around five days in intensive care in the Faro hospital this week, and her condition has thankfully since improved.

‌



Sister-in-law Apryll, 32, says Shereen has taken a few steps but is still unable to talk - and she can't receive speech therapy in English while she remains in Portugal, Glasgow Live reports.

She said: “It was a complete shock. I was devastated to be honest. Shereen is such a nice person. She's the type of person that helps everybody and goes above and beyond."

View 2 Images Shereen and Robert married in March (Image: Supplied/Daily Record)

‌



"She's only 37 - you don't expect things like this to happen at that age. Obviously it can happen to anybody at any age, however you just don't expect it to happen to an otherwise healthy person."

Doctors have advised Shereen, from Provan Hall in the east end of Glasgow, will remain in the hospital for at least two more weeks before she can be transferred on a medically assisted flight home. It will cost the family as much as £25,000.

Apryll has launched a GoFundMe to help raise the money needed to get Shereen home safe. Apryll added her brother Robert, 36, has been "trying to stay positive" and has been issuing regular updates to the family on his new wife's condition.

‌



She added: "He's saying that she will be fine as long as she can keep making progress, and that things are going in a positive direction for her. The doctors confirmed that it had been a stroke through the night, estimating it had happened between midnight and 7am.

"She had been in intensive care since Sunday morning, however she's made some good progress this week. She has been moved today [Friday, September 25] to a normal ward, which is a massive step.

"She has taken a few steps and is actively trying to speak, but being in Portugal and speaking Portuguese, they can't offer any speech therapy for her, which is one of the biggest reasons to try and get her home."

‌



The family have decided to shelter nine-year-old daughter Aria, who is currently staying at Shereen's mum's, from the full details of why her parents haven't returned home from their holiday. Apryll added: "She's obviously quite upset at her mum being away.

"She's used to having her mum all the time, so she'll be devastated about the fact that she's not with her right now. But she's with her gran, who she's really close to, so she's okay and being well looked after."

The concerned family member added the most important thing at the moment is to get Shereen home to her family. She said: "It's hard being so far from home without everyone being able to help out and share the load of visits and the emotional stress..

Article continues below

"I'm just hoping that we can keep going in [a positive] direction and that we can get her home as soon as possible." You can donate to Apryll's GoFundMe to help get Shereen home here.

News.title: Met Office weather maps turn blue as Brits brace for 830-mile downpours on Sunday
News.content:
Met Office weather maps turn blue as Brits brace for 830-mile downpours on Sunday

The latest maps from the UK's Met Office have delivered a bleak picture for the country this weekend, with a huge system of low pressure set to make landfall on Sunday

View 5 Images The Met Office has predicted massive rainfall will hit the coast this weekend (Image: Met Office)

A Sunday washout is on the cards for thousands of Brits this weekend as downpours cascade across the country, new weather maps show.

‌



The latest charts from the Met Office, the UK's national weather forecaster, have captured a mass of rain making its way across all four home nations. The showers, the maps show, will take shape overnight before making landfall in southwest England and Wales, where output will be a gentle 5mm per hour.

‌



They will gather steam throughout the day and eventually unleash between 16mm and 32mm (0.6 and 1.25 inches) per hour, for up to six hours in the worst affected areas. Typically, the affected cities and towns, such as Belfast and Liverpool, see around 75mm of rainfall in a standard September — so Sunday's downpours will be significant.

‌



UK weather maps show temperatures plunging to 3C with 60 counties below 10C READ MORE :

Met Office maps show heavy downpours for 35 areas on Sunday- full list READ MORE :

View 5 Images Rainfall will deliver a Sunday washout for thousands of people (Image: Getty Images)

The Met Office charts show the first signs of rain spattering over parts of South Wales and Cornwall from around 3am on Sunday, with showers moving up over Wales in the following few hours to 7.15am. They will remain calm on the Welsh coast as a much heavier band of rain moves up through St George's Channel and into the Irish Sea.

As the rain moves north, it will come to completely engulf Northern Ireland, leaving no county untouched as it pelts the home nation with between 0.5mm and 30mm from 7am to 2.15pm on Sunday.

‌



The maps show the same system landing in Scotland at around 10am, with the full force of up to 16mm of rain per hour settling down on the southwest coast around Drummore and its surrounds. At this point, the rainy mass will have grown to cover nearly the entire length of the UK, a whole 830 miles lashing the country from Land's End in Cornwall to Stornoway in Scotland.

View 5 Images The maps show the rain settling primarily over Scotland and northern England (Image: Met Office)

The vast bulk of the system will take root in Scotland, with every one of the home nation's major cities at risk of heavy downpours.

‌



According to the charts, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Dumfries, Fort William, Aberdeen, Jedburgh and Dundee could all see rainfall totals of up to 32mm per hour at points throughout Sunday. The rain looks set to remain anchored to the region until 8pm on Sunday.

That doesn't, however, mean that the rest of the country is untouched by the inclement weather, with England and Wales seeing their fair share as well.

View 5 Images Soaking conditions will hit most of the country, but some areas harder than others (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Cardiff, Swansea, Caernarfon, Pembroke and Newtown in Wales will all see rainy showers on Sunday, as will Plymouth, Exeter, Bristol, Swindon, and elsewhere in Southwest England. London, Reading and other communities in the Southeast look likely to see some rain, but in more gentle, periodic showers.

The vast majority of England's rain will likely fall over northern England, according to the Met Office maps, with the heavy shower misery hitting Preston, Kendal, Darlington, Newcastle and other areas around the same time as Scotland.

However, the Environment Agency has issued an amber flood alert for the Essex coast from Clacton to St Peters Flat and the Colne and Blackwater estuaries. The alert states that flooding is possible before the rainy system arrives, between 11.45pm today and 1.45am on Sunday due to "overtopping and spray" on the coast.

‌



View 5 Images The Met Office long-range forecast shows the drought-causing conditions of this summer may well linger into autumn (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

According to the forecaster's long-range forecast, the picture for much of England will be changeable over the next few days, with a mix of high pressure and "settled conditions" meaning rain is less likely as the period continues the pattern established over summer to remain both drier and warmer than usual.

The forecast for October 1 to 10 states: "Higher pressure and more settled conditions look likely to build across across the UK, however it remains finely balanced whether this will become focused across the north or south.

Article continues below

"Lower pressure and interludes of more changeable weather are likely at times, but again, there are mixed signals regarding where this is more likely. However, an overall drier period than average is expected, with shorter periods of rain or showers.

"Winds are also likely to be lighter than average overall, but shorter periods of strong winds remain likely at this time of year, particularly across the northwest. Temperatures are likely to remain warmer than average."

News.title: Andy Burnham says he is more determined to fix social care after death of his father
News.content:
Andy Burnham says he is more determined to fix social care after death of his father

EXCLUSIVE: The Prime Minister said it was painful to see the same failures that impacted his grandmother 25 years ago when his beloved dad Roy needed care as he battled Alzheimer’s

Andy Burnham blames political ‘cowardice’ for social care crisis

Andy Burnham has said he is more determined than ever to fix the broken social care system after the death of his beloved father.

‌



The Prime Minister said it was painful to see the same failures that impacted his grandmother 25 years ago when his dad Roy needed care as he battled Alzheimer’s disease. Mr Burnham’s dad, who had been living in a care home, died earlier this month aged 86.

‌



His father's illness meant he did not know that his son was becoming Prime Minister. However Mr Burnham later said the staff in his care home thought he had shown a flicker of recognition when they showed him the moment the PM entered No10 on TV.

‌



Speaking to the Sunday Mirror from his No10 North office in Manchester, the PM said the experience had fuelled him further. He said: “In a word, yes. I won't leave office without having grasped this nettle.

“I saw what happened to my grandmother. You're going back 25 years ago now. She died in 2002, and she went through the care system, and it wasn't good enough at all. And that really focused me on the issue."

Andy Burnham's father dies less than two months after son becomes Prime Minister READ MORE :

View 3 Images Andy Burnham with his mother Eileen and his father Roy in 2015

‌



Mr Burnham's gran Catherine Murray was forced to sell her home to pay for her care. He previously revealed how her wedding ring was stolen from her hand as she lay in a nursing home.

He told us that the experience had left a lasting mark, and he had tried to bring forward reforms when he was Health Secretary "so that my parents' generation didn't have the same experience as my grandparents' generation had".

The PM said: “But here I am today, having now directly, painfully, personally experienced the fact that that has happened to my parents' generation, and not just [my parents], I'm talking about thousands and thousands of people across the country.

‌



“That is a shameful dereliction of duty by a generation of Westminster politicians who have just shown total cowardice in relation to this issue.

“The idea that it's too difficult. How can the care that we give from one person to another be too difficult for politics? How? I mean, that is terrible, that politics has got itself to a position where it's so superficial and so focus group driven that it won't take on a difficult argument and say, no we have to fix this.”

The PM said failure to fix social care will “break the NHS”, and said stretched care staff are being told to ring 999 to if there is a problem with a patient.

‌



“You cannot fix 21st Century care needs on that basis where there's no prevention and we're just sending everything to hospital” he said.

“In the end, it will sink the NHS if we carry on in this way. So I'm not going to leave office having done what everyone else in my position has done, and pretty much say, 'well, I'm not going to deal with this. It's too difficult. It's not a priority.'

"It is a priority for me, and I will face it. And it may make me unpopular, but I'm going to do it.”

‌



View 3 Images The PM spoke to the Mirror about his plans from his office in No10 North (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Social care will feature in Mr Burnham’s conference speech on Tuesday, where he will address party faithful as Labour leader for the first time.

“It's not the case that there's a complete detailed plan yet,” he said. “I will just go out and make the argument in a front foot way, talking about the experience that I've been through, that we've been through.

‌



“The thing I would say is, my dad could not have been cared for better by the people in the care home where he was, or you know when he was at home, amazing people and some of them from all parts of the world.

“The fact that they do it in a broken system on poverty pay just makes them all the more remarkable that they do that for other people's parents day in, day out.

“When you when you're living it and when you're looking at it through the eyes of your own parent, you look at what they do in a different way because you really observe it.

‌



“It's so moving when you see how they do what they do, and it makes me angry about modern politics actually, that they are invisible to most politicians what they do in their jobs every day, and it just cannot be possibly justified in any way, shape, or form.”

Under the slogan “Hope Again”, the PM will seek to fire up Labour troops at a moment when the party's electoral fortunes appear to be on the up.

He said: “We are going to set out what we believe is a path for the country to feel more hopeful, have a sense of belief and direction.

‌



“It can't be done overnight. But it is about being honest about where we haven't gone right in the right direction in the past, and then saying clearly to people, these are the things we will do to put Britain on the right path, to let the country believe again, let people have hope again.”

But Mr Burnham faces mounting challenges to deliver on his plans to ease the cost of living, as the economic picture darkens ahead of a high-stakes Budget next month.

The PM wouldn’t be drawn on his plans to balance the books but insisted Labour’s manifesto commitments on tax still stand, which rule out hikes to VAT, income tax and national insurance for working people.

‌



And he signalled there would be more help to come on the cost of living.

He said: “Of course it's a hard outlook right now. But I will be pointing very much to the fact that VAT is coming off Mirror Readers electricity bills next week. Now that isn't the be-all and end-all, honestly. Don't get me wrong, but it helps.

“I'll be pointing to the fact that there'll be a cap on bus fares across England for the whole of 2027, two pound cap. That helps, you know. So the thing is, hope comes from doing the small things as well as the big things.”

‌



He said he wanted to do all he can to give breathing space to business too, saying: “I realise it's a hard climate for people out there. But I think all of that can bring a sense of hope. We're not promising people the earth, but you're showing there are things that can still be done, and actually beyond those first steps, there's a direction for the country that will take us to a better place in the long term.”

But Mr Burnham and Chancellor John Healey face a string of unenviable choices to balance the books - tax rises, public spending or more borrowing.

View 3 Images Andy Burnham speaks to the Mirror's Political Editor Lizzy Buchan ahead of Labour Party conference (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



Asked if there could be a return to austerity, he said: “We're obviously trying our best to make sure that we don't go back to those days in the 2010s. The damage that was done in that period actually I think has sometimes been underestimated.

“The hollowing out of council budgets, I think, damaged growth at a local level. So alongside breathing space, we want this to be a growth promoting Budget.”

Mr Burnham will sketch out more of his vision on how to hand people more control over their lives - and the state more control of vital services.

‌



“The country took some wrong turns in the 1980s. Things were broken up and sold off: homes, energy, water, transport, care,” he said.

“Why is Britain not in the place that it should be? How do we give people more control over their lives, the country more control over the basics? That's the theme that I'll be developing in Liverpool.”

Another difficult issue on his desk is the small boat crisis, and the rise of toxic far-right protests on the south coast.

‌



The PM said: “The best thing we can do is to get the overall numbers down, and they are down. Those who want to build public unrest will focus on one issue or one day.

“But the crucial thing is to look at the big picture, and the big picture shows that boat crossings are down by around 50% between where they are now and where they were in the early 2020s.

“So massive progress has been made. I'm not saying it's good enough. I'm not complacent about it.”

Article continues below

He said the gangs were being forced to change their models as the Government cracks down, but said the Home Office would be relentless in adapting.

He added: “I think it's really important that we don't allow those who want a narrative, they will leap on one incident or one day or whatever to suit their political purposes. What we need to do is to point to the broad picture, which is one of progress - not enough, but progress.”

Mr Burnham rubbished speculation in Westminster that he was planning to call an early general election. “There will be no early election, so people may as well forget about that,” he said. “We're focusing on the here and the now.”

News.title: First-time buyers without 'bank of Mum and Dad' to get leg up in major new scheme
News.content:
First-time buyers without 'bank of Mum and Dad' to get leg up in major new scheme

EXCLUSIVE: Andy Burnham will announce plans to help people to buy their first home with a deposit of just 2.5% in his keynote speech to Labour Party conference

PM reveals new plans to help first-time buyers

First-time buyers without access to the “bank of Mum and Dad” will get help to get on the housing ladder in a Help to Buy-style scheme.

‌



Andy Burnham will announce plans to help people to buy their first home with a deposit of just 2.5% in his big speech to Labour Party conference next week. The “Your First Home” scheme is designed to help young people who would struggle to afford a deposit to get on the housing ladder.

‌



The Prime Minister told the Sunday Mirror: “We are coming back at this whole question of helping first-time buyers onto the housing ladder, particularly those who can't call on the famous bank of mum and dad. So we're looking at what was the Help to Buy scheme, which obviously had an impact, but was it as focused as it should have been?

‌



Andy Burnham rules out snap election as Labour surge in polls READ MORE :

View Image Andy Burnham said he wanted to help young people without the 'bank of mum and dad' to get on the housing ladder (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

“We coming back with a proposal that we think will really help those young people who might struggle otherwise or not be able to get on the housing ladder otherwise. Of course, the housing world is really desperate for a scheme of this type to stimulate building. So I'm pretty proud of the scheme that we've brought forward."

He went on: “You know, we are going to build a new generation of council housing, and we're taking big steps there. But also at the same time, it's about people owning their own home, and I absolutely recognize that ambition as well.

‌



“So we're proud of the scheme that we're putting forward. It's quite a significant intervention in the market, and I think it will particularly help some of those young people in their 20s.

"Perhaps a couple who are just starting out, maybe they've got two student loans going on. I absolutely think we've got an obligation to help them a bit more, particularly when they don't have a network of family who can help them with the deposit.”

Developers would pay a fee to allow first time buyers to purchase new build homes helped by a 20% government backed equity loan, with an initial interest-free period to ensure housing costs are affordable.

‌



There will be a cap on household income and the size of the deposit to target the scheme at less well off buyers. Registration for the scheme will open at the end of the year.

It comes after a Government audit found that George Osborne’s Help to Buy scheme in 2013 delivered value for money, rebutting criticism that it pushed up house prices and cost too much.

Osborne's scheme allowed buyers to purchase a new-build home worth up to £600,000 with a 5% deposit, backed by a government loan of up to 20% (or up to 40% in London).

‌



The report, commissioned under Keir Starmer's government, found more than 387,000 people bought their own home through the scheme, more than 328,000 of whom were first-time buyers. It reportedly delivered £25bn in social value to the UK in its final year.

However officials believe it was not properly targeted and asked too little from developers. The full details of the scheme, which will be funded by reprioritising cash from existing budgets, is expected to be set out in next month’s Budget.

Separately, councils will be given strengthened powers to seize empty and derelict homes to meet untapped housing need.

‌



The Government will overhaul Tory changes to Empty Dwelling Management Orders (EDMOs) which allow councils to take over the management of long-term empty homes and bring them back into occupation for an initial period of 12 months, rising to 8 years.

No applications have been made since 2021.

Under new plans, which will be tabled in Parliament within weeks, the amount of time a property must sit empty will be reduced from two years to six months. Red tape will be ripped up to make it easier for local authorities to get the go ahead.

Article continues below

Some 303,185 dwellings in England were classed as “long-term” empty (more than six months) in 2025, according to official figures.

Meanwhile, the number of homeless children in England living in temporary accommodation has hit 177,530, because of long-term shortages in housing supply.

News.title: Labour MPs and dads to protest over 'not good enough' two-week paternity leave
News.content:
Labour MPs and dads to protest over 'not good enough' two-week paternity leave

EXCLUSIVE: The event on the first day of Labour conference has been organised by The Dad Shift in locations across the country - protesting against paternity leave that they claim is the least generous in Europe

View 2 Images Labour MPs are expected to protest on Sunday (Image: Getty Images/Blend Images)

Labour MPs are expected to join dads with their babies today (SUN) calling for better paternity leave.

‌



The event on the first day of Labour conference has been organised by The Dad Shift in locations across the country - protesting against paternity leave that they claim is the least generous in Europe.

‌



As part of the protest, dads and their babies in dozens of towns and cities across Britain will stage the world's first mass "change in" this afternoon, wearing nappies that spell out what their parents think of UK paternity leave in brown ink: "two weeks is sh*t".

‌



Some dads get just two weeks off when their baby is born - paid at less than half the minimum wage. The UK’s paternity leave is also worse than many far poorer countries. Kenya guarantees new fathers two weeks on full pay, as do Colombia and Paraguay.

The campaign stunt comes as the Government's review of parental leave enters its final stages, and at Andy Burnham's first conference as Prime Minister, with campaigners revealing almost half of Labour MPs are now on record calling for change.

New analysis published on the same day shows a huge paternity leave class gap, with nine in ten statutory paternity pay claims in the past decade going to the top half of earners.

‌



Major change to rights for new dads and bereaved parents to be set out today READ MORE :

Paternity leave changes are coming from April 6 - what you need to know READ MORE :

View 2 Images The campaign stunt comes as the Government's review of parental leave enters its final stages, and as Andy Burnham enters his first conference as Prime Minister (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Just one in 10 went to the bottom half, while maternity pay reaches three times (31%) as many lower earners.

The Dad Shift are now warning better-off dads get their pay and duration entitlements topped up by employers, so they can take leave, but dads on lower incomes cannot survive a fortnight on £194, so go back to work while their partners are still recovering, sometimes still in hospital.

‌



Amanda Martin, Labour MP for Portsmouth North and Co-Chair of the Labour Men & Boys group, said: "I don’t blame parents for calling a spade a spade. Our paternity leave system sets up working class blokes to fail at fatherhood by forcing them straight back out the door the minute a baby arrives and it’s not good enough.”

Jon Pearce, Labour MP for High Peak, and one of the authors of a letter of 104 MPs to Andy Burnham, asking for action on paternity leave, said: "I know all too well that feeling as a dad that you’re failing at work and you’re failing at home because the systems just aren’t set up to help you to succeed.

“We need to do better to give working dads every chance to face up to the massive responsibility of fatherhood, to bond with their babies, and support their partners as they recover.”

‌



Also participating in the event are media personalities Anna Whitehouse, aka the Mother Pukka, relationship expert Alex Trippier, and Movember ambassadors Jim Chapman, Gordon Smart and Jason Fo.

The campaign was also backed by Tesco. Emma Taylor, Chief People Officer, said: "The arrival of a new child is a life-changing moment, and time away from work in those first few weeks allows parents to support one another, spend valuable time together as a family and build important bonds with their baby.

"Supporting colleagues through major life moments is fundamental to how you create a great place to work and, at Tesco, we offer six weeks of fully paid paternity leave and see first-hand the difference additional time at home during those formative early weeks makes for colleagues and their families.

Article continues below

"We believe family-friendly policies are not just good for colleagues and their families, they're good for business too, and we'd encourage more employers to explore what further support they can offer."

Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden said: The first few weeks of being a parent can be both some of the most rewarding and challenging. We are determined to make sure dads and partners can be there to provide support as much as possible, especially in those crucial first few weeks and months when mums are often recovering from childbirth.

“That’s why we’ve already changed the law to give 32,000 more partners access to paternity leave, and are carrying out a full review of parental pay and leave to ensure we reflect the realities of modern work and childcare so that parents can spend as much time doing what matters most – caring for their baby.”

News.title: Noel Gallagher begs Premier League bosses not to punish Manchester City fans despite 'breaking financial rules'
News.content:
Noel Gallagher begs Premier League bosses not to punish Manchester City fans despite 'breaking financial rules'

Noel Gallagher, who will tour with Oasis again next year, has responded to the bombshell development Manchester City have been found guilty on 114 of the 115 charges

View 4 Images Noel Gallagher reacts during a Premier League match involving Manchester City (Image: Getty Images)

Noel Gallagher has begged Premier League bosses not to punish fans of his beloved Manchester City for more than 100 alleged breaches of financial rules.

‌



The Oasis star was shocked by reports the football giants have been found guilty of 114 alleged offences and could now face a massive fine, point deductions, stripped trophies, or even enforced relegation. Noel, 59, said: "Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it's nothing to do with the supporters or the players. Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw. They won it on the pitch.

‌



"Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that's nothing to do with the fans. We were there, we know what we saw. Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt."

‌



Man City star's dad left Oasis legend Noel Gallagher with two black eyes after headbutt READ MORE :

Stripping Man City of Premier League titles 'unlikely' as new charges punishment theory given READ MORE :

View 4 Images City won seven Premier League titles when the alleged breaches took place (Image: Getty Images)

Noel, who is pals with the club's former boss Pep Guardiola, added: "I'm sad for the fans and the players and a little surprised because all along the club reassured us and vehemently denied all the charges. It was a shock to hear we were guilty on all but one of them."

Man City, owned by mega-rich Emirati royal Sheikh Mansour, are expected to appeal the verdicts, which were first reported on Friday after a three and a half year probe by an independent Premier League commission. At least four clubs, including Arsenal, Man United, Liverpool and Tottenham, have already reportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation for loss of earnings under Section W of Premier League rules. Other clubs are also tonight understood to be taking legal advice about the possibility of legal action.

‌



Christian Purslow, who has previously held top executive roles at Liverpool, Chelsea and Aston Villa, today warned the verdicts could kick-off a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game". Mr Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss.

"Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3million. Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated.
