Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp forced into immediate Florian Wirtz U-turn after Germany injury blow

New Germany boss Jurgen Klopp had named two squads for the four matches in this international window, but injuries have forced the former Liverpool manager's hand

View 2 Images Florian Wirtz has joined up with Germany earlier than expected (Image: Joe Prior/Visionhaus via Getty Images)

Jurgen Klopp has been required to call up Florian Wirtz earlier than expected after a double injury blow for Germany.

‌



Klopp is taking charge of his first camp as national team manager, after being named as Julian Nagelsmann’s successor. And he joins at a unique time for international managers, with countries facing four games in an extended window of matches.

‌



The former Liverpool boss took the novel approach of naming two different squads, with the first featuring against Netherlands and Greece. Wirtz was selected in the second group to face Serbia and then the return match in Greece.

‌



However, after Jamal Musiala and Kai Havertz picked up injury issues in the draw with Netherlands, Klopp has been forced to react.

Wirtz along with Frankfurt striker Jonathan Burkardt have now joined the squad and will be available for the next three matches, starting with Greece on Sunday night.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

The Liverpool star will be desperate to impress Klopp after an indifferent start to the new season under Andoni Iraola. In 6 appearances, Wirtz has just one assist - although Iraola insists his performances have been better than those numbers.

Iraola said: "He is a good player out of possession who helps us in our press. But he runs the same as the 10 of Arsenal, the 10 of (Manchester) City, the 10 of Fulham and more or less his stats are very similar to the number 10s other teams have.

‌



"But that is why you cannot just play because of the numbers. Whether a striker scores a lot of goals or he doesn’t score a lot of goals, you have to look at the performances. Does he help us to play well? Yes.

View 2 Images Jurgen Klopp is back in management with the German national team (Image: Getty Images)

"Well, someone will score the goals and someone will give the assists. It is not that because you had the last touch, you played better than the other person.”

‌



Klopp was at pains to confirm that Wirtz - and the others included in the second squad - was not in a de-facto ‘b team’ and that his approach was done in order to meet as many players as possible.

"I want to get to know as many players as possible," Klopp explained. "There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience."

Klopp was forced to settle for a point in his first game in charge of Germany, with Cody Gakpo getting one over his old club boss with a 92nd minute equaliser for the Netherlands.

Sports.title: What did Pocognoli change in first Scotland game in charge?
Sports.content:
A draw might not be the most inspiring result for a new era, but there were still plenty of positives for Sebastien Pocognoli to take from his first game in charge of Scotland.

On the surface, 0-0 against Slovenia doesn't exactly scream entertaining. On another day though, Scotland could've either won by four or lost by a couple; such was the nature of the contest.

In the first half they looked vulnerable, but the second completely dominant. So, what exactly did Pocognoli do to change things up for the better, and what does he still need to keep his eye on?

Image: Sebastien Pocognoli singing the Scottish national anthem

High press creates chances, but leaves Scots exposed

Despite his record of qualifying for more major tournaments than any other manager, the one criticism Steve Clarke repeatedly received during his tenure was that Scotland sat too deep.

Pre-match, Pocognoli made a point of emphasising that his ideology was the opposite. "I try to be a little bit higher up the pitch," he said.

"On the ball we need to have patterns, which is the most difficult part. But off the ball, we need to be solid. That doesn't mean dropping off though; we need to be higher."

What that created at the start was far more exposure to Angus Gunn's goal. In the first 30 minutes, Slovenia had a goal ruled out and missed numerous other chances. All it would take was one ball over the top of the Scotland backline, and they were in.

Image: Andraz Sporar had the ball in the net for Slovenia before it was ruled out for offside

Andy Robertson and Stephen Welsh were caught out several times in particular and it was the hosts' poor finishing that kept them from going ahead in that period.

However, when Scotland did finally get to grips with the game, the benefits of the high press came to the fore. It created a glorious chance which Oli McBurnie squandered and helped keep a chaotic tempo which suited Pocognoli's men and kept Slovenia very much on the edge.

It needs some fine-tuning, but with the likes of John McGinn and Scott McTominay when he returns, there's enough energy and quality to make the most of this change in approach.

A different-looking 3-5-2

Pocognoli's formation was similar to what we have seen from Scotland previously. A 3-5-2. However, it was not a defensive set-up.

Aaron Hickey and Andy Robertson had far more license to get forward and the former picked up some lovely areas when entering narrower positions. The wing-backs' main priority was to attack, something that was rarely the case under Clarke. This was further emphasised when Ben Gannon-Doak came on to replace Hickey in the latter stages in search of a breakthrough.

The right and left-sided centre-backs were also a bit more adventurous. On a couple of occasions, Jack Hendry was allowed to roam almost as far up as the Slovenia penalty area to add more numbers.

Image: Scotland defenders Jack Hendry and Scott McKenna

It was also intriguing to see Stephen Welsh operate on the left of the back three. With the left-footed Scott McKenna central, it would've seemed to have made more sense to swap the two around. However, Welsh's passing was key in trying to split Slovenia open. That was most apparent when he managed to slide in substitute Kieron Bowie, who was thwarted by Jan Oblak.

There was a lot more emphasis on Billy Gilmour to pull the strings in midfield and use his technical ability to open up Slovenia after Scotland won back possession in more dangerous areas. And when the game was stretched, John McGinn was the driving force to get the midfield up the pitch.

New chances for a new attack

The front two both had reasons to prove themselves. In Robbie Ure you had a debutant looking to make his mark and in McBurnie you had a man looking for redemption after five years out of the reckoning.

Image: Oli McBurnie made his first Scotland appearance since 2021

Neither scored, but both could've. Ure hit the post, while McBurnie made a mess of a glorious one-on-one and saw a thumping header kept out at point-blank range by Jan Oblak.

The way Scotland pressed, you could see someone like a Lyndon Dykes, who wasn't in the squad, having a positive impact. But Pocognoli is ushering in a new era with new players. And his front two certainly posed questions and had a couple of moments of nice interplay.

McBurnie especially is a good option for the midfielders to play and run off. In one moment where Scotland won the ball back high up the pitch, the Hull City man became a wall for Gilmour, creating a good opening. That is where he shone and could continue to be a nuisance in Pocognoli's search for high-pressing breakthroughs.

Image: Billy Gimour was denied by a good save from Jan Oblak

What the players made of Pocognoli's changes

Scotland striker Oli McBurnie speaking with BBC Sport:

"It took us a little bit of getting used to in the first half, the new formation. I thought once we did, we looked really good. We created enough chances to kill the game. We are really disappointed we didn't get the three points.

"I was asked to play a different position and I quite enjoyed it. I like the manager's ideas; we've had some good chats about it already. It suited me in there, but I won't be able to sleep tonight with those chances. It's a tough one but I'd rather be getting into those positions than not getting the chances.

"We had them pinned for a lot of the game. We put them under waves of pressure. The only thing missing was a goal or two."

Scotland striker Stephen Welsh speaking with BBC Sport:

"We struggled to get into the game in the first half. Obviously it's a new style, some fresh faces and a new way of playing. In the second half, we completely dominated the game. At this level, you need to take your chances. But it's something we can improve on. Definitely positives to come from the game.

"The manager told us at half-time to be a bit sharper on the counter-press. We changed shape at half-time to get more control in the midfield and I thought it worked really well for us.

"I've played on the left-hand side for the last couple of years now. I'm very comfortable doing that. As long as you're in the starting XI, that's the important thing."

Sports.title: Harrison's late try wins thriller for Red Roses over New Zealand
Sports.content:
England 26-19 New Zealand: Zoe Harrison converted try in added time wins thriller and sees Red Roses return to winning way

England's players mob Zoe Harrison after her try in added time sealed a 26-19 win over New Zealand

Zoe Harrison's converted try in added time saw England's Red Roses return to winning ways in thrilling fashion over New Zealand.

Fly-half Harrison intercepted a pass inside the New Zealand 22 as the Black Ferns tried to counter her missed penalty attempt before adding the conversion to seal an epic 26-19 victory.

A crowd of nearly 60,000 at Allianz Stadium were treated to an absolute thriller between the world's top two sides, where the lead changed hands three times before the Red Roses crossed for a fourth decisive try.

England had trailed 12-7 at half-time after New Zealand responded to Claudia Moloney-MacDonald's try with scores from Amy Du Plessis and Ayesha Leti-I'iga.

But in the second half, England regained the lead when Ellie Kildunne burst clear and then Jess Breach stretched their lead to 19-12 as they took advantage of a yellow card for Black Ferns prop Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu for a high tackle on Marlie Packer.

New Zealand weren't done though and levelled the scores at 19-19 when Mererangi Paul crossed with 10 minutes to play.

England looked to have missed their chance for victory when Harrison's penalty dropped short of the posts, but her timely interception was the final act and ensured England bounced back to winning ways and extended their unbeaten run to 41 matches following last week's thrilling 26-26 draw vs Canada.

England's Claudia Moloney-MacDonald scored their first try of the game

September sunshine serves up epic tussle

The Red Roses came into this fixture at Twickenham having seen their 39-game winning run halted by World Cup runners-up Canada at Sandy Park seven days earlier.

New Zealand, the last side to beat England back in the 2022 World Cup final, were in fine form having won all seven of their Test matches this year so far.

It was the visitors who started with greater intent and gave England, who for the first time were benefitting from the tutelage of iconic defence coach Shaun Edwards, plenty to think about.

Winger Leti-I'iga looked to have given them the lead in the opening 10 minutes only for her try to be ruled out for a double-movement on review.

England did finally find their groove when Moloney-MacDonald crossed for the opening try from Kildunne's pass and it looked to be setting the tone.

But the Black Ferns responded stoutly. First up, centre Du Plessis reduced the deficit when she chased down her own kick forward from Lucy Packer's poor clearance and dotted down unopposed.

They would then take the lead soon after when Leti-I'iga scored just after the half-hour when she received fly-half Hannah King's clever inside pass following a burst through the England defence.

The Red Roses had to withstand more pressure before the break and were fortunate to escape falling further behind when New Zealand knocked-on inches from the tryline.

Zoe Harrison crosses for England's winning try in their thrilling 26-19 victory over New Zealand

Harrison writes last act of thriller

John Mitchell's side came out after the break fired up and were rewarded by Kildunne scoring a trademark try as she had too much pace for the Black Ferns to handle out wide.

After a yellow card for tight-head prop Mahutariki-Fakalelu reduced them to 14 players, Breach went over for England's third try in the corner and a 19-12 lead which looked set to be further built on.

But when New Zealand were back to full strength, they were threatening again and were rewarded with their third try as winger Paul finished off concerted pressure to make it 19-19.

Ellie Kildunne crossed the line to score and restore England's lead in the second half

Chances looked to have gone begging for both sides to win it, no more so than when Harrison's penalty attempt from 40 metres back was well short of the posts.

Instead of kicking for touch and taking the draw, New Zealand chose to run it from their own line and go for victory.

But an intercepted pass from Du Plessis was pounced on by Harrison, who crossed to then be mobbed by her team-mates and lauded by a jubilant Twickenham crowd.

Reaction: 'An amazing Test'

England captain and centre Megan Jones:

"What an amazing honour to play the Black Ferns. They set down a challenge for us from the beginning; we responded really well and we accepted that challenge.

"An amazing Test match for us. We're playing the top teams now and you're just going to get everything thrown at you, tested in every avenue and today we prevailed and were able to stay on top.

"Massive credit to our defence, probably my favourite part of the game. But credit to the girls, they showed a lot of character today."

England captain Megan Jones tries to break free from the New Zealand defence at Allianz Stadium

On Zoe Harrison's winning try: "I just said to her, 'you create your own luck in this game', and that was her moment.

"We were putting so much pressure on them. They clearly wanted to play and huge credit to them for putting on a spectacle. But we were just able to capitalise and the pressure we put on them in defence gave us that opportunity and it was an amazing way to finish."

England head coach John Mitchell:

"It was topsy-turvy. I just need to commend the New Zealand girls; they threw the kitchen sink at us and we just gave them too much possession.

"It was just simple messages at half-time to say that the game can turn on a moment and there's just so much credit to the defence as they held in there."

'Proud' Black Ferns excited for future

New Zealand came close to ending the Red Roses' unbeaten run having been the last side to inflict defeat on them in the 2022 World Cup final

New Zealand captain Georgia Ponsonby:

"I was on the bench at the end, but the overwhelming feeling at the end is just pride. It was neck and neck the whole way through and the girls just put so much on the line.

"It was an absolute tussle, the Test match of our dreams in many ways. We were just really unlucky towards the end, but I'm so hugely proud of my team.

"We didn't come out here to lose, we came to win and be brave and I think that's exactly what we did."

New Zealand head coach Wendy Hansen:

"To be really honest, the biggest feeling I've got at this moment is pride.

"We have an amazing group of people, athletes, coaches and family, who work really hard and we're at the beginning of a journey of what Black Ferns rugby looks like.

"We always said this week was going to be a real big test for us, it was going to draw a line in the sand and give us some things and show us how we're special and built different.

"Those watching the game will have seen it was exciting and but it also showed us how and where we can and need to be better.

"It's an exciting space to be in. Obviously, you always want to win but for us, it's about chasing a performance and we know we've got greatness in us, but we'll continue to stay humble on that journey."

What's next for the Red Roses?

The WXV Global Series resumes next month with the North American leg of the competition for John Mitchell's side.

Two more Tests against World Cup runners-up Canada are followed up by a match against USA in successive weeks.

Sports.title: 'I was driving like my grandma' - Antonelli admits to lack of confidence
Sports.content:
World championship leader Kimi Antonelli says he was driving "like his grandmother" during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix because of a lack of confidence at the Baku City Circuit.

Antonelli staged a decent recovery in Saturday's race to come from 16th on the grid, following a crash in qualifying, to finish fifth, but his championship lead over his Mercedes team-mate George Russell was reduced to 66 points as the Brit claimed victory.

The 20-year-old Italian has shown remarkable consistency to build a commanding lead at the top of the standings, but struggled in Baku after missing a significant chunk of practice due to technical issues with his car.

"I was driving a bit like my grandmother today, just damage save mode," Antonelli said. "I didn't take risks. Before making a move, I was making sure that I could go for it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Expectations were high given Antonelli had remarkably come from 19th on the grid to win his home race at Monza earlier in September, but his progress was far more steady this time around.

"If I had the same pace as at Monza or in previous races, it would have been different," Antonelli said.

"It would have been like just full attack. But today, I realised very early that first of all, it was a lot harder to overtake with a train of cars all in Overtake Mode, then I didn't have the same pace as I had previously, so the mindset changed very quickly."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli hits the wall during qualifying at the Azerbaijan GP.

Antonelli actually dropped a place at the start, and it took him 17 laps to work his way up into the top 10.

He then benefitted from errors made by drivers ahead as he made further progress. He also survived a near-miss at the first of two rolling restarts following Safety Cars as he avoided a crash that took three cars out of the race, and was able to continue despite contact with the Haas of Oliver Bearman.

Antonelli said: "After the restart, I had big floor damage. My whole left side was gone with the contact.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player There was carnage on the safety car restart after contact between Alpine team-mates resulted in Lando Norris crashing out of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

"After that, the car was very sketchy to drive, and I still tried to get to P4, but all in all, it's one of those days where you have to be happy with P5.

"Also seeing so many people doing mistakes, you kind of pull back a little bit because I just took advantage of everyone else's mistakes and just move forward."

'My worst weekend of the year'

Antonelli doesn't have to wait long to return to the track with the second of a triple-header of races coming next weekend with the Bahrain Grand Prix, which is being hosted by Malaysia amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Russell produced his most complete weekend since the opening round of the season in Australia, taking a victory that would have been dominant without the Safety Car interruptions.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Azerbaijan GP saw a dramatic ending as Valtteri Bottas crashed on the final lap as George Russell just beat Max Verstappen to victory by one tenth of a second.

Antonelli remains a heavy favourite for the title, especially given Russell must take a grid penalty for changing his engine between now and the end of the season.

It was therefore unsurprising that the championship leader was retaining a positive outlook ahead of the next race.

"It's exciting," Antonelli told Sky Sports F1. "George has done an incredible weekend, he's driven incredibly. He had a lot of confidence.

"And this weekend was my worst of the year by far in terms of performance. I wasn't there, I wasn't really present, especially with what happened so early on."

Formula 1 heads to Malaysia for the first time since 2017 as it hosts the Bahrain Grand Prix at the Sepang International Circuit - watch live coverage from Friday morning, live on Sky Sports F1. Stream Sky Sports with NOW - no contract, cancel anytime

Sports.title: England v Spain: Nations League football – live
Sports.content:
4m ago 13.57 EDT Jacob Steinberg Anthony Gordon has sided with Thomas Tuchel’s assertion that controlling games through possession is not part of English football’s DNA. Although Gordon revealed surprise at being substituted when England were 1-0 up in their World Cup semi-final against Argentina, the winger refused to blame the defeat on Tuchel’s decisions and argued that wider cultural issues influenced the side’s collapse. England’s perennial struggle to keep the ball when under pressure flared when a place in the final was within touching distance in July, allowing Argentina to fight back and go through with two late goals. The pain has not gone away and there has been intense scrutiny of Tuchel’s role in Atlanta. The head coach’s tactical choices were criticised and he faced a backlash after saying “ball possession” was not in his team’s DNA. But Gordon, who thinks he will always be scarred by losing against Argentina, sided with Tuchel’s observations about England’s style as he looked towards the Nations League game against Spain on Saturday. The 25-year-old admitted the side had an ingrained inability to control games but argued they should stop trying to copy other nations. Gordon has gained an insight into the Spanish understanding of how to use the ball since his move to Barcelona. His view is that England should lean more into their physical strengths. ‘It’s not in us’: Anthony Gordon backs Tuchel over England’s possession problem Read more Share

10m ago 13.52 EDT “Hello Rob,” writes Krishnamoorthy V. “Were you assigned this game or did you opt for it? This important piece of information would let me decide if you are merely unfortunate or a steadfast masochist.” Opt for it indeed. The Man giveth, and The Man taketh away. Share

14m ago 13.48 EDT Jacob Steinberg Thomas Tuchel has thrown Cole Palmer’s England future into major doubt by questioning whether the Chelsea attacker wants to be part of his squad. England’s head coach did not hold back on Palmer’s latest withdrawal from international duty, warning that the 24-year-old has missed too many opportunities to play for his country. Palmer has only 14 caps and his decision not to join up with the squad this week, because of a minor muscular injury, caused disappointment given he was left out of Tuchel’s World Cup squad after struggling with form and fitness last season. Tuchel has put a lot of store in team spirit and is clear about wanting commitment. The German has rarely been able to work with Palmer, who had earned a high-profile recall after making a strong start to the campaign, and did not go down the diplomatic route when it was suggested the former Manchester City player does not seem desperate to play for England. “Hard to argue against what you’re saying,” Tuchel said. The line came with a warning for Palmer. “He misses too many camps,” Tuchel said. “That’s the overall headline. We have a lot of invitations and he couldn’t make this one. It is what it is. I am not ready to focus on players who are not here. The players that are here have my full attention. Thomas Tuchel warns Cole Palmer about ‘missing way too many’ England camps Read more Share

19m ago 13.43 EDT Sid Lowe “I’m going to tell you a story,” Luis de la Fuente said. “As soon as the game finished on 19 July, before anyone had cooled down at all, just two or three minutes after the final, one of the players – and you’ll have to forgive me for not telling you which one, but it was one of those who has been with us for the longest time – came up to me and said: ‘Mister, now what? What’s left to win?’ And I said: ‘Bloody hell, the game against England at Wembley on 26 September.’” It was a Friday afternoon at Las Rozas and Spain’s coach had just named his first squad since that day in New Jersey. It was a familiar one, full of history makers. Of the 26 from the World Cup, only four had been left out and there was an explanation for each: Marcos Llorente has announced his international retirement; Joan García is injured; Borja Iglesias, who always felt the likeliest to leave first, is not fully fit; and Gavi is suspended for Wembley, although he could have faced Croatia and Czechia. De la Fuente brings insatiable Spain to England knowing World Cup is not enough Read more Share

24m ago 13.37 EDT Team news: Trafford preferred to Pickford Leeds goalkeeper James Trafford starts ahead of Jordan Pickford, a selection that few people saw coming. Pickford is among the subs, so this might be the end of his long spell as England’s undisputed No1. Myles Lewis-Skelly covers for Declan Rice in midfield and Jarell Quansah is preferred to Trent Alexander-Arnold at right-back. Ferran Torres and Nico Williams, the substitutes who combined for Spain’s World Cup-winning goal against Argentina, start ahead of Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal. The only other change from that game is in defence, where Eric Garcia replaces the injured Pedro Porro at right-back. England (4-2-3-1) Trafford; Quansah, Konsa, Guehi, O’Reilly; Anderson, Lewis-Skelly; Saka, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane. Subs: Pickford, Steele, Alexander-Arnold, Scott, Chalobah, Hall, Branthwaite, Rogers, Garner, Calvert-Lewin, Gibbs-White, Eze. Spain (4-2-3-1) Simon; Garcia, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella; Rodri, Ruiz; Yamal, Olmo, Williams; Torres. Subs: Raya, Martinez, Huijsen, Grimaldo, Merino, Lopez, Pino, Pubill, Baena, Zubimendi, Pedri, Oyarzabal. Referee Davide Massa (Italy) View image in fullscreen Anthony Gordon of England and Spain’s Eric García talk before kick-off. Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty Images Share Updated at 13.57 EDT

33m ago 13.28 EDT David Hytner Thomas Tuchel has pictured the scene. It comes after the final whistle has blown on England’s Nations League opener against Spain on Saturday night, the first post-World Cup fixture for both teams, and it has Wembley swaying to the strains of Wonderwall. It is a moment of communion, a reconnection with the Oasis classic that was the soundtrack to England’s World Cup campaign, which delivered so much only to end in such disappointment. “Do I think it will happen tomorrow?” Tuchel said, when asked if Wonderwall would play again afterwards. “I think it will happen if we win.” There are a couple of counterpoints. The visit of Spain is certainly a glamour fixture and Wembley is sold out in anticipation, but it is not a World Cup knockout tie. The emotion cannot pulse to the same levels. Furthermore, Tuchel has first-hand experience of the vagaries of the Wembley crowd; its hard-to-please restlessness. England aim to win over Wembley and revive Wonderwall in Spain glamour fixture Read more Share

Sports.title: Pocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in Slovenia
Sports.content:
Sébastien Pocognoli grimaced on Friday when recalling his debut as an international player for Belgium. Alessandro del Piero and Italy discovered favourable opposition when preparing for the 2006 World Cup. Pocognoli will also look back, in time, at his first game as the manager of Scotland.

Blue skies, a dainty stadium in Ljubljana and a second-half display that provided glimpses of optimism in respect of Scotland’s world, post-Steve Clarke. The best-forgotten first 45 minutes can be explained away by a squad operating under a new regime. By full time, Slovenia were grateful for their point. Scotland’s players took deserved applause.

Scotland’s failing here was a familiar one. A lack of goals haunted Clarke. Nonetheless, this version of Scotland did at least create a series of openings. Scott McTominay, a key attacking threat, was missing. Instilling ruthlessness in a team is no easy task; it is one, however, Pocognoli has the coaching credentials to meet. Slovenia, on this evidence, have the more significant challenges.

“The feeling in the dressing room is positive because of the second half,” said Pocognoli. “We should have scored but I am very happy with the general performance of the strikers. It was only the last details we missed.” His demeanour was upbeat.

Ninety-four days had passed since Scotland’s loss to Brazil all but confirmed World Cup elimination. When that meek exit was certain, Clarke announced his resignation. Players and supporters alike seem caught between being highly grateful to Clarke for materially altering Scotland’s fortunes and heralding regime change.

In Slovenia, Pocognoli sampled international management for the first time at the age of 39. Slovenia failed to reach the World Cup, with the rows of empty seats telling the story of a country that is not at all convinced by its footballing outlook. The absence of Benjamin Sesko did nothing to help a shot-shy side.

Scotland could hardly bemoan poor preparation. Pocognoli had whipped his squad and mini-army of backroom staff to La Manga in the buildup to this Nations League game. With a sense of revolution in the air, the head coach unleashed a hitherto unseen front two: Robbie Ure was making his international debut while Oli McBurnie returned after years in the wilderness. The opening half only proved there is little point deploying multiple strikers if there is no adequate means of supplying them.

Scotland were awful in that first period. The football was passive and directionless. Players looked well-enough drilled off the ball, but descended into a state of panic when in possession. Slovenia, who were little better than ordinary, should have seized upon these shortcomings. To his credit, whatever message Pocognoli forcefully pressed home during the break had an effect.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli barks instructions during his first game in charge of Scotland. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Andraz Sporar had the ball in the net for the hosts in the eighth minute only for an offside flag to go up. Sporar subsequently missed a golden opportunity from six yards after fine work from Danijel Sturm. As Aljosa Matko shanked wide of Angus Gunn’s goal, the Tartan Army’s groans were audible.

Save a Ure shot from 20 yards that clipped the outside of a post, Scotland were nonexistent as an attacking force. An overhit Billy Gilmour pass that flew out of play when intended for the marauding Andy Robertson rather summed things up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McBurnie should have marked his Scotland return with a goal within five minutes of the restart. He opted to try to jink around Jan Oblak rather than slam a shot past the goalkeeper. Oblak morphed into Inspector Gadget, stretching out his arms while grounded to pinch the ball from McBurnie’s feet.

This triggered Scottish improvement; Gilmour forced a save after a one-two with McBurnie. Aaron Hickey could not quite divert a John McGinn corner on target. Oblak had to be sharp to deny the Scotland substitute Kieron Bowie before doing likewise to McBurnie from the resultant corner.

Second-half Scotland involved a huge upturn. McBurnie said he would not be able to sleep due to his profligacy. Seventeen Scotland caps are yet to yield a goal.

Bowie’s miss, 12 minutes from time, was in the category of howler. Gilmour, increasingly influential as Scotland dominated, had fed his teammate. Pocognoli was emboldened, sending on Ben Gannon-Doak to replace Hickey. In old money, that represented a winger for a full-back.

Scotland huffed, puffed, pushed and wheezed. Slovenia stood firm. Pocognoli nodded with approval as the whistle blew. Next up, a Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland players to wear black armbands after agreeing to play Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will fulfil their fixture against Israel in Hungary on Sunday night, but only after lengthy deliberations between the players resulted in a “significant majority” voting to play.

After a week in which the Irish team and officials have come under increasing domestic pressure to boycott the match due to Israel’s military actions in Gaza, training was delayed by five hours on Saturday while the squad discussed whether to go ahead.

“This morning, a player expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad,” said the FAI’s chief David Courell, referring to a player understood to be the goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu.

“What proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves, but also at times with the coaching staff and the executive. Ultimately we carried out a vote amongst the squad ... and it was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue.”

Courell said the squad had also agreed a number of measures to signal their unease with the fixture taking place. Players are to wear black armbands “in recognition of all the lives lost in the conflict” he said, adding that there will be “elements of the pre-match ceremony” that will “not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland” players, namely the pre-match handshake and exchange of pennants.

View image in fullscreen Gavin Bazunu is believed to be the player who withdrew from the Republic of Ireland squad to play Israel. Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PA

The Republic’s head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, said “nobody is comfortable playing these games for many reasons” as he was once again put under pressure over remarks in which he described his team as “playing against genocide” earlier this week.

Hallgrímsson said he had used a “strong” word and now regretted it. “It was a wrong word for me to use,” he said, arguing that he had meant to say that “by playing we are not accepting what is happening”. If a player chooses to play in the fixture “he is not supporting or agreeing with anything in Gaza” Hallgrímsson said. “We are not playing with that word, we are playing against it.”

The leadership of the Israel team used their press conference to read a statement congratulating Ireland on their decision to play. “What we have seen today is that football has won,” it read. “The separation between football and politics must continue. Anything else spells chaos and creates consequences for the game we love. The Irish took the right decision in agreeing to this. Even if it took longer than it should, it was welcome.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Israeli officials said they would engage in all of the pre-match formalities with the head coach Ran Ben-Shimon confirming: “I will shake hands with Hallgrímsson.”

The Israel FA will also appeal both yellow cards awarded to Saied Abu Farchi during Thursday’s defeat to Austria. Farchi was given a second yellow after he celebrated scoring an equaliser by uprooting the corner flag, an action interpreted by officials as mimicking the firing of a rifle.

Israel dispute this interpretation. “Anyone familiar with him knows it was an imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty,” their spokesperson said.

Sports.title: Manchester City chair Al Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the Manchester City chair, has spoken for the first time since the club was found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules. He said “nothing has changed” and “our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began”.

News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied.

The club did not comment on the verdict until Saturday afternoon when Al Mubarak said on social media: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.

“We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family. Thank you, as always, for your constant support.”

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon Al Mubarak (right) has been Manchester City’s chair since the Abu Dhabi takeover of the club from Thaksin Shinawatra (left) in 2008. Photograph: Nigel Roddis/Reuters

Earlier, City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, posted a cryptic message on social media reading “I know nothing”.

On Saturday morning, Maresca was approached for comment about whether he is seeking reassurance from the club on their continued stance of innocence. The Guardian was sent by his representatives a screenshot of a quote attributed to Socrates, the Greek philosopher, which Maresca posted on Instagram.

The quote reads: “The only thing I know is that I know nothing.” Maresca also wrote: “Time to breathe. Time to analyse. Time to learn.”

Elsewhere, there wwere contrasting reactions to the outcome of the Premier League investigation. Oasis’ Noel Gallagher, a longtime City fan, described his shock at the news, while the club’s former chair David Bernstein believes any potential punishment should not be only financial. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, described the case as unsettling.

On the Let Me Talk podcast, Gallagher said: “A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.

“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really just quite sad. Sad for the fans and for the players.”

View image in fullscreen Noel Gallagher, a longtime Manchester City fan, maintains that even if the guilty verdict stands, the club’s fans will not feel any differently about their success. Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty Images

Asked if it changes the context of moments like Sergio Agüero’s title-winning goal in 2012, Gallagher said: “Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw.

“Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it’s nothing to do with the supporters or the players. The players won that game and won that title on the pitch. Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that’s nothing to do with the fans.

“Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt.”

Bernstein, City’s chair from 1998-2003, told Times Radio: “I felt absolutely awful, I felt in shock yesterday. You’ve asked me on the programme because of my time as chair of City and the FA, but basically I’m a fan of Manchester City and have been a fan for 70 years.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“When I was chair I think I helped get the club out of a very difficult period and started the road to better things. But to see all this tarnished in this way is very sad.

“I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who’ve stayed with the club through thick and thin. It’s a pretty bad day for the fans in blue of Manchester.”

As for the correct punishment, Bernstein said: “First of all, the timing is crucial. This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process has to be done quickly because you’ve got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it’s just not viable.

“The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, that would be a disaster. Not just for this particular case, but for English football generally.

“I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty. All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”

On BBC Radio 5 Live, Nandy said: “Most football fans will be feeling this is not a good moment for football as a whole and Manchester City fans will be feeling very anxious about what happens next. This is a really longstanding investigation, it dates all the way back to allegations that begin in 2009.

“The football fans need to know the rules are applied fairly and consistently, they need to know they’re upheld and they need to know the right decision has been reached.

“We do have a way to go with this, it’s very unsettling for football fans and I hope it can be resolved as swiftly as possible.”

Nigel Huddleston, who was the shadow secretary of state for culture until last month, said on social media: “Whatever the next steps are, they must be conducted in an accelerated and more transparent manner or risk further damage to the reputation and integrity of English football and more unnecessary anxiety for millions of football fans.”

A City spokesperson said on Friday: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.” In that statement, City said they had a ‘comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence’ of their innocence.

Friday’s statement from City continued: “The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Sports.title: Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?
Sports.content:
What happens next?

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 134 disciplinary charges brought against them by the Premier League.

In keeping with the history of this case which has been conducted exclusively in private and with every party sworn to secrecy, there is a lot we don’t know. We do not even have an official confirmation that the three-person judicial panel has reached a verdict. All of football is acting as if they have, however, and that reports of a big win for the Premier League are correct.

If these assumptions are accurate, and neither party have formally denied them at least, then the immediate thing to watch out for is news of an appeal. Under Premier League rules, City would have 14 days from the announcement of the verdict to submit an appeal and the process that follows should be completed in less than 12 weeks from then. Once the appeal has been heard – which should happen in one block of no more than five days – and a verdict reached, the appeal panel are also expected to publish written reasons behind their decisions. We should also see the written reasons from the original judicial panel too, but the unique scale of this case has meant that normal procedures have not always been followed, and the date of publication for these reasons remains unknown.

If City do appeal, what happens?

The club would be submitting an appeal based solely on the decision and not any resulting punishment, which is yet to be determined. In hoping to make the case that the judicial panel were wrong in their observations, City would be allowed to submit new evidence, providing it had not been previously available to them, and make new oral presentations. Once the hearing is concluded, a verdict would be expected in 30 days.

If an appeal fails, what then?

According to Premier League rule W.97, “the decision of an Appeal Board shall be final”, but even this is subject to one final route, that of arbitration. This would mean appearing in front of another panel of eminent legal figures, but the criteria for any hearing would be a lot stricter and successful arbitration only possible in the main if the judicial panel or appeal board was found to have abused the legal process. City have recently been through the arbitration process with the Premier League over its rules related to associated party transactions and, after an initial verdict challenged two applications of the rules but otherwise found them to be sound, City and the Premier League reached a settlement which stopped the case from going to court.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When and how would City be punished?

If City managed to overturn the verdict, there would of course be no sanction. If City’s appeals failed, there are a number of measures available to the panel. They start at fines and end at complete expulsion from the league, with a variety of sporting sanctions including point deductions falling in between. Given the magnitude of the verdict, City can expect to receive a punishment at the sharper end of the scale should any appeal not prove successful.

Could relegation be the end of it?

It seems unlikely. Premier League clubs and those who have been relegated from the division are understood to have been assessing any financial losses they may have incurred during the period City were winning and, appeal pending, breaking the rules. A wave of lawsuits is likely to follow, with Manchester United, for example, having finished second behind City in 2017-18 and potentially denied a record-breaking 21st league title in the process. It is possible that clubs who were relegated could argue that they were sent down because of points denied them by a City side subsequently found to have cheated. Premier League clubs reportedly lost their appetite for legal action after an estimated £50m cost to the competition last season, but if the verdict against City revealed this week is ultimately upheld, a new wave of lawsuits will surely follow.

Sports.title: We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rights
Sports.content:
It couldn’t have been more prophetic. In 2008, 15 years before Manchester City were charged with financial fraud, fans started singing “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” to the tune of Yellow Submarine. This was because the former Thailand president Thaksin Shinawatra’s 15-month ownership of City had come to an abrupt end when more than £1bn of his assets were frozen. And although Sheikh Mansour of the UAE had stepped in to save City, we were sinking fast.

Despite the UAE’s untold riches, by December we were in the relegation zone. It’s called Cityitis – shorthand for our tendency to self-destruct when things appear to be going well. In fact we won trophy after trophy. But we continued to sing the song about going down with a billion in the bank. When the financial fair play investigation was launched in 2018, the chant got louder. Then in 2023 we learned there were more than 100 charges. The chant became even louder and more cavalier. And now that our grubby, griftin’, cheatin’ chicken has come home to roost, you can bank on one thing (if banks still deal with us) – the chanting will be louder and more cavalier than ever.

After all, this is a club that believes schadenfreude starts at home. We brag about our failings. Other songs we sing include “Empty seats at home” (to the tune of the Beautiful South’s Rotterdam) because we can’t sell out our tickets and “Is This the Etihad?” (to La donna è mobile from Verdi’s Rigoletto, natch) at deathly quiet away grounds.

It’s not about tempting fate. Nor is it hubristic irony – we can’t sell out despite winning all these trophies. It’s simply an acceptance that one way or another we’ll always be City, always suffer from Cityitis, and come the day, despite our endless UAE riches, we’ll do a City.

And that day has come. We don’t know what our fate, or sentence, is yet. When I interviewed Wayne Rooney recently he suggested we would have 60 points docked, making it virtually impossible for us to avoid relegation.

It could be worse, of course. We could lose all eight trophies we won in the period (2009-10 to 2017-18) we flouted fair play, including three Premier League titles and our record-breaking centurions season when we won with 100 points in 2017-18. To me, that would be disproportionate and would in effect mean the Premier League eating itself.

But is the verdict itself unjust? City will say yes because they don’t want anything as petty as fair-play rules thwarting their bid for global domination. The lawyers will say yes because they’re paid to do so. Many fans will say yes because they’re fans. But some of us believe we’re bang to rights.

Everton and Nottingham Forest have been docked points for lesser offences, so it would be embarrassing if City had got away with it; an undeniable case of one rule for the rich. Despite City’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed. Although it appears this is not the end because City intend to appeal.

View image in fullscreen The 2017-18 Premier League title may be one of eight trophies that Manchester City fear losing. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

Our behaviour has been pretty outrageous at Dodge City. Failing to provide accurate and up-to-date financial reports, concealing salary details and bonuses, inflating sponsorship revenues and failing to cooperate or supply requested documents during the investigation all feature on the charge sheet. We used lawyers to royally take the piss. And when it comes down to it, that is not very City. After all, this is a club founded in 1880 as St Mark’s (West Gorton) by members of St Mark’s Church of England for humanitarian and social rescue purposes to serve the deprived area of east Manchester, where Shameless was filmed a century later.

So what happens next? We may lose trophies. We will almost certainly get relegated. We almost certainly lose our best players and say ha det bra to Erling Haaland, the great Nordic God of goalscoring (having said that he may stay just to see how many he could get in a Championship season). And we start building again.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

If the very worst happens, and we lose all those trophies, at least we still have our anni mirabiles when we did the unprecedented domestic quadruple (2018-19), and treble including the Champions League (2022-23). There was barely a whiff of scandal in these years. We were simply obscenely wealthy, brilliantly run and managed by the world’s numero uno Pep Guardiola.

And plenty of positives will come out of our disgrace. The biggest being that justice is done. But there is so much more. City may get to play in the Championship where we enjoyed some of our finest moments (“We’ve got Kevin Keegan 100 goals a season,” sung to the tune of Let’s All Do the Conga a mere 24 years ago). League One? Halcyon days. For City fans of a certain age and disposition, beating Gillingham in the playoff is our top footballing memory. League Two? Thrill of the unknown. The only way is up, as the song goes.

Ticket prices come down, allowing regular civilians back into the Etihad. Prices become so low that we fill the ground. Fans begin to realise Wembley visits and winning trophies are to be treasured. Pep has already gone so there’s no danger of losing him. We learn some humility and stop coming over all sullen because we’ve only won the League Cup and FA Cup in one season.

Perhaps the biggest positive is that rather than simply pulling out the chequebook and signing the world’s best, we learn to think imaginatively. I noticed the God of Bermudan goalscoring Shaun Goater this year left his job coaching Aston Villa Women. He’s only 56, never relied entirely on pace, and I bet he’s a free agent.

Sports.title: Liverpool rehire Julian Ward as sporting director to replace Richard Hughes
Sports.content:
Liverpool have appointed Julian Ward as their sporting director for a second time after the departure of Richard Hughes to Al-Hilal. Ward, who was Liverpool’s sporting director for the 2022-23 season, has spent the past two years as technical director for Fenway Sports Group, the club’s owners.

The process of finding a successor to Hughes, who left for the Saudi Pro League after two and a half years at Anfield when the summer transfer window ended, was led by the FSG president, Mike Gordon.

Ward has worked in various capacities for Liverpool over the past 14 years, including European scouting manager, assistant sporting director and sporting director.

His appointment offers continuity at a time of upheaval in the Liverpool hierarchy with Hughes and Michael Edwards, the former chief executive of football at FSG, leaving this year and the owners in the process of selling a 38% stake in the club to 1892 Holdings for £2bn. The consortium, fronted by Amit Bhatia and including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, has an option for a full takeover should FSG decide to sell up.

View image in fullscreen Jürgen Klopp signs a contract extension in April 2022 with FSG’s Michael Gordon (left) and Julian Ward, then Liverpool’s assistant sporting director. Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

The 45-year-old Ward replaced Edwards as sporting director in 2022, but told FSG he wished to step away for personal reasons a few months into the role. Luis Díaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Núñez were signed during his first spell although the manager at the time, Jürgen Klopp, had a greater say on transfers after Edwards left.

Ward remained highly regarded by FSG, however, and Gordon, who had resumed the day-to-day running of Liverpool after Hughes’s departure, considers his extensive knowledge of the club and of squad planning as invaluable. As FSG’s technical director, Ward had oversight of the global talent strategy that has led Liverpool to sign several highly rated young prospects this year.

Liverpool’s new sporting director will lead the club’s football operation alongside the assistant sporting director, David Woodfine, the chief scout, Barry Hunter, FSG’s director of football development, Pedro Marques, and Andoni Iraola’s senior leadership team.

Sports.title: George Russell wins Azerbaijan Grand Prix by ONE tenth of a second: Mercedes star back to winning ways - and denies Max Verstappen his first triumph of the season by razor-thin margin
Sports.content:
George Russell wins Azerbaijan Grand Prix by ONE tenth of a second: Mercedes star back to winning ways - and denies Max Verstappen his first triumph of the season by razor-thin margin

Only just. By one tenth of a second. Practically a photo-finish. But victory for George Russell at the Azerbaijan Grand, pulled off with Max Verstappen right alongside him, means the Briton can just glimpse the prize on the horizon – the world title he craves.

Hmm, it still requires binoculars to detect it clearly, but it is no longer out of sight.

After this dramatic win, one of the best of Russell's career, he remains 66 points behind his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli, who finished fifth.

But the team's senior driver, 28, felt rejuvenated enough afterwards to delve into the box of mind games regarding the 20-year-old Italian who leads him.

'There is much less pressure on me than there is on him,' said Russell, who vowed to aim for victory in each one of the remaining eight races.

'It is the most dominant weekend I have had in my career. And it has come at a really great moment. I am really proud of this.

George Russell claimed his first win in three months as he claimed the Azerbaijan Granx Prix

He beat Max Verstappen by less than a second, denying the Dutchman a first win of the year

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli could only finish fifth, having crashed in qualifying and started 16th

'It would have been easy for me to lose the faith, not about winning the championship, but in terms of my ability, and that never happened.'

Russell had not stood on the top step of the podium for three months almost to the day, in Austria, and confidence was hissing out of him like a punctured tyre. Antonelli was the coming kid, an unstoppable Exocet, or so it seemed.

So this was a magnificent afternoon of cheer for Russell. There are 208 points to fight over yet, including one sprint race in Singapore, which follows 'the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia' next weekend, reassigned owing to war in the Middle East.

It's precisely in Kuala Lumpur that Russell needs to put his foot on Antonelli's larynx again, and then to keep it there.

Here, it was the boy wonder who stymied himself by crashing in qualifying and starting 16th. Is that the pressure about which Russell talked, and tried to quadruple?

Antonelli dropped a place at the start but revived his race slice by slice. He was not too impressed with his own performance, though, saying: 'I was driving a bit like my grandmother today. I was taking no risks. It was about saving points.

'If I'd had the pace I did in Monza (where he won earlier this month from 19th on the grid), I could have raced differently but I realised I didn't and that it would be hard to overtake. I just took advantage of others' misfortunes.

'It wasn't the usual Kimi.'

Perhaps, he was a bit harsh on himself even if, yes, he was helped by a couple of safety cars, the first bunching up the field when he was running ninth.

This punctuation in proceedings, brought about by Alex Albon bashing his Williams into the wall at Turn 5, allowed everyone to stop for fresh rubber. Nobody had pitted by this stage.

Russell had priorly been sailing ahead from pole, the man ruling the race by a distance. His advantage at the time of the safety car's maiden tour stood in double figures, 10 or 11 seconds. Yes, his Mercedes was mighty quick but he was making full use of its potential around Baku's tight streets.

Returning to Antonelli's situation. The safety car peeled off and the next moment Franco Colapinto of Alpine came rolling into the first corner like a 10-pin bowling ball. He crashed into his team-mate Pierre Gasly and took him out. Gasly then ricocheted into Lando Norris, a second helpless victim of the recklessness. The world champion was out, as was Gasly, and the safety car was recalled.

Norris called afterwards for Colapinto to be banned for a race. The stewards instead handed down a five-place grid penalty for 'Bahrain in Malaysia'. Which was about justice.

Anyway, the incident gifted Antonelli seventh place. He later passed Lewis Hamilton and Oscar Piastri, who ran off the road, to claim his finishing position.

Russell was too fast for everyone all weekend. Yet having established his huge lead that was eroded by the crashes, he found himself in a battle with Verstappen at the end.

Ironically, Verstappen had been struggling for speed earlier but was then flying, having moved on to soft tyres, just as Russell had, the pair on the same strategy.

The Dutchman, for all his harrying, had to settle for second place, though it looked as if he might just pass Russell as they roared to the line wheel-to-wheel. It was touch and go in one of the closest finishes in Formula One history.

Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar finished third. Ferrari's Charles Leclerc came fourth, holding off Antonelli's charge by 0.3sec, with Hamilton sixth.

But the only man smiling ear to ear was George Russell… with his binoculars out.

Sports.title: Devastating untold story of Tom Brady and Gisele Bundchen's marriage: Read every ugly detail, the secret letter stashed in a drawer... and her savage last three words that left him so ruined, friends feared he had cancer
Sports.content:
Devastating untold story of Tom Brady and Gisele Bundchen's marriage: Read every ugly detail, the secret letter stashed in a drawer... and her savage last three words that left him so ruined, friends feared he had cancer

Tom Brady and Gisele Bundchen's divorce in 2022 shocked America. The greatest quarterback in history and the woman who was once the world's highest-paid model were a fairytale match made real.

Now, after years of extensive research speaking to friends, eyewitnesses and teammates, bestselling author Lars Anderson's new book Brady: An American Story and the Price of Greatness reveals how it all went so terribly wrong.

Tom Brady longed to stay connected to his old life, to keep feeling that high-voltage climax of competition he'd been chasing since he was a teenager.

But he was also tormented by the mounting feeling that it was almost immoral to keep playing because the job essentially rendered him an absent father and husband for half the year.

His brain dictated one course of action. His gut chartered another – a problem similar to trying to walk in opposite directions at once.

'It's not always what I want,' he said in January 2022. 'It's what we want as a family. And I'm gonna spend a lot of time with them and figure out in the future what's next.'

In particular, Brady felt that his Victoria's Secret model wife Gisele Bundchen 'deserved' more of his time as a husband and a father.

Brady's unrelenting desire to continue playing football had placed enormous strain on the marriage. At first, she tried to gently nudge him into retirement.

In 2017, minutes after Brady had just masterminded the greatest comeback in NFL history to win his sixth Super Bowl, Gisele and their two children ran onto the field to celebrate.

But the first words Gisele said to her husband of eight years had nothing to do with the game and everything to do with the future: Would now be the perfect time to retire?

Brady didn't know what to say. He hugged his wife and acted as if he hadn't heard the question.

A new book by Lars Anderson has revealed the untold story of Tom Brady and Gisele Bundchen's shock divorce that shocked America

When Brady first met Gisele, whose net worth was close to $400 million and had graced more magazine covers than anybody on earth, he said he was only planning to play in the NFL for 10 more years

As his wife's career faded into the background and her yearning for him to be at home with their family grew, Brady built a dynasty with Bill Belichick and the New England Patriots

Later that night in Houston, as the team celebrated, Gisele pressed her husband a second time. Brady was unresponsive.

After a third attempt, he finally answered. 'Too bad, babe,' he said. 'I'm having too much fun right now.'

Weeks later, the couple and their children went on vacation with Jay Feely, a former teammate of Brady's with the Michigan Wolverines.

Gisele asked Feely to do what she could not: persuade her husband. Gisele pressured Feely to frame retirement as Brady's final and most important act of leadership – one for his family.

'She was dead serious, too,' Feely later said.

'Play as long as you want,' he told Brady.

Brady winked at his buddy.

Gisele went for a more direct approach in 2018, days after Brady and the New England Patriots had suffered a gut-wrenching Super Bowl loss to the Philadelphia Eagles.

Gisele wrote her husband a letter – serious, handwritten. She explained that their marriage wasn't working. She needed more of him, more of his time, more of his attention, more of his heart.

She needed him to be present when he was at home, not responding to text messages on his constantly buzzing cell phone or replaying a game in his mind.

She needed more help with the kids. She needed the chance to sleep in just a few days a week. She needed more time for her own career.

Gisele ran onto the field to celebrate with Brady after he had just completed the greatest comeback in NFL history, only to immediately question him on a potential retirement

Brady and Gisele have son Benjamin (left) and daughter Vivian (right). But she also helped raise Jack (center), the son Brady shares with actress Bridget Moynahan: pictured in 2021

'People need to understand that Gisele was a bigger international star than Tom,' said a former Brady teammate. 'She was getting tired of living on Tom's schedule and being somewhat in his shadow during football season. She has a lot of pride, too. And, I mean, how many times did you see Tom supporting her career? There clearly were imbalances there.'

The couple went to marriage counselling, but Brady eventually filed the heartfelt letter in a drawer.

He'd pull it out on contemplative nights and reread every word, wanting to be reminded that he needed to tend to his marriage with the same tenacity he tended to his job.

In early 2020, the family relocated to Florida when Brady signed for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

'Think about being married to Tom,' said one of Brady's friends, a former NFL player. 'The guy gets up at the crack of dawn, thinks all day about a game that is foreign to his wife, comes home and is in bed each night by nine. He can't really eat out or go out without causing a scene. Everything he puts in his mouth tastes like s***. The whole lifestyle had to be getting tiresome for Gisele.'

BRADY: AN AMERICAN STORY AND THE PRICE OF GREATNESS Lars Anderson's new Brady biography is released on Tuesday September 29 and is available to purchase HERE

Worried that enrolling their young children at a new school would be 'too much change,' Gisele committed to homeschooling Benny and Vivian in Tampa. 'We were only going to stay for a year,' she said.

One year turned to two.

And so it was that, in January 2022, America's most famous quarterback found himself weighing the case of Brady vs. Brady – the sportsman vs. the family man.

He deliberated for nine days. It was close to a hung jury; Brady leaned 55 percent one way, 45 percent the other.

But on February 1, he announced the verdict: At the age of 44 and after 22 years in professional football, his NFL career was over.

That decision lasted just 40 days.

On March 13, Brady announced he would return for a 23rd season, his sights set on an eighth Super Bowl win.

'I've realized my place is still on the field and not in the stands. That time will come. But it's not now,' he said.

At first, Gisele made the right noises, expressing public support for her husband's decision to play on.

'I don't think relationships just happen. It's never the fairytale people want to believe it is,' she said that summer.

'When you love someone, you don't put them in a jail and say, "You have to live this life." You set them free to be who they are.'

But when Brady walked into One Buc Place in July for the start of training camp, the sight of him – gaunt and cadaverous – was that of a man worn thin, reduced to bone and sorrow.

Brady and Gisele looked smitten on vacation in 2022, just weeks before he announced his un-retirement

Gisele paid an emotional tribute to Brady after he announced his retirement for the first time. She also initially supported his decision to return publicly but things quickly turned sour

Nearly everyone in the building worried he was ill, maybe even battling a serious disease. His teammates estimated he'd lost close to 20 pounds, and the vibrancy of his spirit had dimmed like a candle running low on wax.

'For Tom to lose that much weight, on his frame, it was a lot,' said his former Buccaneers head coach Bruce Arians. 'It was very clear that the reason for the weight loss was the stress from the personal issues he was dealing with.'

'His cheekbones had freaking cheekbones,' said another coach. 'With all respect, he looked like a cancer patient with really good hair. He just seemed miserable, not even close to the Tom we all loved. He was so stressed.'

In truth, Gisele had been so upset at Brady's U-turn that she had flown off to Costa Rica.

Brady wound up taking Benny and Vivian, then 12 and 9, to their first day of class at a new private school in Florida.

During practice on July 28, center Ryan Jensen, one of Brady's closest friends and his biggest defender on the field, collided with another player.

Crashing to the ground, Jensen screamed 'F***!' and clutched his left knee. Practice stopped. Brady lifted off his helmet and ran to Jensen.

Kneeling by his side and knowing the meaning of that scream – torn ligaments, fractured bones – he watched as the medical staff tended to his friend. Getting visibly upset, Brady stood and walked away.

He wandered around the eerily quiet field, hands on his hips. 'It was pretty clear he was asking himself, "Why the f*** did I come back?"' said one Buccaneers staffer.

'I think that's when he realized he'd made a horrible decision. He didn't come back and risk adding more troubles to his marriage to get the s*** kicked out of him!'

In late August, for the first time in his career, Brady asked his head coach if he could take an extended leave from camp.

He said he'd come back; he just didn't know when.

Things had got so bad that he and Gisele now required a serious discussion in a remote location.

There was a noticeable change in Brady when he walked into One Buc Place in the summer of 2022 for training camp

Brady had lost so much weight that his Buccaneers coaches and teammates thought he looked like a cancer patient

'I've got to take care of some personal things,' Brady told coach Clyde Christensen with a lifeless stare.

Christensen later speculated that Brady may have been experiencing a form of serious psychological shock.

Something had blindsided him – something very bad and something that had completely devitalized him.

Brady's absence from camp was excused, but only a few at One Buc Place knew he was traveling to a private resort in the Bahamas to make one final, desperate attempt to keep his family together.

With just six months left in his football career, the bond he and Gisele had was flickering out like a match in a strong gust of wind, the fragile illusion of forever now fast fading.

'Tom didn't know what the heck was going on,' said an assistant coach. 'And we didn't know if he was ever coming back.'

When he returned to Tampa after 11 days away, his spirit seemed more broken than before.

It was evident that a scarring incident had transpired.

The frantic, nearly two-week effort to rescue his marriage had failed. Those close to Brady feared the countdown to divorce was on.

But Brady remained utterly captivated by Gisele, still lost in the enchantment of her.

'Tom was an empty shell of who he was when he got back,' Christensen said. 'There was no joy. Everything was hard work.'

'Everything was going good between Tom and Gisele,' one eyewitness close to Brady said. 'Tom was FaceTiming with Gisele during the day between meetings, just checking in to see if she needed anything. These were normal conversations, and she seemed happy.

'Then one day, Gisele, who is really into astrology, basically looked into the stars and told Tom, "We're not compatible." And just like that, she was done.

'But what triggered that? Was it the years of feeling like she wasn't his top priority? That he kept playing when she'd asked him to step away? Maybe.

'Or was there a particular spiritual adviser telling her, "Hey, this relationship is bad for you. Get out of it now. Even the stars are telling you that." One thing is certain: In no way, shape or form was this a normal marital breakdown.'

Brady and Gisele announced their divorce on October 28, 2022, after 13 years of marriage.

In February 2025, Gisele gave birth to her third child, her first with boyfriend Joaquim Valente, her former jiu-jitsu instructor.

According to one of Brady's friends, he was absolutely 'stung' that she had become pregnant just two years after divorce.

In February 2025, Gisele gave birth to her third child, her first with boyfriend Joaquim Valente, her former jiu-jitsu instructor

According to one of Brady's friends, he was absolutely 'stung' that she had become pregnant just two years after divorce

Just over a month after the birth, Brady shared a photo of himself on Instagram – his preferred form of mass (and often cryptic) communication.

In the color photograph, Brady's right arm is extended and a ball has spiraled out of his hand. He is silhouetted by the sunset's golden glow.

Underneath, Brady wrote: 'True Love.'

To those who knew him well, there was no ambiguity. As one friend described it, that was 'the softest middle finger.'

PART TWO COMING NEXT WEEK: The shocking sex incident that left Brady's college teammates questioning everything...
