World.title: Estonian Military Orchestra marks anniversary with concerts in Viljandi and Tallinn
World.content:
The Estonian Military Orchestra will celebrate the 108th anniversary of Estonian military music and the fifth anniversary of operating within the Estonian War Museum with birthday concerts on 7 October at Viljandi Pauluse Church and on 8 October at the Estonia Concert Hall in Tallinn.

The concerts are also an expression of continued support for Ukraine: guest conductor will be Major Lyubomir Sukennik, head of the Military Music Center of the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

The program includes works by Estonian composers as well as Ukrainian national music. Both concerts are charitable in nature. The ticket revenue from the Viljandi concert will be donated to the NGO Sõdurilt Sõdurile, which supports Ukrainian frontline units primarily by purchasing non‑lethal equipment and medical supplies.

According to Samuel Jalakas, head of the Estonian Military Orchestra, the five years within the Estonian War Museum have been active. "State ceremonies and official events are our daily work, but all the more we are pleased to give two public concerts for this year's birthday, to thank our audience and supporters who have stood by us in turbulent times," Jalakas said. "It is also a great joy that Major Lyubomir Sukennik from Odesa can join us on stage, with whom we already had good cooperation at the jazz ensemble concerts held in Tallinn this spring."

The Ukrainian orchestra has been familiar to the Estonian public since May 2022, when Ukraine's largest classical music festival in exile was held in Tallinn for the first time. During the concerts broadcast on ETV and ETV2, television viewers donated a total of 30,000 euros, half of which was directed specifically toward purchasing bulletproof vests for members of this orchestra. This spring, a smaller ensemble of the orchestra visited Tallinn, with a series of concerts and charity performances, also together with the Estonian Military Orchestra.

The beginning of Estonian military music is considered to be the founding of the 1st Infantry Regiment's orchestra on 24 November 1918. This is also the birthday of the Estonian Military Orchestra, which over more than a century has carried the names of the Ministry of War, the Ministry of Defense, the Tallinn Garrison Orchestra, and the Defense Forces Orchestra. Since 1 October 2021, it has operated under the name Estonian Military Orchestra within the Estonian War Museum.

World.title: Cyberattack gains access to University of Tartu library's online store customer data
World.content:
The University of Tartu Library informed users of its e‑bookstore that an external attacker gained access to their online store and most likely downloaded the store's customer data.

The Director of the University of Tartu Library, Jaanika Anderson, told online store users that on 11 September they detected a data security incident: an attacker had illegally accessed the store.

The university immediately notified the Information System Authority (RIA) of the incident and suspended access to the online store. The Data Protection Inspectorate was also informed.

"In additional analysis of the incident, the university determined that the attacker very likely also illegally downloaded the online store's customer data, which includes your first and last name, email, phone number, online store username and the encrypted version of the password associated with it, as well as data related to the use of the online store, such as purchase history, IP addresses, etc.," Anderson wrote to online store users.

The attacker likely also accessed customers' usernames and passwords, and although passwords were stored in encrypted form, the library recommends changing them as soon as possible if the same username‑password combination has been used for other accounts, and monitoring for any suspicious activity.

Anderson added that the attacker did not gain access to payment instrument data related to purchases.

The university has suspended access to the online store and will restore it only after a full security analysis has been carried out and security vulnerabilities have been eliminated.

World.title: Kristian Sirp: Estonia's bigger defense budget requires smarter procurers
World.content:
Estonia has good reason to invest heavily in security in the coming years, but a larger budget also means greater responsibility for the technological choices we make, as more equipment does not automatically translate into greater capability, Kristian Sirp writes.

Drone technology is currently developing faster than the state can procure it through conventional procedures. A solution that appears to be the best when technical specifications are being drawn up may already be yesterday's technology by the time the contract is signed. Therefore, Estonia's next important drone capability is not necessarily a new radar, sensor or counter-drone system. At least as important is the ability to establish, based on evidence and before making a purchase, what actually works under Estonian conditions.

The more Estonia invests in security, the more costly mistakes become. Purchasing millions of euros' worth of equipment without knowing how it works with other systems, what information it provides, who receives that information and what decision a person makes based on it is a matter of governance, resilience and the use of public funds.

The war in Ukraine has made drones one of the fastest-developing fields of technology. A countermeasure is found for a sensor, communications methods are changed, software is upgraded and algorithms are adjusted, while a cheaper and more effective alternative to a costly solution can emerge within a matter of months. The technology cycle has become considerably shorter than the traditional public-sector procurement cycle.

The Estonian government itself has acknowledged this change. Prime Minister Kristen Michal noted in the spring that drones have significantly changed airborne threats in a short period of time and that Estonia needs both multilayered drone defenses and an environment in which companies can develop new counter-drone solutions.

A single radar cannot create situational awareness

When discussing the drone threat, we tend to talk about equipment. Do we need radar, a radio-frequency sensor, an optical camera, a jammer, an interceptor drone and so on? But none of these creates an operational capability on its own. First, a drone has to be detected and then it has to be identified. Information from multiple sensors must be brought together, an assessment must be made as to whether the object poses a threat and someone must receive and understand that information in time to make a decision. Only then can action be taken if necessary.

What needs to be established is which model of detection, data exchange, decision support and cooperation actually works. This distinction becomes especially important at a facility providing an essential service. Imagine a (malicious) drone near an electrical substation, hospital, port or other critical facility. One sensor issues an alert, another does not confirm it and a third detects the object but classifies it differently. Who receives the information? Who decides whether it is a threat? Which agency is responsible? When should the police be involved? When should the facility's security team be involved? What information is sufficient to justify intervention in the first place?

The same problem arises when different agencies procure different solutions at different times. Each piece of equipment may be good on its own, but their data formats, operating models, threat assessments and command-and-control systems may not be compatible. The result may be that the state has a great deal of technology but still lacks a common operational picture. This is precisely the kind of fragmentation that should be avoided before major investments are made.

Developments among Estonia's allies show that the problem is increasingly well understood. In March this year, NATO launched its new Innovation Range in Latvia with its first campaign to test, assess, verify and validate drone and counter-drone technologies. Companies from allied countries and Ukraine, operational users and public-sector representatives were brought together at the Sēlija Military Training Area. It was the first of several testing activities planned for 2026.

NATO has applied the same principle elsewhere on the eastern flank, jointly testing drones, counter-drone systems, unmanned ground systems and communications solutions in an operational environment. NATO is conducting these tests because there is a vast amount of technology available and it is necessary to quickly determine what actually works, how it integrates with other systems and how it can be used operationally.

The European Union is moving in the same direction. The European Commission's new Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security, adopted in February, addresses incident prevention, drone detection, responses to malicious activity and strengthening European defense readiness together. The Commission's action plan places particular emphasis on secure equipment, command-and-control capabilities, industrial cooperation and the broader deployment of drone and counter-drone solutions. Testing and validation are becoming a core part of capability development.

Estonia has good reason to invest heavily in security in the coming years, but a larger budget also means greater responsibility for the technological choices we make as more equipment does not automatically translate into greater capability.

If organizations define their needs separately, conduct separate procurements and evaluate solutions according to different criteria, the result may be a collection of technological islands. One sensor operates in one place and another elsewhere, one agency has one operational picture and another has a different one, data is exchanged only partially or manually and the final operational decision-making process remains to be worked out after procurement.

The state's ability to act as a smart customer is becoming a key competency. A smart customer knows how to compare alternatives under the same conditions before making a major investment, make different components work together, measure results and involve the end user.

In public-sector innovation, the purpose of testing is precisely that learning on a limited scale makes it possible to avoid larger and more costly mistakes before full-scale implementation. Documents underpinning Estonia's public-sector innovation policy likewise treat testing as a means of evaluating new solutions before widespread deployment and reducing the risk of costly mistakes on a large scale. In the case of drone technology, this principle may prove particularly valuable.

Ability to make "small" mistakes needed before the next major tender

Estonia therefore needs a permanent capability to test solutions designed to mitigate drone threats under controlled conditions before they are relied upon to handle a real crisis or become the subject of a major investment.

The technology needs to be tested in real-world environments. An urban area, a port, energy infrastructure or the surroundings of a hospital all place very different demands on sensors. Interference, buildings, other radio signals and people's everyday activities all affect performance.

Data from different sensors must also be integrated. The detection accuracy of an individual device is of little use if an operational user has to monitor four different screens at once and determine whether they are showing the same object.

Not every threat scenario can be recreated in the real world and physically testing every combination would be too expensive. A digital model makes it possible to repeat the same scenario, change parameters and compare the performance of different solutions and processes.

A good counter-drone test examines whether the system correctly understood what it detected, whether the information reached the right person at the right time and whether that information enabled the right decision to be made. This is where technology and governance intersect.

Estonia's small size makes it possible to bring operational agencies, essential service providers, technology companies, researchers and government policymakers into a single testing framework. Estonian businesses would benefit as well. If a solution developed in Estonia can demonstrate that it works not only in a laboratory but in a real energy, port or other critical infrastructure environment and as part of an integrated decision-making chain, that is valuable to both the state and the company.

World.title: Lenin promised nations the right to secede, but built a centralized state
World.content:
As the Russian Empire collapsed, self‑determination became a powerful political tool. It was used to demand autonomy and independence as well as to justify new systems of governance. A doctoral dissertation defended at the University of Tartu examined how and why different political forces harnessed self‑determination for their own interests in the early 20th century.

A hundred years ago, a major political struggle surrounded the concept of self‑determination. It was used to demand a state and autonomy, but the same term was also used by forces that considered it their right to decide how much self‑determination other nations should be granted at all.

Oliver Rowe, who defended his doctoral dissertation at the University of Tartu, studied how self‑determination was used in the collapsing Russian Empire between 1914 and 1924. His work shows that the meaning of the concept depended largely on who used it, to whom it was offered, and in what kind of document the promise was written.

What did self‑determination actually mean?

Although today self‑determination is primarily associated with a people's right to decide their own political future, the meaning of the term has changed significantly over time. Before it entered the vocabulary of nations and collective rights, it referred mainly to individual autonomy and inner development. Only in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries did the term begin to denote the political rights of groups and nations.

Even then, no single clear understanding emerged of what self‑determination meant in practice. Russian liberal Kadets spoke of cultural self‑determination and used the term in their 1917 party program. In the socialist movement, national self‑determination was discussed instead, but its content was sharply contested. Vladimir Lenin linked national self‑determination directly to the right to secede from the state — a position that was more exceptional than self‑evident in contemporary politics.

This plurality of meanings led Rowe to focus on political forces that did not demand self‑determination for themselves but claimed the right to grant it to others. In his view, this reveals the imperial mindset shared by many political actors of the time. Both the Bolsheviks and several of their opponents assumed that the center would decide in what form and to what extent the empire's peoples could govern themselves.

This decision‑making power was reflected clearly in how politicians formulated self‑determination on paper. In an election speech, self‑determination could remain a political promise, but in a constitution it became a written right. "When a politician mentions self‑determination in a campaign, it is something entirely different from writing the same right into a constitution," Rowe explained. Thus, the weight of self‑determination depended not only on its wording but also on where and with what force it was written.

Lenin, Stalin and the limits of self‑determination

The self‑determination debate of the final years of the First World War is often associated with two names: Vladimir Lenin and U.S. President Woodrow Wilson. Their views were, of course, different. Lenin tied national self‑determination directly to the right to secede, while Wilson's name became linked in international politics with a broader understanding of peoples' self‑government.

Every history‑minded Estonian likely knows that Lenin's approach contained a tension. He defended the right of nations to secede, yet envisioned a future socialist society as strongly centralized. According to Lenin's logic, merely recognizing the right to leave should reduce the desire to actually use it. If a people are not held in the state by force, the feeling of oppression diminishes and "fraternal trust" can emerge.

"According to Lenin's logic, merely recognizing the right to leave should reduce the desire to actually use it."

Lenin's ideas received a cold shower after the 1917 revolutions, when secession in the empire's borderlands became a real possibility rather than a theoretical one. In Ukraine and Georgia, left‑wing national forces wanted to separate from Russia for real. "This is the million‑dollar — or million‑ruble — question. Lenin supported the right of nations to secede, but could not fully reconcile it with his vision of a centralized socialist state," Rowe explained.

After the civil war, the Bolsheviks changed their political vocabulary. Whereas the broad concept of self‑determination had previously included autonomy, federation and secession, Stalin began narrowing it already in 1918. Soon he argued that one should speak specifically of the right to secede — the right of a republic to leave the union. "Stalin said outright that self‑determination had become problematic and should be replaced with the right to secede," Rowe added.

The shift was partly driven by the changing reputation of self‑determination in international politics. At the end of the First World War, the concept was associated with Wilson, but after the Paris Peace Conference many were disappointed in the expectations tied to him. The narrower concept of the right to secede was politically useful for the Bolsheviks. They did not intend to allow actual secession within the Soviet state, but the same right could be used to support revolutionary and anti‑colonial movements elsewhere, such as in Ireland.

Estonia, Ukraine and the Treaty of Tartu

How much the meaning of self‑determination could depend on the form in which it was written became sharply evident as the Russian Empire collapsed. After negotiations with the Provisional Government failed to produce the desired result, the Ukrainian Central Rada declared autonomy in its First Universal. A debate erupted in Petrograd over whether the declaration was merely a political statement or a step with legal weight. According to Rowe, this shows how the content of self‑determination was shaped by the type of document in which it appeared.

"The legacy of the empire directly influenced how different peoples were described and classified in the Soviet Union."

Events unfolded differently in Estonia. In 1917, the Provisional Government agreed to reorganize the borders of the Governorate of Estonia on a national basis. Rowe sees timing as a possible explanation. At that moment, influential supporters of local self‑government were present in the Russian government. Jaan Tõnisson's activities and Estonian demonstrations in Petrograd may also have played a role. Thus, the fate of national demands depended greatly on when and in what political situation they were presented.

The Bolshevik coup and the continued disintegration of the Russian state changed the aims of national movements. When the Bolshevik government sought a way out of the war with Germany and began negotiations, independence became a much more realistic possibility for several movements. According to Rowe, this must be considered when interpreting the independence efforts of the time. "These independence efforts should be seen more as a response to the collapse of the state than as its cause," he explained.

When independence became reality, self‑determination also became a diplomatic tool for Estonia. During the Treaty of Tartu negotiations, the Estonian delegation demanded that the right to self‑determination be explicitly written into the treaty. This was intended to justify Estonia's independence and improve its chances of broader international recognition. The wording of the Treaty of Tartu later served as a model for other peace treaties the Bolsheviks concluded with neighboring states.

Traces of old thinking

The collapse of the Russian Empire did not erase imperial thinking. Rowe describes the early Soviet Union as a hybrid regime in which revolutionary socialist ideology intertwined with centralized power. The legacy of the empire directly influenced how different peoples were described and classified in the Soviet Union.

This contradiction was illustrated by the Soviet nationalities policy of korenizatsiya, which promoted local languages, cadres and national institutions. According to Rowe, the policy carried forward the earlier logic of self‑determination, even though the term itself disappeared from the Bolshevik elite's political vocabulary after 1921. "On one hand it was a revolutionary socialist state; on the other hand it often interacted with other peoples in clearly imperial ways," he added.

Rowe sees a similar contradiction in today's Russian rhetoric. He finds it notable how the war against Ukraine is justified with talk of "liberation," "oppression" and the protection of various groups' rights. Putin's relationship to the Bolshevik legacy is also telling. He has blamed the Bolsheviks for creating Ukraine, linking the country's emergence to Lenin. At the same time, Putin's view of Russia as a natural great power resembles, in Rowe's assessment, the views of the Bolsheviks' opponents — including the movement of Aleksandr Kolchak.

Thus, although the language of self‑determination may change over time, a great‑power belief in the right to decide the fate of other nations persists stubbornly alongside it. "Ideology may be only a smokescreen or rhetorical device. Behind it lives the conviction that an empire has the right to decide for others," Rowe said.

Oliver Rowe defended his doctoral dissertation "Self‑determination in theory and practice: the reconfiguration of the 'Russian' Empire, 1914–1924" ("Enesemääramine teoorias ja praktikas: 'Vene' impeeriumi ümberkujundamine 1914–1924") on 24 August at the University of Tartu. The dissertation was supervised by Professor of Political Theory Eva Piirimäe. The opponent was Lara Douds from Northumbria University.

World.title: Health Insurance Fund chief: healthcare pay rises must reflect real possibilities
World.content:
The head of the Health Insurance Fund's management board, Siiri Lahe, said regarding the healthcare unions' demands for pay increases that they do responsible and important work and their pay must keep pace with the times, but at the same time one must proceed from real possibilities.

Healthcare workers' unions announced on Friday that they are turning to the national conciliator, because collective bargaining negotiations with the Health Insurance Fund — in which they sought a rise in minimum pay faster than the Estonian average for the next two years — ended without results.

Siiri Lahe said that healthcare workers do very important and responsible work for the people of Estonia, and their pay must keep pace with the times.

"At the same time, one must proceed from real possibilities and ensure that health insurance funding is sufficient both for salaries and for the availability of necessary healthcare services and medicines for people," Lahe said.

She emphasized that the Health Insurance Fund's forecast for the next four years continues to account for pay increases for healthcare workers in line with the projected growth of Estonia's average wage.

"According to the current plan, the next increase in the wage component included in healthcare service prices will be postponed by nine months — from April 2027 to January 2028," the Health Insurance Fund chief added.

The Nurses Union, the Healthcare Workers' Professional Union, the Doctors' Union, the Clinical Psychologists' and Clinical Speech Therapists' Professional Union, and the Physiotherapists' Union — who signed the healthcare workers' appeal — cited as the reason for the failure of negotiations the decision by Social Minister Karmen Joller and the Health Insurance Fund that in 2027 the amount needed to raise minimum wages for healthcare workers will be used to bring the Health Insurance Fund's budget into balance.

The Nurses Union pointed out that although the average nurse's salary is often highlighted, they earn it through many overtime hours, working nights, weekends and holidays, and often at multiple jobs.

The union also noted that the base salary of care workers is more than one‑third lower than the national average, and their pay approaches the average only thanks to night and overtime work.

World.title: Tartu researchers develop blood test to identify genetic causes of pregnancy loss
World.content:
Researchers at the University of Tartu's Institute of Molecular and Cell Biology are testing a solution that makes it possible to determine the cause of pregnancy loss based on a blood test.

Those involved are hopeful that the method will reach practice already in the coming years.

Approximately two‑thirds of pregnancies that end in the first trimester are caused by chromosomal errors. To determine the exact genetic cause of the loss, medical researchers have until now analyzed removed abortive tissue, that is, the product of conception.

However, this is emotionally and physically exhausting for both the patient and the analyst, expensive, and often technically difficult, because the laboratory sample may contain the woman's own cells, leaving the exact answer unattainable.

According to the study's lead, Professor Ants Kurg, the new method is based on cell‑free fetal DNA that enters the mother's bloodstream during pregnancy. "It is an interesting phenomenon that when a woman is expecting a child, fetal DNA also reaches her bloodstream. There is very little of it, but it can still be analyzed. This has laid the foundation for an entirely new application called non‑invasive prenatal testing," Kurg explained.

The blood test is made difficult by the fact that cell‑free fetal DNA is extremely scarce in the mother's blood, and researchers must find it against the background of the mother's own DNA. The pilot project, which ended in August, demonstrated that the blood‑based method is sufficiently accurate and that the results largely match tissue analyses.

A clear answer brings peace of mind

A precise genetic cause is important for families who have experienced pregnancy loss, primarily to restore peace of mind. "This is always the main question when a pregnancy loss occurs: what did I do wrong and why did this happen to me?" Kurg said.

If the blood test identifies a cytogenetic cause — a random chromosomal error — it relieves parents of unjustified guilt. "For doctors, it is also important that if a cytogenetic cause can be shown, there is a fairly high likelihood that when planning a new child, the next pregnancy will go well. But if no cytogenetic cause is found, additional investigations are needed, and these are much more complex," the professor added.

A three-year research project

To bring the blood‑based analysis into everyday medical practice, researchers together with the University of Tartu Women's Clinic and the health‑technology company Celvia CC are launching a large applied research project supported by Estonian Business and Innovation Agency (EIS).

The three‑year project begins this autumn. "There is a whole series of questions we want to continue working on. For example, how early in pregnancy the analysis can be performed, and how maternal comorbidities and medications affect it. Another separate question is missed miscarriage — within what time frame after a missed miscarriage it is still possible to determine the cause based on cell‑free DNA," Kurg explained.

World.title: Gallery: Lennart Meri's epic 'Silverwhite' journey brought to life
World.content:
50 years after its publication, the Estonian Maritime Museum has brought Lennart Meri's epic "Silverwhite" journey to life with a new exhibition at Tallinn Seaplane Harbor.

First published in occupied Estonia in 1976, "Silverwhite" ("Hõbevalge" in Estonian) weaves together history, research, myths and imagination, becoming a landmark work of Estonian cultural history.

The anniversary exhibition, "Silverwhite 50," takes Meri's journey from the pages of the book into the hangars of Tallinn Seaplane Harbor, tracing the route of ancient Greek explorer Pytheas from the Mediterranean to Saaremaa through sound, space and light.

"We wanted to invite people to read the book again and discover its many layers," said curator Martti Helde.

"Silverwhite 50" unfolds as a journey through a series of spaces, culminating in the story of the Kaali meteorite, which has left a lasting mark on Estonia's cultural history. Like Meri's book, it also explores the mystery surrounding the island of Ultima Thule.

Bespoke experience

At the heart of the exhibition's sound design is NOUS Sonic, an Austrian-developed system being used for the first time in the Baltic and Nordic regions.

Finnish sound artist Janne Laine's soundscapes, heard through headphones, change according to each visitor's movements, pauses and choices.

Lennart Meri and ETV editor Martin Viirand at Meri's Nõmme home in 1976. Source: Jaan Rõõmus/ERR

"Each visitor gets a personal 'Silverwhite' experience," said EMM director Urmas Dresen. "No two sound experiences are exactly the same."

The exhibition also features rare artifacts, items from Meri's family collection and even meteorite fragments.

Helde said it is designed for both readers familiar with the book and those encountering it for the first time, inviting visitors to explore its many layers rather than providing any definitive answers.

"'Silverwhite' is at once an exhibition, an expedition and a state of being," the exhibition team said. "It is an opportunity to step into a world where time moves at a different pace and where each visitor creates their own journey."

Pre-presidential legacy

Lennart Meri was a traveler, published writer, documentary filmmaker and statesman before being elected in 1992 as Estonia's first president following the restoration of its independence the previous year. He was reelected as head of state in 1996, serving two terms over ten years.

Originally published in 1976, "Silverwhite," Meri's best-known work, was published in Finnish in 1983, Italian in 2016, Russian in 2020 and English in 2025.

A new, 50th anniversary edition of the Estonian-language book is set for release, while filming also continues for a feature film adaptation of the same name.

"Silverwhite 50" will remain open to visitors at Tallinn Seaplane Harbor through October 31, 2027.

World.title: Iraq beats Kuwait 3-2 in Gulf Cup thriller with dramatic late winner
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq claimed their first victory of the 27th Arabian Gulf Cup with a thrilling 3-2 win over Kuwait on Saturday at the Prince Abdullah Al-Faisal Stadium in Jeddah, as substitute Karrar Nabeel struck a thunderous stoppage-time winner to settle a dramatic encounter between the two Gulf rivals.

After opening their Group A campaign with a 1-1 draw against Oman, Iraq needed a win in Kuwait and got one in dramatic manner, with coach Graham Arnold’s changes transforming the final moments.

Following a goalless first half, Zidane Iqbal put Iraq ahead in the 52nd minute, giving the Lions of Mesopotamia the breakthrough after starting the match in midfield.

Kuwait equalized in the 75th minute when Yousef Nasser scored from the penalty spot, setting up a tense final 15 minutes.

Iraq reclaimed the lead eight minutes later when Saif Rashid scored a fantastic acrobatic goal from a cross to make it 2-1.

As the game progressed, Arnold’s replacements added new energy to Iraq’s offensive.

Jussef Nasrawe shined after coming on, giving speed and direct running down the right flank while regularly putting pressure on Kuwait’s defense.

Karrar Nabeel also came off the bench and would later provide a crucial contribution.

Kuwait refused to give up, as Nasser scored again in the 90th minute to complete his brace and tie the game at 2-2, seemingly winning his team a point.

Iraq replied nearly instantly.

Nabeel fired a tremendous shot deep into stoppage time to make it 3-2, igniting jubilation among Iraqi players and fans and capping off an incredible encounter.

The contribution from Iraq’s bench was especially significant.

Nasrawe provided Iraq with additional offensive danger down the right, and Nabeel’s entrance resulted in the game-winning goal.

Iraq now has four points from their first two Group A matches, after a tie with Oman in which Mohammed Qasim scored the only goal.

Saturday’s success also extended Iraq’s current undefeated streak against Kuwait, who last defeated the Iraqi national team in 2014.

The match brought another unforgettable chapter to one of Gulf football’s long-standing rivalries.

Kuwait is the competition’s most successful country, with ten trophies, while Iraq has won the Gulf Cup four times, most recently in Basra in 2023.

The style of Iraq’s victory offered an added boost: Iqbal scored the first goal, Saif scored a fantastic second, Nasrawe helped fuel the assault from the bench, and Nabeel scored the winner at the end.

Iraq will now focus on their last Group A encounter against Saudi Arabia on September 29, with Arnold’s team aiming for a spot in the Gulf Cup semifinals.

World.title: PM Al Zaidi meets UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih in New York
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi met with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Barham Salih, and his accompanying delegation in New York to evaluate the status of refugees and internally displaced persons (IDPs), alongside joint humanitarian relief programs.

The diplomatic discussions were held on the sidelines of Al-Zaidi’s active participation in the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

The talks centered on deepening institutional coordination between the Iraqi Federal Government and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), with a particular focus on mobilizing technical resources and international assistance to support vulnerable displaced populations.

Prime Minister Al-Zaidi underscored that Baghdad places human rights and humanitarian protection at the forefront of its national priorities, maintaining consistent cooperation with the UNHCR and relevant multilateral agencies to enhance living conditions, deliver targeted welfare services, and rebuild stability across liberated and crisis-impacted areas.

Al-Zaidi emphasized the necessity of tackling the root causes driving involuntary displacement and asylum seeking, calling for cohesive regional and international coordination frameworks to safeguard the fundamental rights of displaced groups in strict alignment with international conventions and statutory humanitarian laws.

In response, High Commissioner Salih confirmed the agency’s commitment to supporting Iraq through comprehensive relief and developmental operations, stressing that the UNHCR will continue working with Baghdad to fulfill all operational and financial benchmarks necessary to permanently resolve the internal displacement file.

World.title: PM Al-Zaidi asserts state monopoly on arms and outlines economic vision at UNGA81
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi delivered a wide-ranging policy address before the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, presenting Baghdad’s strategic vision for national sovereignty, economic restructuring, and regional stability.

Reaffirming Iraq’s adherence to the principles of the United Nations Charter, Al-Zaidi framed the nation as an ascending economic force and an essential bridge for multilateral dialogue and cooperative diplomacy. He declared that the country’s immediate priorities stem from a decisive national will to restore the prestige of the rule of law, consolidate constitutional governance, and rebuild public confidence in sovereign state institutions.

Addressing the nation’s security architecture, the Prime Minister emphasized that the federal government holds the exclusive authority to determine matters of peace and war, asserting that all arms and instruments of legitimate force must remain strictly confined to the command of constitutional institutions.

Al-Zaidi underscored that current executive and regulatory enforcement measures are rooted in statutory mandates and supreme national interest, aimed at defending territorial integrity, consolidating security gains, and establishing the stable environment required to support sustainable socio-economic development and incoming international investments.

Highlighting a pivotal sovereign transition, Al-Zaidi noted that the conclusion of the U.S.-led International Coalition’s mission in Iraq marks a strategic evolution in Baghdad’s foreign partnerships, pivoting defense-centric alignments toward multifaceted economic and developmental cooperation.

He stressed that Iraqi forces have built the requisite autonomous military and intelligence capabilities to defend the nation’s borders, land, and people in the post-defeat era of terrorism. To sustain this regional equilibrium, the Prime Minister called on international partners and neighboring states to enforce rigorous border management, eliminate security gaps, and maintain constant counter-extremism coordination.

Turning to economic governance, Al-Zaidi outlined Iraq’s ongoing campaign against administrative and financial corruption, identifying the recovery and safeguarding of public funds as an indispensable pillar of institutional reform. He articulated an ambitious modernization agenda designed to transition Iraq away from the vulnerabilities of a rentier economy toward a dynamic, open-market framework integrated with global digital and technological systems.

To realize this transition, the federal government has established legal, tax, and customs incentives aimed at empowering private enterprises, attracting foreign direct investment, and leveraging Iraq’s strategic geographical crossroads to expand commercial flows.

In the energy sector, the Prime Minister reaffirmed comprehensive plans to boost crude oil production, capture and process natural gas reserves, and scale up refining capacities alongside downstream petrochemical industries, aiming to cement Iraq’s standing as a dependable global energy supplier.

Al-Zaidi voiced grave concern regarding disruptions to freedom of navigation and commercial shipping routes that have triggered sharp increases in global energy prices. To insulate national revenues and reinforce global market stability, he confirmed that Baghdad is actively advancing strategic pipeline corridors linking Iraq with Turkey, Jordan, and Syria to diversify crude export outlets away from maritime chokepoints.

Concluding his address, the Prime Minister presented Iraq’s multibillion-dollar Development Road project as an overarching blueprint for regional integration, characterizing the multimodal transit corridor as a vital artery connecting East and West through trade, logistics, industry, and energy networks.

Finally, Al-Zaidi invited neighboring states and global investment partners to participate directly in the transit corridor, reiterating Iraq’s conviction that shared economic interests, reciprocal trade ties, and cross-border infrastructure constitute the most durable foundation for lasting regional peace and prosperity.

World.title: Basra tribesmen liberate hijacked oil tanker in Gulf of Aden
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A tribal dignitary from Basra Governorate revealed on Friday, September 25, 2026, that approximately 40 members of the Al-Shaghanba tribe from the Abu Al-Khaseeb district successfully liberated a hijacked crude oil tanker in the Gulf of Aden, freeing the crew and capturing seven armed pirates.

Sheikh Ali Al-Shaghanbi stated that the commercial vessel, owned by an Iraqi businessman belonging to the Al-Shaghanba tribe, was intercepted and boarded by maritime pirates while transiting strategic maritime lanes off the southern Arabian Peninsula.

According to the tribal leader, the pirates seized control of the tanker, took the crew hostage, and issued ransom demands as a condition for their release.

In response, an expeditionary group of roughly 40 armed tribesmen from Abu Al-Khaseeb and the village of Jaykoor mobilized to mount a direct recovery operation, coordinating logistics and tracking through international contacts positioned outside Iraq.

The intervention concluded with the tribal forces successfully storming the vessel, regaining full command of the tanker, and securing the safe release of all detained crew members unharmed.

Sheikh Al-Shaghanbi confirmed that the clash resulted in the capture and detention of seven armed pirates found aboard the vessel, while remaining members of the pirate group managed to flee the maritime perimeter.

World.title: Al Zaidi courts US banks in New York targeting 10M bpd oil capacity
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Under the auspices and in the presence of Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, the Permanent Mission of the Republic of Iraq to the United Nations in New York hosted a high-level roundtable meeting bringing together representatives from premier American commercial banks and financial institutions, Iraqi banking delegates, senior government officials, and economic analysts.

Held late Thursday evening Baghdad time on September 24, 2026, the diplomatic engagement was convened to re-establish institutional communication between Iraq’s financial sector and the international banking architecture, with a particular focus on direct correspondent relationships with major U.S. lenders.

In his address to the executive gathering, Prime Minister Al-Zaidi stressed that Iraq has embarked on an irreversible trajectory of structural economic transformation and banking sector modernization. He acknowledged that past vulnerabilities within Iraq’s domestic banking ecosystem were partly rooted in institutional isolation and restricted interaction with global financial hubs, particularly American banking conglomerates.

Al-Zaidi extended an open invitation to U.S. financial institutions to establish direct operational footprints in the Iraqi market, emphasizing that their market entry would represent a qualitative leap toward elevating local banking practices, adopting international compliance standards, and deepening Iraq’s integration into global capital networks.

Highlighting Iraq’s macroeconomic foundations, the Prime Minister noted that the country currently produces approximately 4.5 million barrels of crude oil per day, with federal energy policies actively targeting an expansion toward 10 million barrels per day over the long term.

This hydrocarbon expansion strategy is designed to maximize sovereign revenues and channel critical liquidity into national development, industrial manufacturing, and cross-sector economic diversification. Al-Zaidi assured participants that the government is actively engineering an investor-friendly environment with streamlined regulatory, customs, and fiscal frameworks, underscoring that American banks hold vast opportunities to structure project financing, issue commercial credit, and underwrite major capital ventures across energy, logistics, and real estate.

Detailing administrative reforms underway, Al-Zaidi outlined the government’s clear operational blueprint for comprehensive institutional restructuring across state-owned commercial banks. The initiative aims to enforce corporate governance benchmarks, upgrade anti-money laundering and know-your-customer compliance mechanisms, and build an agile banking framework capable of supporting modern commercial activities.

The Prime Minister affirmed that statutory anti-corruption proceedings, asset recovery drives, and fiscal protection measures are advancing effectively, reiterating Baghdad’s commitment to institutional transparency and the safeguarding of public and private investment funds.

World.title: Iraq and US sign accord handing over diplomatic center at Baghdad Airport
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Government and the United States signed a formal agreement on Thursday, September 24, 2026, transferring full control of the Baghdad Diplomatic Support Center (BDSC) at Baghdad International Airport to the Iraqi side, marking a significant step in the systematic restructuring of bilateral ties between both nations.

The signing ceremony, hosted at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs headquarters in Baghdad, brought together Iraq’s Undersecretary for Bilateral Relations, Muhammad Hussein Bahr Al-Uloom, and the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad, Steven Fagin.

The foreign ministry stated that the handover forms an integral milestone in federal efforts to fulfill the technical and sovereign prerequisites for concluding the mission of the U.S.-led International Coalition and drawing down foreign military presence across Iraq, aligned with the established September 30, 2026, deadline.

By transferring authority over the high-profile logistical installation at the capital’s international gateway, the sovereign transition moves forward on schedule toward the formal cessation of coalition combat missions.

Undersecretary Bahr Al-Uloom emphasized the strategic weight of the agreement, framing the handover as an operational pivot toward an expanded bilateral era centered on mutual economic partnerships, energy infrastructure modernization, and broad-based development projects.

In response, Fagin reaffirmed Washington’s support for advancing bilateral collaboration within agreed strategic frameworks that uphold mutual sovereignty, with both diplomatic delegations concluding the ceremony by noting that the handover establishes practical foundations for deeper institutional cooperation and coordinated regional security frameworks.

World.title: Iraq targets first Gulf Cup win against Kuwait
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq will take on Kuwait on Saturday, looking for their first victory in the 27th Arabian Gulf Cup, after drawing 1-1 with Oman in Jeddah.

The Group A match will take place at Prince Abdullah Al Faisal Stadium in Baghdad at 6:55 p.m. local time, with Iraq starting the second round with one point and Kuwait aiming to rebound from a 1-0 loss to Saudi Arabia.

Iraq started quickly against Oman on Wednesday, with Mohammed Qasim scoring in the sixth minute with a strong left-footed finish.

Oman answered in the second half with Nasser Al-Rawahi, who equalized in the 67th minute to give both sides a draw.

News from Iraq’s Coach Graham Arnold said that preparations for the first match had been restricted, with his group having little time together before playing an Oman team that had been in camp for many days.

Arnold mentioned that Iraq’s players are physically, tactically, and emotionally ready for Kuwait. Arnold may make changes to his team for the match against Kuwait due to exhaustion and the hot weather in Saudi Arabia.

Half of Iraq’s Gulf Cup roster had competed in the 2026 World Cup, with the remaining being younger players given a chance with the national team.

Arnold said that Mustafa Saadoun and Mohammed Qasim are available for the match, while defender Akam Hashim’s fitness is being examined.

Saturday’s encounter is crucial after Iraq’s two-point loss to Oman. Saudi Arabia leads Group A with three points, Iraq and Oman have one apiece, while Kuwait has no points after the first round.

The top two teams advanced to the semifinals.

Iraq’s last group encounter is against Saudi Arabia on September 29, making it crucial to win against Kuwait before facing the current group leaders.

World.title: Iraqi PM calls on US firms to seize investment opportunities
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi called on US companies on Wednesday to seize investment opportunities available in Iraq, particularly in the petrochemicals, glass, and phosphate industries, as well as the gas and clean energy sectors.

Al-Zaidi’s remarks took place during his meeting in New York with a delegation from the US Chamber of Commerce, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

The prime minister stated that Iraq has considerable natural resources, human resources, and a key geographical position, all of which serve as necessary foundations for successful partnerships. He explained that the government is seeking to use these resources to promote economic development and increase investment possibilities.

Al-Zaidi emphasized the government’s commitment to providing support for businesses and investors, such as granting ownership of land for investment projects in accordance with Iraqi laws, as well as access to tax and customs exemptions for up to ten years.

Iraq is working on infrastructure and transportation projects, notably the strategic project of the Development Road, which will improve Iraq’s position as a corridor connecting the East and West, according to al-Zaidi.

The prime minister affirmed that the government looks forward to establishing factories and setting up projects to diversify the economy and create job opportunities.

Al-Zaidi also asked members of the US Chamber of Commerce and specialized firms to attend the Baghdad Energy Conference and capitalize on the prospects offered in the country. He added that Iraq aspires to establish economic partnerships based on collaboration, mutual interest, and long-term investment.

World.title: Wangchuk apologises for comparing Ladakh situation with Tibet
World.content:
SRINAGAR: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk walked back his comparison between Ladakh and Tibet, saying he meant only to highlight the gravity of the violence in Leh on Sept 24 last year and had no intention of hurting Tibetans.

The Leh Apex Body member apologised Saturday after the Central Tibetan Administration in Dharamshala objected to his remarks as âmisplaced and inaccurateâ.

âI was only comparing a specific incident on a particular day and of course not with decades of sufferings that Tibetan people have gone through,â Wangchuk said. âI have no intentions whatsoever to cause any hurt to anyone, least my dear Tibetan friends... I deeply apologise from the core of my heart,â he said in a Facebook post.

CTA spokesperson Tenzin Lekshay said Friday that comparing Ladakh with Tibet was inaccurate. âTibet continues to remain under Chinaâs authoritarian rule,â he said, adding that Tibetans face systematic repression of fundamental rights and religious freedom, along with measures aimed at erasing their distinct cultural identity.

Wangchuk made the comparison Thursday while addressing people in Leh on the first anniversary of Sept 24 police firing on protesters demanding Sixth Schedule status and statehood.





Four people were killed and nearly 90 injured after demonstrations turned violent.

He said he feared an âencounterâ for speaking out against what he called atrocities in Ladakh. âToday, such atrocities are being committed in Ladakh that even China is not doing in Tibet,â he had said.

World.title: ‘Damage control’ after EC row: Congress demands SIR rollback, CEC’s resignation
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Saturday demanded the immediate suspension of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and called for chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation or prosecution.

Their demand comes after the Election Commission issued a fresh statement defending its decisions amid reported differences within the poll body.

Congress leaders Pawan Khera and Jairam Ramesh accused the EC of going into "damage control" mode following an Indian Express report and subsequent media coverage on differences between the three election commissioners. The party alleged that the SIR exercise had led to the "disenfranchisement" of crores of voters and questioned the Commission's explanation on changes to Form 6, used to add names to electoral rolls.

"The ECI's press note today is too lame, too little, too late," Congress' head of media and publicity department Pawan Khera said.

Ramesh said the Commission had issued the statement only after the media reports and nationwide protests seeking Kumar's removal.

"It has just issued a wishy-washy Press Note that raises further questions on its intent, integrity, impartiality and credibility," he said on X.

"The ongoing SIR, which has turned out to be a method of massive disenfranchisement of several crores of Indians, must be suspended immediately without delay.





"In the meantime, nothing short of the CEC's resignation or prosecution will suffice," he said in a two-page statement.

Congress questions EC's explanation

The Election Commission said all SIR orders were issued after approval from all three Election Commissioners. It also said changes to Form 6 had been upheld by the Supreme Court.

The Commission further said letters written by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi to the Cabinet Secretary were not related to any policy decision of the Commission or its IT division.

According to the EC, the letters concerned the functioning of an officer deputed to the poll body.

Ramesh said the EC statement did not directly deny the findings reported by the Indian Express.

"First, the Press note does not directly deny the story or its findings. It makes a defensive attempt to downplay the same in paragraph 3(i) and 3(ii) but does not say that the allegations are baseless," he said.

On Goa, he said the EC's response showed that 81 of the 97 deleted voters had already filled Form 6 to be included again in the electoral rolls.

"To put this another way, you disenfranchise voters through a broken and corrupt system, and when caught say that they are being added back," Ramesh said.

Khera also alleged that the EC had not addressed objections raised by the other two Election Commissioners over changes to Form 6.

"That objection was not resolved then. It was not resolved since. And this 'mother of all objections' has still not been addressed - even after today's so-called unanimous meeting," Khera said on X.

"So until the ECI answers this specific legal objection, no length of press notes, no claim of unanimity or any other clownery can save Gyanesh Kumar Gupta's face," he said.

"It is still not too late for him. He should resign and turn approver, or prepare for jail," Khera added.

Congress raises questions over voter deletions

Ramesh also questioned the EC's reliance on a Supreme Court order of May 27 saying the order had preceded the recent media revelations.

"The order which was pronounced well before the recent revelations will not save the CEC for the malicious deletion of targeted voters, for the incompetence that has resulted in citizens being wiped off the roles, for the crores lost in both expenses and man-hours due to the confusion and harassment caused to entire families," he said.

He also questioned the extension of voter registration deadlines in Delhi and Maharashtra and asked what would happen to voters in Karnataka, Telangana, Bihar and West Bengal.

"What happens to the voters disenfranchised in Bihar and West Bengal? Do the voters of these and other states who were deleted due to one man's corruption not deserve answers," Ramesh said.

The Congress leader also criticised the EC's decision to involve experts from IITs and IIITs to review the ECINET portal and submit a report on whether it complies with rules.

"Aside from being a meaningless safeguard (since the concern is not about the technical soundness but rather the centralization which prevents voter addition at ground level) this confirms the concerns attributed to the two other Election Commissioners per the reportage," he said.

Dispute over Gen Z voters

Ramesh alleged that the EC's statement had not addressed concerns over the deletion of young voters.

"The Press Note avoids answering the questions regarding the deliberate targeting of Gen Z voters.

The ECI has no answer for its targeted disenfranchisement, beginning mid-July through wholly illegal changes made to Form 6 (unseen and unapproved by Parliament) which placed an unfair burden on them to find and disclose their parents and/or grandparents' details," he said.

He listed several allegations that he said required answers, including the "unilateral nature of decision making by the CEC", alleged bias against the Opposition, alleged participation in "vote chori", the enrolment of Gen Z voters and alleged negligence in the deletion and updating of electoral rolls.

Ramesh said the CEC could not avoid scrutiny through bureaucratic procedures.

"He stands exposed and is now petrified as an entire country seeks to hold him accountable," Ramesh said.

World.title: 'India calls for restraint': Jaishankar on ship attacks in Gulf, seafarers at UNGA - top quotes
World.content:
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Saturday and called for exercising restraint amid continued attacks on commercial ships and seafarers in Gulf region amid the Iran-US war.

"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault of theirs. Those most impacted often have the least say. This assembly must face up to the true state of affairs. This year, we are witnessing a conflict in the Gulf, one that is exacerbating an already difficult situation. We remain deeply concerned over continuing hostilities," he said.

"The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers, transiting international waterways, is simply unacceptable.

India calls upon all parties to exercise restraint, de-escalate tensions, ensure protection of civilians, and uninterrupted flow of energy and commerce...," he added.

Taking aim at Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, he said: "Yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this assembly. Arguments were invoked to normalize terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences.





That will not stand. Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised. Friendship and goodwill cannot coexist with terrorism, and understandings premised on that will naturally be called into question.

It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend its ways."

Here are top quotes from Jaishankar's speech:

The conflict in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, is equally concerning. As Prime Minister Narendra Modi stated, endless war must give way now to an end to war. India supports ongoing initiatives to bring peace. Even as this is underway, there is an urgent need to address the security of seafarers and the supply of food, grains, and energy.

India is prepared to do everything possible to ameliorate this situation, especially with regard to food and energy security. Tensions and violence also regrettably continue in West Asia or the Middle East. We strongly believe that a durable and lasting peace requires a two-state solution.

In the meanwhile, India is contributing to humanitarian assistance and relief efforts for the Palestinian people. Let us recognize that peace is not just the absence of war. If the world is subjected to continuous threats and pressures, then we are really living on the edge of an abyss. All it takes is one more step to push us over. Therefore, it is imperative to strengthen stability, security, and predictability. These are crucial elements of the enabling environment for peace...

A persistent threat to peace has been the scourge of terrorism. That this could be state-sponsored, with cross-border purpose, makes it a direct affront to the global order. Governments indulging in such practices must be held accountable. There must be no dilution in our zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism. Its financial aspects, in particular, should be exposed and should be countered...

After eight decades of the UN, this should have become second nature. Instead, what we are actually seeing is a weaponization of everything. A mindset of extreme competition has set in, undermining institutions and establishing choke points. It extends from the world of finance to constricting market access, disrupting supply chains, and withholding technology. Resources and connectivity have become particularly subject to leveraging. As a result, nations are now more focused on de-risking and diversifying. Now, while this may secure their interests to varying degrees, the overall atmosphere is no longer that of trust or goodwill...

The predicament of the Global South is particularly acute. It faces a 4F crisis concerning the security of food, fuel, fertilizer, and financeâthe combined impact of a super El NiÃ±o compounding fertilizer shortages and now impediments to grain movements. All these are a cause for alarm. Moreover, SDG progress is under increasing pressure. The Global South's right to industrialize is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial. The march of technology that was meant to instill hope has now become a source of anxiety. The misuse of AI is sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect...

Earlier, he held discussions with Russia and Iran on the sidelines of the high-level UNGA session, days after US President Donald Trump signed a new law providing for sanctions on countries purchasing oil and gas from Moscow and Tehran.

Jaishankar met his Russian and Iranian counterparts, with talks covering bilateral ties, cooperation in the Brics grouping and the Gulf conflict.

NEW DELHI: The Federation of Indian Pilots (FIP) has urged the civil aviation ministry to ensure that its technical submissions on the Air India AI171 crash are formally considered before the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) finalises its probe report.The AAIB investigation into the June 12, 2025 crash in Ahmedabad, which killed 260 people, is at an advanced stage.In a letter to civil aviation minister K Rammohan Naidu on Friday, FIP sought to be nominated as an âindependent technical participant in the review of the draft AI171 final investigation reportâ.FIP said it had âreliably learnt that the government/ ministry has directed or is considering requiring the draft report to undergo examination by an independent committee before it is circulated/ finalisedâ. It said that if such a review mechanism is being constituted, the pilots' body should be formally nominated and represented as an independent technical stakeholder representing the professional pilot community.The federation also requested that its technical submissions receive formal and documented consideration before the final report is issued.The FIP had last week urged the AAIB to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of electrical-system evidence related to Boeing 787 aircraft as part of the AI171 investigation.The Air India Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, registered as VT-ANB, crashed shortly after taking off from Ahmedabad for London Gatwick on June 12, 2025. Of the 242 people on board, 241 died, while 19 people on the ground were also killed. All 12 crew members died and one passenger survived.The aircraft, manufactured in 2013 and powered by GE engines, had flown 41,868 hours. Its Airworthiness Review Certificate was valid until May 23, 2026.In its latest update on the investigation, the AAIB said significant progress had been made and that the final report would be released after completion of all investigative activities and the required international review and consultation processes.The bureau has said the investigation team has examined technical, operational, organisational and human factors associated with the accident, without disclosing specific findings from the probe.

World.title: Albanese credits PM Modi for expanding energy access, bats for stronger India-Australia ties
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Australian PM Anthony Albanese has credited PM Narendra Modi with providing energy access to India's population on a scale that, he said, no other country has achieved before.

Talking to former Australian PM Kevin Rudd on Sept 24 at an event organised by Asia Policy Institute in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly meetings, Albanese said, âTo give Prime Minister Modi credit, more people have been connected with access to energy in India under his reign than has occurred in any decade in any country or any region in human history.â

Under the Ujjwala scheme, over 10.5 crore domestic cooking gas connections have been provided since 2016, while the Saubhagya scheme helped electrify over 2.8 crore rural and poor urban households.

The PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, the worldâs largest domestic rooftop solar initiative, has connected over 50 lakh households with solar energy. Nearly 2.5 million farmers have also benefited from the PM-KUSUM scheme, which promotes solar energy in agriculture through solar-powered irrigation systems.

Albanese's statement comes at a time when energy security is high on Indiaâs agenda, with global supplies facing disruptions amid the ongoing war in West Asia.





India diversified its energy supplies from 27 to 41 countries over the past decade to ensure energy security for its population of over 140 crore. This helped it tide over supply disruptions linked to the Strait of Hormuz, which carries a fifth of the worldâs total energy trade, amid the West Asia conflict and, more recently, disruptions in the Red Sea. India also imported LNG from Australia when supplies from Gulf nations were scarce.

Albanese spoke about India's growing economic strength and efforts to deepen bilateral ties. He said the India-Australia partnership had been âunder-utilisedâ and that he and PM Modi were âvery keen on rectifying thatâ.

âHe is someone who we have a strong relationship with. I think thereâs a lot more can be done in our economic partnership,â Albanese said.

During PM Modiâs visit to Australia in July this year, the two countries issued a joint statement calling for stronger cooperation on reliable energy supplies, renewable energy, supply-chain resilience and electrification. They also agreed on Australian uranium exports to India for its nuclear energy programmes and reaffirmed cooperation on critical minerals and renewable energy.

Commerce minister Piyush Goyal recently said that bilateral trade between the two countries stood at $21.09 billion in 2025-26.

World.title: As Trump hugs Xi and plugs Sharif, India feels the squeeze
World.content:
TOI correspondent from Washington:

The clearest sign yet of a widening US-India diplomatic rift came this weekend from the White House and the United Nations, where India was denouncing Pakistan for what it called a litany of âfalsehoodsâ and âdeceit,â even as US President Donald Trump appeared to give those very claims a presidential imprimatur.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had used his UN General Assembly address to revive Islamabadâs account of the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, crediting Trump with a âtimely interventionâ that, he said, prevented a wider war. On Friday night, shortly after Chinaâs President Xi Jinping had departed for Beijing, Trump posted an 87-second excerpt of Sharifâs speech on Truth Social without comment. The clip included Sharifâs praise of Trump and Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir.

The timing was striking. India had just exercised its Right of Reply, with First Secretary Petal Gahlot accusing Islamabad of peddling âfalsehoodsâ and âdeceitâ and describing Pakistan as a âpuppetâ regime. New Delhi has also rejected Trumpâs repeated assertion that he mediated the cessation of hostilities in May 2025, saying the fighting was halted after direct military-to-military communication between India and Pakistan.





For India, however, the larger concern may be less about one Truth Social post than about a pattern. The Xi visit to Washington this week appeared to underscore how dramatically the strategic geometry of US foreign policy has shifted. Rather than organizing its Asia policy principally around building India as a counterweight to China â a two-decade old Washington objective that resulting in an âIndo-Pacificâ focused QUAD â the Trump White House increasingly appears willing to deal with Beijing as a peer whose cooperation is indispensable, and whose confrontation carries costs Trump is reluctant to incur.

Following the Xi visit, Washington and Beijing extended their trade truce and agreed on tariff reductions covering $30 billion of less-sensitive goods in each direction, according reports in the Chinese media. They also operationalized bilateral boards on trade and investment and agreed to pursue an artificial-intelligence dialogue.

Analysts say none of this amounts to a formal US-China condominium, and deep disagreements over Taiwan, technology, trade and strategic competition remain.

But the emerging arrangement has prompted comparisons with a de facto G-2: Washington and Beijing managing their rivalry directly while other powers, including India, find themselves having to adjust to decisions made in a room in which they are not present.

âOne totally unsurprising consequence of this US-China trade truce is that Trump is not even thinking about implementing the Lindsey Graham Russia sanctions legislation he just signed, which would have required penalizing China's support for Russia's war machine,â Tom Malinowski a former New Jersey lawmaker noted, even as Republicans close to Trump have been champing at the bit to punish New Delhi.

The Graham bill, signed by Trump on Sept.

18, gives the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian crude or natural gas under specified conditions. The law specifically covers countries among the five largest Russian oil or gas importers that make new purchases, as well as countries identified among the top facilitators of sanctions evasion.

India is plainly exposed to that provision, as is China. Yet the contrast in Trumpâs handling of the two relationships has become difficult for New Delhi to ignore: Beijing is being courted into a new economic accommodation even as India faces the prospect of punitive trade action.

The message was reinforced this week by a senior State Department official who said the Graham law gives Trump âa new tool in his toolbox,â while emphasizing that its use is not automatic. The official pointed to a broad national-security waiver but added that Washington expects India to help the US end the Ukraine war.

More revealing was the official's description of what Washington now wants from India: not necessarily strategic alignment against China, but access to the enormous Indian energy market.

âWe are looking to also become a huge source of India's energy needs,â the official was quoted as saying, pointing to expanding US hydrocarbon exports and urging faster diversification away from Russian supplies.

All this is consequential because for two decades the bipartisan American strategy had been to help India acquire the economic, military and technological heft to balance China's rise. As recently as May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who will be back in New Delhi in October, was describing India as one of America's most important strategic partners, while US officials continued to characterize New Delhi as a critical Indo-Pacific counterweight.

The language now coming from Washington is noticeably more transactional.

For New Delhi, the resulting unease is not simply about tariffs or Pakistan. It is about whether a strategic partnership painstakingly built across successive administrations is being replaced by a transactional relationship in which China is too powerful to punish, Pakistan is useful to cultivate, and India is expected to accommodate. And as New Delhi watched Washington kiss up to Beijing as an indispensable peer and embrace a country New Delhi views as a terrorism sponsor, the strategic space India once occupied in the American imagination appeared to be shrinking.

World.title: 'Avoids issue of Gen Z voters': Congress attacks EC's 'wishy-washy' press note, seeks pause in SIR
World.content:
"The CEC thinks he can hide behind âbureaucratiseâ and protocol. He stands exposed and is now petrified," claimed Jairam Ramesh

First, the Press note does not directly deny the story or its findings. It makes a defensive attempt to downplay the same in paragraph 3(i) and 3(ii) but does not say that the allegations are baseless.

Second, in the case of Goa, after having been caught out the ECI has sheepishly stated that Form 6 has already been filled out for inclusion by 81 of the 97 deleted voters. To put this another way, you disenfranchise voters through a broken and corrupt system, and when caught say that they are being added back.

Third, it seeks to justify the Commissions actions by appealing to the Order of the Supreme Court dated May 27th, 2026. The Order which was pronounced well before the recent revelations will not save the CEC for the malicious deletion of targeted voters, for the incompetence that has resulted in citizens being wiped off the roles, for the crores lost in both expenses and man-hours due to the confusion and harassment caused to entire families.

Fourth, it extends the deadlines for voter registration in Delhi and Maharashtra. But what happens to the voters of Karnataka and Telangana? What happens to the voters disenfranchised in Bihar and West Bengal? Do the voters of these and other states who were deleted due to one manâs corruption not deserve answers?

Fifth, the Press Release also states the ECI will now involve experts from IIT/IIIT to review the ECINET portal and submit a report to ensure it complies with rules. Aside from being a meaningless safeguard (since the concern is not about the technical soundness but rather the centralization which prevents voter addition at ground level) this confirms the concerns attributed to the two other Election Commissioners per the reportage.

Sixth, the Press Note avoids answering the questions regarding the deliberate targeting of Gen Z voters. The ECI has no answer for its targeted disenfranchisement, beginning mid-July 2026 through wholly illegal changes made to Form 6 (unseen and unapproved by Parliament) which placed an unfair burden on them to find and disclose their parents and/or grandparentsâ details.

NEW DELHI: Congress hit back at the election commission over the statement they issued amid the ongoing SIR row, claiming they're in "damage control mode" and adding that EC didn't deny the media report claims and gave a "wishy washy" statement which "avoids answering the questions regarding the deliberate targeting of Gen Z voters. ""The Election Commission is in damage control mode after it has already caused massive damage to our democracy. It has just issued a wishy-washy Press Note that raises further questions on its intent, integrity, impartiality and credibility," said Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh on X, while sharing his full response to the EC press note.He raised 6 points in his statement as below:Further continuing the party's "vote chori" allegations, he added, "The revelations regarding (1) the unilateral nature of decision making by the CEC, (2) his open hatred and bias against the Opposition resulting in a clear bias, (3) his willing participation and abetment in Vote Chori by the ruling regime, (4) his specific attack to prevent the enrollment of Gen Z voters, (5) his corruption exposed ironically by his negligence in purging and pruning voter lists, needs to be answered for. "Jairam Ramesh also called for suspension of SIR and prosecution against Gyanesh Kumar, saying, "The CEC thinks he can hide behind âbureaucratiseâ and protocol. He stands exposed and is now petrified as an entire country seeks to hold him accountable. The ongoing SIR which has turned to be method of massive disenfranchisement of several crores of India must be suspended immediately without delay. In the meantime, nothing short of the CECâs resignation or prosecution will suffice.Congress has took multiple jabs at EC, since the report of 2 election commissioners disagreeing amid the SIR process came out. In another development, Rahul Gandhi, questioned the EC over former kerala chief secretary Jiji Thomson claimed in a media interview that Gyanesh Kumar approached and asked him to contest on a BJP ticket, even offering a ministerial position. The LoP added to those claims, saying on X, "First, Gyanesh Kumar - then a serving IAS officer - was used to recruit for the BJP. Then Modi and Shah made him the umpire and put him in charge of match-fixing India's elections."This comes as the Election Commission (EC) issued a clarification on Saturday amid reports of differences within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The EC said all decisions on SIR, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously by the Commission.It also announced measures to ease the process for voters who receive notices over unmapped names or discrepancies. BLOs will visit their homes to collect documents, while hearings will be held only in exceptional cases, preferably online.The EC said SIR has been completed in 20 states and UTs, while excluded voters and first-time voters can seek inclusion through continuous updation.The Commission also extended claim and objection deadlines in Delhi and Maharashtra and said an IIT/IIIT expert would be part of a committee reviewing the ECINet system.

World.title: Arguments by serial practitioner of terrorism will not stand: EAM Jaishankar slams Pakistan at UNGA
World.content:
India strongly hit back at Pakistan in the UN General Assembly on Saturday (September 26, 2026), asserting that arguments by the “serial practitioner of terrorism” to normalise the scourge and claim immunity from its consequences will not stand.

“Yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts before this Assembly,” External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said in his address to the General Debate at the high-level 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

Without naming Pakistan or the address by its Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at the UN on Friday (September 25, 2026), Mr. Jaishankar said arguments were invoked to "normalise terrorism, and claim immunity from its consequences."

"That will not stand," he stressed.

“Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised,” Mr. Jaishankar said, asserting that “friendship and goodwill cannot co-exist with terrorism".

“And understandings premised on that will naturally be called into question. It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend its ways,” he said.

Mr. Jaishankar told world leaders that a persistent threat to peace has been the scourge of terrorism. “That this could be state-sponsored, with a cross-border purpose, makes it a direct affront to the global order,” he said.
