World.title: James Reyne has never been Australian Crawl's biggest fan
World.content:
The forthcoming "reunion" of legendary rock band Australian Crawl has been anything but smooth sailing.

In March, founding frontman James Reyne and guitarist Simon Binks filed an application to the Australian Federal Court challenging the acquisition of Australian Crawl trademarks by Bill McDonough, the band's drummer from 1978 to 1983.

James Reyne, Simon Binks and David Reyne in the 1980s. (Supplied)

Three months later, a version of Australian Crawl announced its first Australian tour since splitting in 1986. Reyne and Binks would lead the charge, with former drummers David Reyne and John Watson also onboard.

In September, the ship took on water: Binks bailed, saying he couldn't fit these gargantuan outdoor shows into his schedule.

"No hard feelings but life has merely moved on from the early eighties," the guitarist wrote in a statement.

Loading Instagram content

None of this surprised anyone who'd followed the band's four decades apart, when frosty relationships, and at times outright animosity, were the norm. A reunion was never going to be simple.

Oh no, not you again

Reyne has never been his band's biggest champion, and often regards the songs he wrote as a teenager — even classics like Beautiful People and The Boys Light Up — with a kind of personal cultural cringe.

"Even back then I thought some of the songs were pretty clunky," Reyne says.

"There's a song called Hoochie Gucci Fiorucci Mama. I mean, I wrote it when I was 17 or 18 or something. It's really clunky, lyrically especially. It's a young guy trying to be smart. It's just not smart."

Australian Crawl, seen here performing on Countdown, released a string of multi-platinum albums in the early 1980s before splitting up. (ABC)

Four decades on, that tension lingers. He's grateful fans still cling to these songs; he just doesn't quite get why.

"As I've got older, I find it incredible and quite gratifying to be able to do what I do at my age on the level that I get to do it," he says. "We pull big crowds and I go, 'Really?'"

"There's a song called Reckless that's become quite well known. The crowd will sing every line, and they're louder than the band.

"Recently, I've just gone, 'That's beautiful. I really like that'. I get these genuine, emotional responses to it. Whereas before I used to go, 'Oh, that's some silly old song I wrote when I was a kid'."

Loading Instagram content

Now 69, Reyne has decades of life and musical experience under his belt and feels more confident for it.

"I knew nothing then," he says. "I don't know anything now, but I know a lot more now."

The Australian Crawl album James Reyne doesn't hate

It was all happening for Aussie Crawl in 1983. Bill McDonough left the band, and Angels drummer Buzz Bidstrup stepped in to ensure the band didn't lose any momentum.

A new deal with Geffen Records in America dangled the prize that had eluded peers like Cold Chisel and Mental As Anything: genuine American success.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

It never came. But the pressure forced rare discipline on the band and produced the one record Reyne still rates.

"We made an EP called Semantics, Reckless being one of the songs on that," he says.

With The Boys Light Up, Sirocco and Sons of Beaches already hits in Australia, the band cherry-picked their finest moments for American ears.

"We re-recorded six songs that we'd already released in Australia and added the four songs of the EP to that as an album for America," Reyne says.

"We'd been playing so much by then, that was when we were most cohesive musically."

To Reyne, it's the strongest case for Australian Crawl as a world-class rock'n'roll band.

"That's about the only record of Australian Crawl's I could probably listen to now," he says. "I just think it's well done.

"It's a band that was actually pulling together, because we had this deal and we were smart about it for once. We sat down and thought about it, rather than going, 'let's go and get drunk and do a vocal'. We knew a lot more about being in the studio.

"This was probably the first time we really pulled together as a band and were quite mature about it."

It was a long way from the band's humble beginnings on the Mornington Peninsula.

"The first record we ever made… I can't listen to it now, it's awful," Reyne says.

"I'm not talking about the band, I'm talking about the singing. It's just barely controlled yelling. I didn't know what I was doing."

Things seem to be going right

There will be Australian Crawl shows around Australia starting in October. The rocky road back is, in a way, true to form.

"I always called Australian Crawl my apprenticeship," Reyne says.

"The personal dynamics of being in a band that every band goes through… They can get tricky and they can be interesting and they can be wonderful and they can be supportive…

"It's like having fights with your brother. Sometimes you have a fight, but you would fly in front of a bus for your brother."

Speaking of brothers, David Reyne, better known for The Flying Doctors, Sweet and Sour and The Chantoozies than his brief Crawl stint, returns on percussion and backing vocals.

"My brother was the original drummer in the band, he left because he got accepted into film school in Melbourne when the band hadn't done anything, I don't think we'd even made a demo," Reyne says.

"His role is just to come out and have a whole lot of fun."

Loading...

The rest of the band will feature members of Reyne's solo band — Watson, Brett Kingman, Josh Owen, Andrew McIvor, Sean Johnson, Melinda Jackson and Nicole Kurta — who have been playing Australian Crawl songs for years.

All but three of the initial dates have sold out, with tens of thousands of eager punters ready to use Aussie Crawl as their early soundtrack for summer.

No one is harder on Australian Crawl than James Reyne, but even he has caught the fever surrounding these shows.

" Usually I'm a bit cynical about these things," the frontman says. "But I genuinely feel excited about it. "

The shows will also honour absent friends: guitarists Brad Robinson and Guy McDonough, Bill's brother.

"I really want to pay credit to Brad and Guy, who unfortunately are no longer with us. I just really want to pay total respect and credit to them.

"No bullshit, no agenda. Let's just have a lovely time with some of these funny old songs and let's just really enjoy them. That's my attitude towards it."

Above all, Reyne wants to offer a few hours' reprieve from the doom scroll.

"The world is inundated with bullshit from the minute you wake up to the minute you go to bed. This is hopefully just a really honest experience: you come along and go, 'That was a great thing. I could forget about all this rubbish for a while'."

Australian Crawl's tour begins in Toowoomba on Saturday October 17, before shows around the country throughout October and November.

World.title: Reading fiction has unique benefits for language and empathy
World.content:
For author Melanie Saward, stories are so much more than words.

"I think it's a safe way of confronting the parts of ourselves that we don't often like and that we need to sit with in order to grow," she says.

Dr Saward is a Bigambul and Wakka Wakka woman, academic and publishing all-rounder, who writes across multiple genres including Aboriginal romance novels.

She recognises the power of fiction to unpack biases.

"We all have these biases — I have things that I have to unpack that make me really, really uncomfortable — it's just because of society and how you're raised, your standpoint, and all those things that make you, you.

"Fiction is such a powerful way of privately confronting you with those things."

Melanie Saward's novels include Burn (2023) and Love Unleashed (2024). (Supplied: Jill Kerswill Photography)

Studies show reading can increase empathy as we experience new perspectives and is linked with better brain health, cognition and mental wellbeing.

It is associated with a lower risk of dementia and slower cognitive decline in adults, and better attention, memory, executive function, academic achievement and mental health in children and adolescents.

So how does reading work in the brain?

Reading is an invented skill, according to Lili Yu, senior lecturer of psychological sciences at Macquarie University who studies how people read.

Dr Yu says reading uses parts of the brain, such as our attention and memory systems, we used for other purposes prior to the invention of the skill.

"Because reading is kind of a recent invention, that essentially means the processes involved in reading rely on lots of the cognitive systems we have already," she says.

Loading...

Put simply, when we encounter written text, the first thing our brain observes is the shape, or the "orthographic information", of the word.

We attach that visual information to what the word sounds like, known as the "phonological information".

Then we take those two different forms of information and mentally attach it to the meaning of the word. This is called lexical processing, Dr Yu explains.

Although this is the most common way to read, some people do this process slightly differently.

"Sometimes people see the form and go straight to the meaning, a tendency more commonly seen in logographic scripts like Chinese," she says.

While reading, we're using the same mental processes we would normally use to understand others, says Professor Mar. (Pexels: nam mau)

Reading sentences is more complicated, requiring multiple cognitive systems to work together, including our memory, language and visual processing systems.

Dr Lili Yu says reading can strengthen our memory. It also increases our vocabulary and allows us to better understand nuances between words, she tells All In The Mind.

"The way we organise the words in our head becomes more sophisticated, and we know more of the nuances between different words."

What is Australia's Top 100 book? Vote now Radio National's annual Top 100 books countdown is on. Vote for your favourite 10 books by 1 October, then tune into Radio National on 17-18 October to hear how Australia voted.

Reading narrative fiction comes with its own unique benefits, Raymond Mar, a professor of psychology at York University in Toronto, adds.

"Fiction is a much stronger predictor of verbal abilities than non-fiction," he says.

"We know that language abilities are a great predictor of things like educational achievement and then later on, career achievement and success.

"So, given that we all recognise how important our verbal abilities are, I think it's really interesting that fiction is the one that seems to have the stronger influence."

Despite the benefits of reading for developing language, Australians are reading less than ever before and literacy levels in many OECD countries are declining or stagnating.

Beyond developing literacy, reading introduces us to different perspectives.

The relationship between reading and empathy

Professor Mar says there are two ways stories help us become better at navigating the world we live in.

"We know that reading fiction can help to hone the same sort of mental processes that we use to understand other people, including empathy and perspective-taking."

This effect has been observed in brain studies.

"What we find is parts of the brain that become active while we're reading narrative fiction are the same parts of the brain that are activated when we're trying to understand other people."

Reading can help foster social connections. (Pexels: cottonbro studio)

As reading improves empathy, increasing empathy may improve our reading skills.

"The better our empathy, the better our perspective-taking, the easier it is for us to understand stories," Professor Mar says.

Stories also may contain social knowledge about the world we can learn from.

For example, in one study, adolescents talk about how books helped them reflect on their emotions and gain greater insight into some of the challenging parts of their life.

And for older adults, reading can foster social connection, such as through book clubs.

"Getting together to discuss different perspectives on a novel that everyone's read is a great way to spend time and a great way to bond with others."

The benefits of reading aren't limited to physical books, Professor Mar says.

Listening to audiobooks can also boost empathy.

"The content matters so much more than the modality so I don't think people should feel guilty at all for listening to audiobooks.

"As long as what we have is a representation of other people, their experiences, their interior life, we would see kind of similar results, similar benefits."

Reading to expand your world view

Dr Saward remembers a book that was particularly impactful for her: Claire G Coleman's Terra Nullius.

"It just was a moment where you go, 'Wow, even me, with my brain, I've still got things to unlearn and learn,' and that's kind of exciting.

"I love that every book you pick up could have something like that in there," she says.

Her advice to readers is to diversity your bookshelf.

"Find the thing that you like and then try and find it from a perspective outside your own," she says.

"If it's a hockey romance and you're a straight woman, maybe read one of the queer hockey romances.

" Try and read a little bit outside of your comfort zone, you never know what you might find. "

Listen to All In The Mind to hear the episode and subscribe to the podcast for more stories about mental health and wellbeing.

World.title: Roosters earn shot at perfect NRLW season with win over Canberra
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters are into their third consecutive NRLW grand final after halfback Tarryn Aiken's late try helped subdue the Raiders 20-10 at Sydney Football Stadium.

The final eight minutes of Saturday night's game were fairly frantic, with only a converted try between the sides after a four-pointer by Canberra's England international Hollie-Mae Dodd.

But Aiken might have wanted to ensure her team got to the decider after she missed out last year with an ACL tear.

The Roosters, who led 10-4 at half-time, have made it a celebratory weekend for the Tricolours after the NRL side's preliminary final win over the Dolphins in Brisbane on Friday night.

The Roosters' NRLW team are still nursing the hurt from losing the 2025 decider to the Broncos and would dearly love to add to their 2021 and 2024 premierships in the October 4 grand final.

It only took two minutes for the Roosters to start asserting their dominance.

Winger Jayme Fressard, after missing three matches with a hand injury, accepted a pass from her skipper Isabelle Kelly to score in the left corner.

The Roosters' second came off the back of a penalty against Raiders fullback Sheridan Gallagher for pulling Kelly's hair in stopping her 50-metre line break.

The ensuing set allowed prop Rima Butler through the front door.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

After a Jocelyn Kelleher conversion, the Roosters had sprung to a 10-0 lead.

The Raiders' first points came in the shadow of half-time from a battered and bruised Krystal Blackwell, who had been off the field for a minute to treat a bloody nose and grab a clean jersey.

The five-eighth returned in jersey No.25 and accelerated through a gap set up by her halves partner Zahara Temara to score in the 32nd minute.

In the second half, Blackwell needed the trainer to bring a towel to stem the blood flow.

The Roosters kept the pressure on, with Brydie Parker's boot denying Lili Boyle a try, before a swirling kick by Kelleher was allowed to bounce by Raiders winger Isabella Waterman.

Centre Jessica Sergis swooped to score her 17th try of the season and put the Roosters up 16-4.

Sergis then had a one-on-one steal on Blackwell with the Raiders on the attack as the Green Machine desperately tried to narrow the gap.

They did it with a Chante Temara short pass close to the line for Dodd to bust through to make it 16-10.

But Aiken made sure the Roosters were heading back to the premiership decider with an angled run to the line.

AAP

World.title: 'Trump Strait' post follows Iran offer to reopen peace discussions
World.content:
Iran has proposed a deal to the United States that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week, according to its Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

Mr Araghchi said the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar, and revisited parts of the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.

"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding that it could be done "if the necessary conditions are met".

However, Mr Trump said the US wasn't ready to accept Iran's terms when he spoke to reporters at the White House on Saturday local time.

"I reject the proposal," he said.

Earlier, the Wall Street Journal reported that the 80-year-old president was sceptical that Tehran would meet his demands and added he saw a renewed bombing campaign as likely.

Donald Trump took to Truth Social to rename the strategic waterway. (Supplied: Truth Social)

Mr Trump also posted an image to his Truth Social platform of a map showing the Strait of Hormuz circled and labelled "Trump Strait".

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guard, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."

Iran's plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon, according to Mr Araghchi.

The MOU, signed with the US earlier this year, calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $US12 billion ($17 billion), as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran.

Masoud Pezeshkian, who addressed the UN this week, wants June's MOU revisited. (Reuters: Caitlin Ochs)

On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.

Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian told US broadcaster CBS that the "process will begin from the very day they accept it".

"We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan," he said.

"If the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before.

Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran's nuclear program.

But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.

Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the US sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Russell wins Azerbaijan GP after Piastri disaster in Baku
World.content:
George Russell has claimed a nail-biting victory in Baku, holding off Max Verstappen by just 0.196 seconds to secure his third victory of the season.

Russell, who had never led a race from start to finish before in his career, narrowed the gap to his teammate Kimi Antonelli, who recovered from a 16th place start to finish fifth.

The Englishman was successfully holding Verstappen at arms length right up until the final moments of the last lap, when waved yellow flags for a Valtteri Bottas crash through the old town section of the track saw Russell lose power.

That allowed Verstappen to rapidly close the gap, but the Dutch four-times world champion ran out of time and had to settle for second.

George Russell led from start to finish for the first time in F1. (Getty Images: LAT Image/Alastair Staley)

"The first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing," Russell said.

"After the safety car I saw Max behind me, I knew he wasn't going to make it easy.

"He drove incredibly at the end of the race.

"When the yellow flag came out, I lifted off the power and, when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power.

"Max nearly got me on the line, which would have been a real shame.

"It is amazing to be back on the top step of the podium."

Earlier, Oscar Piastri let a promising position slip, locking up and spinning onto the run off area during his 40th lap to drop from third to 15th.

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 26: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes locks up heavily under braking during the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 26, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Alex Pantling/LAT Images) (Getty Images: Alex Pantling/LAT Images)

The Australian eventually finished in 14th and cut a dejected figure on what was a disappointing day for McLaren.

"I need to go and look because it certainly took me by surprise," Piastri said of his lock up.

"I didn't think I braked super late or super hard, just instantly locked both fronts.

"Just a disappointing end to the day, the first half of the race was very strong, so a shame to not have anything to show from it."

Piastri's teammate Lando Norris crashed out of the race on lap 36 when he was knocked out by the pair of Alpine cars, who collided at Turn One on a restart following a second safety car period of the race.

A turgid opening half of the race gave little indication of the drama to come in the second half.

Piastri, starting third, darted up the inside of Charles Leclerc on the opening corner and then led a procession of the two Red Bulls as Russell disappeared into the distance.

Verstappen appeared to be struggling with his medium tyres but did not allow his teammate Isack Hadjar to overtake, despite plenty of discussion taking place via the pit wall.

The action seemed set to continue in a static holding pattern until Alex Albon sent his car into the wall, precipitating the first safety car.

The restart caused chaos, Franco Colapinto locking up as he darted up the inside of Turn One, collecting teammate Pierre Gasly, who in turn knocked Norris out of the race.

Verstappen, who started eighth on the grid, had already overtaken Piastri at that point to move into second, but it was at the second restart that disaster befell the Australian, Piastri locking up his wheels while defending Hadjar and spinning into the run off area.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: CNN barred from Trump trip after judge strikes down White House ban
World.content:
The White House has signalled that CNN would be left off Air Force One for Donald Trump's upcoming trip, in the latest media restriction from the administration.

The news organisation was replaced by Real America's Voice, a conservative network, for the US president's trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, according to White House guidance.

Mr Trump is scheduled to attend a college football game between the University of Tennessee and the University of Texas at midday Saturday, local time.

The news came just after journalists from CNN, along with MS NOW and Politico — which Mr Trump banned last week from the White House grounds — returned to the executive complex with TV cameras in hand after a judge handed the organisations a reprieve.

Judge orders reversal of Trump's media ban A federal judge has ordered US President Donald Trump to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, saying his ban was likely unconstitutional.

US District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily struck down the ban in an overnight ruling early Thursday, saying it was likely unconstitutional.

Judge Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organisations filed contesting the ban, which argued it violated the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.

The judge's decision addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds but did not directly address pool duties nor Air Force One.

Theodore Boutrous Jr, the news outlets' attorney, did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for comment.

Earlier Friday, on "The Lead with Jake Tapper," Mr Boutrous had said the plaintiffs believed the recent court ruling also covered the issue of pool access.

The White House did not immediately respond to an AP email requesting additional details on the decision.

For a while during the day, the US network video pool for the White House was back in operation for the first time since Mr Trump banned the three news outlets in an extraordinary showdown over media access.

At noon on CNN, viewers could see Mr Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping touring the National Archives, along with Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan, Xi's wife.

It was a routine report from a state visit — except that CNN had not aired live video of Mr Trump in several days.

The pool consists of five major US broadcast outlets that take turns shooting and sharing video.

CNN reporters were allowed back on the White House grounds for Xi Jinping's state visit. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

When the White House banned CNN — which belongs to the pool — from White House grounds, along with MS NOW and Politico, the other four pool providers declined to participate in a show of solidarity.

The spot meant for CNN on the Air Force One flight has long been saved for a member of the US network video pool, which Real America's Voice is not a part of.

CNN did not comment directly earlier Friday, referring instead to its editorial coverage.

But Brian Stelter, the network's media analyst, posted on X that CNN had a pool assignment at the National Archives event and that the White House had approved the network's credentials.

Throughout his second term, Mr Trump has increasingly targeted media outlets whose coverage irritates him, taking administrative or legal action against several.

Early last year, he banished AP reporters from White House events because the organisation was not abiding by his executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America".

The AP's guidance says to acknowledge the new name when relevant.

The case is on appeal after a federal district judge ruled in AP's favour.

The press pool was created decades ago by the White House Correspondents' Association, a group of journalists who cover the president, to make sure a rotating roster always travels with the president.

The pool distributes in-person reports and imagery to the broader press corps and is designed to hold the nation's chief executive accountable on behalf of the American public.

AP/ABC

World.title: In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed
World.content:
Where do you start? How do you confront the challenge of making sense of the 2026 AFL grand final?

Perhaps one's reaction to this game, this nonsensical overdose of a game, can stand as some sort of Rorschach test.

When you look at these pictures, do you see the Brisbane Lions and their titanic force of will, the outrageous talent and nerve, an accomplishment to match any seen in the modern AFL era?

Or do you see Fremantle, inconsolable and bewildered, an unfathomably cruel loss among the most heartbreaking inflicted on a single club in the game's history?

Which of these narratives are you most drawn to? What emotion is drawn out of you most acutely? Because you definitely felt something. Nobody who witnessed this grand final, no matter their allegiances or knowledge of the sport, could claim to have felt nothing.

The Lions celebrate the most incredible grand final victory. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Crucially, you cannot have one without the other. The overwhelming weight of Brisbane's accomplishment needs to fall somewhere, and it just so happened to drop squarely on the soul of the Fremantle Dockers.

We can speak safely about the Dockers here, because you can be sure not one of their long-suffering fans will take the step of entering into this or any other media about this grand final for as long as they live.

There have been close grand finals before, heartbreaking defeats, joy snatched away just as it was poised to erupt. But nothing like this.

As Patrick Voss set off in celebration of his goal, as the bells tolled to signify what must surely be the last ever Wharfie Time and as tears erupted at last from the tortured purple throngs, nobody could possibly have been so heartless as to deny them now.

The next five minutes will go down in football folklore, dissected to the millisecond, but in the immediate aftermath felt like a blur of sound and colour. Charlie Cameron teed up Country Roads, Zac Bailey squeezed one out of nowhere, Logan Morris took the biggest mark and kicked the biggest goal of his life.

In amongst it all was Will Ashcroft, again and again and again. With a ferocity perhaps even he didn't know he was capable of, but with the grace nobody has ever doubted. He willed that team off the canvas, Ashcroft.

He didn't win the medal this time, but make no mistake. This was Will Ashcroft's finest hour.

The Dockers suffered one of the most heartbreaking grand final defeats of all time. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

There wasn't time for Fremantle to process what was happening to them. Suddenly, and without warning, they were bystanders in what was meant to be their own story.

It was gone. It was there; it was theirs. Then it was gone.

Justin Longmuir wept in the coaches' box before the final siren had even sounded. By now, he was as helpless as the many hundreds of thousands of Dockers around the country who wept with him.

They were probably the better team on the day, the Dockers. They obliterated the Lions in the clearances, owned the airways and the territory. The in-house review of the game will be made more galling by the fact the Dockers did so much right.

To the great relief of Fremantle fans and neutrals alike, it was clear within 15 minutes of the first bounce that the grand final lights weren't likely to blind the Dockers.

Fremantle leant on its barometers early. The colossal figures of Josh Treacy and Voss, the unique talents of Luke Jackson, the relentless ferreting energy of Caleb Serong and Andrew Brayshaw.

The Dockers, on an unfamiliar stage, belonged. And with that minor business out of the way, a truly great grand final was allowed to unfurl.

Played in a shoebox, compressed at times within an inch of its life, the brief moments of game-breaking skill elevated the contest. Morris's invisible but very real handball to Kai Lohmann, Murphy Reid making up for an error with the cleanest hands imaginable, Conor McKenna seeing an angle few others could.

Hayden Young turned the tide with two third-quarter goals. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The first little sign of concern for Freo came in the third quarter, after a period of dominance that produced more behinds than goals. Windows of opportunity are rare in grand finals such as this, and when Charlie Cameron kicked the Lions in front, it felt like the Dockers had missed a big one.

But even then, Fremantle had an answer. Hayden Young, outstanding on the day, kicked two sensational goals to turn the tide again. The Lions were throwing punches, the Dockers were wearing them and sending them back.

The Dockers were winning the arm wrestle in the last. Treacy's miss from the goal square was set right by Voss's true set shot minutes later. For all intents and purposes, they had at last put the Lions away.

Was Wharfie Time a mistake? Another of the great unknowns about this game. It's cursed forever now, those bells now more likely to trigger an untimely bout of PTSD than to inspire the Freo faithful.

What is also certain is that the Lions fed off it, saw it as a sign the Dockers had an eye on celebrations when five decisive minutes remained on the clock.

These Lions, of course, need no invitation. The self-belief and composure and character required to win this premiership — a journey that extended well beyond those final five minutes or this grand final or even the start of the season — is the envy of the entire AFL.

The Lions enjoy the three-peat spoils. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

One problem with dynastic greatness in sport is you can sometimes run out of things to talk about. Once you've ascended to the peak and set up camp, the story of how you got there can lose its lustre.

They'll tell this story forever. The day the Lions won the unwinnable, the day the world collapsed upon the Dockers, among the greatest and most horrible days footy has ever seen.

World.title: Australian senators summon OpenAI boss as hack expands beyond Medicare
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaOpenAI Australian senators summon OpenAI boss as hack expands beyond Medicare Brittany Busch September 27, 2026 — 12:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian senators are demanding OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman appear before a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence as the tech giant reveals its rogue agents have hacked dozens more organisations around the globe. OpenAI confirmed on Friday (US time) its bots had infiltrated United States government websites and leaked more than 50 ChatGPT user photos just days after Anthony Albanese revealed to the world the company had hacked Medicare. The prime minister on Saturday pointed to the broadening security breaches as more evidence humans risked losing control of the technology without a co-ordinated international response, while insisting the AI rollout was inevitable and Australia must get on board. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addressed the US hack fresh off his flight from New York. ABC News Albanese has been walking a tightrope between muscling up to tech giants – with the teen social media ban, a digital duty of care and now the OpenAI hack – and racing to shore up data centre investment worth billions of dollars to the Australian economy.



But the rollout is facing backlash from communities, which have last week railed against the expansion of the towering facilities in Australia’s suburbs in a Greens-led Senate inquiry. The inquiry is now summoning Altman and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to appear on Thursday to answer questions about their companies’ growing footprint in Australia, and the Medicare hack. “This can’t all be done behind closed doors – the public has a right to know what went on here,” committee chair and Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said. The inquiry does not have the power to compel foreigners to appear, but it could turn up the pressure on their Australian representatives if the chief executives refuse to front. Hanson-Young said while the tech leaders warned their agents posed an existential threat to humanity, they were also lobbying the Australian government to water down copyright laws and grant them access to domestic resources.



“If they truly believe their own warnings, they must front up, face the Senate’s questions and

have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should

look like,” the Greens communications spokeswoman said. Related Article Opinion

AI Why Australia simply cannot afford to miss this AI wave Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Albanese said on Saturday Australia had acted in its national interest in going public with the Medicare breach, and he was unsurprised the autonomous agents had struck again. He called on OpenAI to explain the burgeoning number of security incidents. “We now know that it wasn’t just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation, but that there are dozens of cases, including US government sites,” the prime minister said, speaking on his return to Sydney from the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “You can’t stop it happening. It’s here now and the revelations this week just confirmed this.”



Albanese said international collaboration would be essential to ensuring human control was maintained as AI technology rapidly developed. “The key risk is humans not being in charge of the rollout,” he said. In a lengthy blog post on Friday (US time), OpenAI said it had notified dozens of organisations that its agents may have bypassed security controls, impaired availability or “negatively impacted” websites. Sam Altman, addressing the UN Security Council in New York earlier this week, is in the spotlight as his company comes under intense scrutiny. Bloomberg The tech giant also disclosed agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. The company did not clarify if the images were AI-generated or identified real people, or when the images were posted.





Altman dodged questions from this masthead about the Medicare hack earlier this week, refusing to apologise or explain why it took months for OpenAI to detect and report the intrusion. However, in a social media post on Friday (US time), Altman admitted that OpenAI had not been prompt enough in keeping affected organisations informed. “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organisations,” he said in the post. View post on X Albanese announced earlier this week that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to a Medicare portal in June, using the hack to highlight at the UN the urgent need for countries to develop standards to ensure that AI worked for people, not the other way around.



While the agent broke into a defunct database and did not access any personal information, it still marked one of the first publicly disclosed cases of an AI agent breaking into a government website. Loading The prime minister is increasingly at odds with Donald Trump over the issue, with the US president remaining a staunch believer AI companies should continue developing their technology without the fetters of excessive regulation. The Coalition has argued Labor needs to urgently obtain the most advanced US frontier AI models to bolster Australia’s cybersecurity defences. Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said on Saturday morning the breach was more likely a “cock-up” than a conspiracy, but Australia could not bank on the next hack being as benign.



Related Article Exclusive

AI ChatGPT’s evil twin: How criminals and extremists are using AI to lay traps “I’m a little bit worried that the government’s using this as an opportunity to finger-wag at the big tech companies, or try and gazump Donald Trump on the world stage,” she told 2GB. “This is the wake-up call that we need. We’ve got to make sure that we get those AI companies working with Australia, not imposing ridiculous rules upon them that they simply will not abide by, which means that they go and set up elsewhere.” The New York Times reported OpenAI’s agents gained unauthorised access to the US Department of Education, the Department of Commerce and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). OpenAI confirmed the Commerce Department and SEC incidents, while saying the investigation into the Department of Education breach was ongoing.

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Michelle Stillman Why has the quiz changed?



Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Tell us what you think about the new experience here. We’re keen to hear from you. Although it has a new look, this is the same Superquiz you know and love. Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? World.title: Roosters book third consecutive grand final spot with victory against Raiders
World.content:
SportNRLNRLW 2026 Roosters book third consecutive grand final spot with victory against Raiders Billie Eder September 26, 2026 — 9:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Roosters will have two teams come grand final, with John Strange’s NRLW side booking their October 4 spot less than 24 hours after Trent Robinson’s men did the same up in Brisbane. The Tricolours prevailed 20-10 in a dramatic preliminary final against Canberra at Allianz Stadium on Saturday night, that included hair pulls and bloodied faces. It will be the Tricolours’ third consecutive NRLW grand final, after their 2024 premiership and 2025 heartbreak, where they will meet the winner on Sunday’s clash between the Gold Coast and Brisbane. It took the 2026 minor premiers just two minutes to score their first try on Saturday, but they were in real jeopardy of losing their first game of the season until the final moments of the match, when halfback Tarryn Aiken sealed the deal, scoring with two minutes to spare.



“It was good, it’s what we needed,” Roosters coach John Strange said after the match. “Haven’t played a game in 16 days, and the girls were definitely feeling that – the match fitness, sort of not having it. But that’s definitely what we needed going into the grand final next Sunday.” Tarryn Aiken scores the try that seals the deal for the Roosters. Getty Images Their narrow victory means the Roosters remain undefeated this year, with their only loss in the past two years coming in the 2025 grand final against Brisbane. When Canberra’s Chante Temara put Hollie-Mae Dodd across in the second half, there were 10 minutes left in the match with just one converted try the difference, but an epic from Jess Sergis and Aiken’s late try quashed any concerns of an upset.



When Roosters winger Jayme Fressard scored in the second minute of the match, it was entirely possible for a finely-tuned Roosters side to deal some heavy damage ahead of the grand final. But after teammate Rima Butler barged across in the 19th minute, the Raiders fought back while the Roosters attack fell to pieces. Five-eighth Krystal Blackwell scored the Raiders’ opening try – an impressive feat given she was left bloodied enough by a head clash with Rima Butler that she had to change her jersey mid-way through the first half. Krystal Blackwell scores after getting banged up in a head clash. NRL Images



After the Raiders played a set a woman down, as Blackwell changed into the No.25 jersey, she returned to score a beauty that kept her team in the game. Fressard was left banged up trying to make the tackle on Blackwell and did not return for the second half with a shoulder injury. It’s a worry for the Roosters on grand final day, with Fressard – a NSW representative – only just making her return from a hand injury. “She’ll go for scans tomorrow on the shoulder,” Strange said. “Just had a quick chat to her there, she’s pretty positive, but we’ll see what it comes back with. Looks like an AC joint injury at the moment.” The Roosters celebrate Rima Butler’s try. Getty Images Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly was on her way to a long-range try earlier in the half, before she was brought to ground by her hair by Canberra fullback Sheridan Gallagher.



Related Article NRLW 2026 Corban and her son started playing league in the same year. Now they’ve both called time Gallagher was lucky enough to avoid the sin bin despite it appearing to be an act of foul play. “I don’t think it should have been a penalty try, I think it should have been 10 in the bin as a professional foul,” Strange said. “I’ve got no idea what a professional foul is then, if that’s not one.” Canberra’s Lili Boyle was controversially denied an equaliser with 24 minutes left in the match because Roosters winger Brydie Parker had her foot under the ball, which Canberra coach Darryn Borthwick said could have swung momentum in the Raiders’ favour had it been awarded.



“Every day of the week [that’s a try]. Our game is going crazy,” said Borthwick. “We looked at it 10 times, and she got the ball down. I find that hard to believe it wasn’t awarded a try.” Sergis gave the team some breathing room with a try from an impressive kick chase after Canberra winger Isabella Waterman let the ball bounce. And, despite a quiet night from Aiken and halves partner Jocelyn Kelleher, the Roosters No.7 made it count when they needed her most, scoring to seal her team’s spot in the final. World.title: ‘Time is of the essence’: Melbourne hiker, 30, missing for days in remote Peru mountains
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMissing person ‘Time is of the essence’: Melbourne hiker, 30, missing for days in remote Peru mountains Eleanor Campbell September 26, 2026 — 9:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Peruvian rescue team is scouring a remote part of the mountains for a Melbourne man who set out on a solo hike 13 days ago and has not been heard from since. Jordan Yap (right) with his partner Anita. Jordan Yap, 30, embarked on a hiking trip through the remote Huayhuash mountain range on September 14. He told friends and family he was going to be off the grid for 10 days to complete the high-altitude trek, but failed to check in back at his hotel and missed a scheduled flight several days later. Family reported him missing after he failed to check in with his partner, Anita. Private rescuers later told them that other hikers last reported seeing him on day three of his hike.



“It is extremely out of character for him to be out of contact, and if he could manage to, he would know how worried we all are and make every effort to get a message across,” Anita said. “So that’s why we’re very, very worried right now.” Jordan (right) pictured with a friend. Supplied The Huayhuash circuit is known for its steep, rugged terrain and is considered one of Peru’s most challenging mountain routes. According to his family, Jordan is an experienced traveller and previously solo hiked across Australia, China, Turkey and Jordan. “He’s an avid outdoor person. In winter time, he will spend most weekends on the snow field, even though he didn’t have a lot of luck with the weather, he loves hiking,” Jordan’s father, Vinh Dao, said.



Before leaving for Peru, Jordan attempted to find other people to join him on the trek, but decided to go on his own when no one was available. Jordan Yap (left) works as a food regulation specialist for a dairy company. After struggling to get in contact with Peruvian authorities to help search for their son, the family hired local mountain rescue organisation, Socorro Andino Peruano. The family said a rescue team was deployed Friday at 3am Melbourne time. Vinh said he and his wife were preparing to fly to Peru and are urging the Australian government and the Department of Foreign Affairs to liaise with local authorities to assist with search efforts.



“We’re very concerned. While we’ve had some progress we’d really like it for DFAT to apply pressure on the local police and the government because time is of the essence, and it’s really critical now,” Vinh said. A DFAT spokesperson said they were providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Peru. World.title: This Lion pulled off the tackle of the grand final, but he barely remembers it
World.content:
The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories .

In the grand final briefing, your wrap of footy news Brisbane Lions defender Ryan Lester says his goal-saving tackle on Josh Treacy is little more than a blur.

The Brisbane Lions can thank Charlie Cameron for making “Wharfie Time” a grand final flop.

Retiring Fremantle forward Sam Switkowski prefers a titanic, heartbreaking defeat to Brisbane to being on the wrong end of a one-sided drubbing.

Fremantle are shattered for captain Alex Pearce, whose devastating game-ending Achilles injury in the Dockers’ heartbreaking grand final defeat will likely also eat into his 2027 campaign. The desperate tackle that halted Freo’s premiership momentum Hannah Kennelly

Brisbane’s Ryan Lester was desperate. With less than seven minutes to go in the final quarter, Fremantle’s Josh Treacy sprinted towards goal and looked certain to extend the Dockers’ lead and help them clinch their maiden premiership.



But Lester was right behind him. The 34-year-old launched himself towards Treacy’s legs, performing a tackle that left the Docker flat on his back and sent his kick wayward, preventing what would have been a crucial goal. Standing wide-eyed in the beer-soaked change rooms after the Lions’ extraordinary seven-point win on Saturday afternoon, Lester was lost for words when asked about the tackle. “Oh God, I don’t even know what happened,” he told this masthead. “I got him and the rest is a bit of a blur.” With his daughter Georgie clutching his leg, Lester said he found it difficult to articulate the magnitude of what the Lions had just achieved. In the early 2000s, the Lions achieved a historic hat-trick under Leigh Matthews. Fast-forward 23 years, and Chris Fagan’s team have repeated history, clinching a third straight premiership and cementing themselves in AFL history.



The significance was not lost on Lester. “Growing up, I looked at the Brisbane Lions and Hawthorn and those teams were just immortal … like unbelievable, and for us to join them is pretty cool,” he said. “Particularly for me, like in 2022, I only played three games in the senior team ... so I feel really lucky the way my career has turned out and so lucky to be a part of this special team.” When the bells from AC/DC’s Hells Bells blared, and with huge waves crashing on the big screen, Fremantle fans in the crowd rose to mark “Wharfie Time”. But Lester said the Lions were ready.



“We spoke about that [Wharfie Time] and then we tried to obviously use that for their motivation,” he said. Related Article Updated

AFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented Bomber turned Lion Sam Draper said the team had rehearsed for Wharfie Time and they were prepared for a hostile crowd. “We thought when they hit that trigger, that’s when we go up a notch,” Draper confirmed. “I think the boys responded well. I think like last week we handled that well [against Hawthorn]. That was a hostile environment, and today the same.



“So, yeah, the boys went crazy at the end of there.” Just 12 months ago, Draper was preparing to leave Essendon and enter the trade period as an unrestricted free agent, after another injury-plagued year at the Hangar including a devastating Achilles rupture in mid-April that ended his season. On Sunday, he stood with a premiership medal around his neck and was overcome with emotion. “It doesn’t feel real,” he said.“I got really emotional towards the end when I saw the high-performance team,” he said referencing his bought of injuries. “I just thanked them for believing in me.”



Charlie seizes his moment and history Marc McGowan

The Brisbane Lions can thank Charlie Cameron for making “Wharfie Time” a grand final flop. The evergreen small forward kicked the opening goal of the match – before unleashing his engine-revving celebration as Take Me Home, Country Roads blared across the MCG – but it was his third that turned the game. Charlie Cameron of the Lions celebrates kicking a goal. AFL Photos via Getty Images Eighty-one seconds after Fremantle cult hero Patrick Voss thought he had blasted through the sealer, Cameron swooped and snapped truly. It provided a swift end to Wharfie Time, the Dockers’ trademark fan-driven activation, which the AFL approved them to use just once in the match.



“As a forward, your job is about creating opportunities and moments,” Cameron told this masthead. “I was like, ‘If I get an opportunity here, I’m going to back myself in’. That’s the good thing about playing finals footy – you get the spotlight to showcase yourself, and when I had that snap, I was like, ‘I’m ready to go again, give me another one’.” Charlie Cameron takes his opportunity. Joe Armao Cameron needn’t have worried. Zac Bailey kicked another shortly after before Logan Morris became the match-winner with the last two goals to transform what had largely been a dirty day for him until then. These Lions now join Leigh Matthews’ and Michael Voss’ 2001-03 immortal teams as three-peat premiers.



Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Lion who scored a perfect 10 – and the Docker who scored just one: AFL grand final player ratings Cameron has played a major role in Brisbane becoming a juggernaut under Chris Fagan, including 410 goals – 64 in finals – in 208 matches for the club. “We spoke about it at the start of the year – do we want to go for a three-peat?” he said. “We said, ‘We have the opportunity here [to create history], with the list we have’, and it just came down to a lot of hard work. It’s pretty crazy to be a three-time, back-to-back-to-back premiership player. It’s unbelievable.” Retiring Docker proud despite devastating grand final loss



Steve Barrett

Retiring Fremantle forward Sam Switkowski accepted how cruel football can be, but would still prefer Saturday’s titanic, heartbreaking defeat to Brisbane to being on the wrong end of a one-sided drubbing. Despite the harrowing result and narrow margin, Switkowski can walk off with his head held high one last time. Retiring Docker Sam Switkowski. AFL Photos “I think we all know footy can be cruel like that,” he said after his 131st and last game. “But I’d still rather the way the game played out than have lost by 10 goals.



“It’s a bit hard to get over the disappointment and devastation of it, but I’m just so proud of everyone gave it their all. “I haven’t been in this position before, clearly – grand final loss, career’s at an end. “But I’m just so proud to have played nine years at this club.” Switkowski spoke with emotion, before walking over to Fremantle great Nat Fyfe – who he now joins in the retired footballers club – for a warm embrace. “I said to the guys in the rooms, after ‘JL’ [coach Justin Longmuir] spoke, that I’m so proud of each and every one of them.



Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Dockers had one hand on the premiership cup. Then came four minutes that turned the grand final “I thanked them for their efforts this season and giving it everything today. “I feel like we gave that our best shot. “I thought we played a Freo brand of footy. We would accept whatever the result is if we did that. “I’m trying to get a bit of perspective and know you’d rather be here today and hurt than not be here at all.”



Wingman Corey Wagner could almost touch and feel the club’s maiden flag – as Patrick Voss’ goal deep into the fourth quarter stretched the Dockers’ lead to 17 points – before it was brutally snatched out of the Dockers’ grasp. “It’s a hard pill to swallow,” Wagner said. “It was that close you could almost grab it and feel it. “The crowd was going nuts and you could almost believe it was going to happen. “We were thinking ‘we’re going to bring it home to Freo’.”



Wagner conceded the Lions played those crunch-time final stages better than the Dockers. “I don’t think we handled the last three minutes as good as we should have,” he said. “Credit to Brisbane – they’ve been here, they’ve done it and they’ve seen these moments before. “Brisbane had to come through this situation [2023 grand final loss to Collingwood] before having their three-peat.” Star midfielder Andrew Brayshaw was confident his team would learn and burn from this, but knows – from his own family’s experience – that contesting multiple grand finals isn’t guaranteed.



Related Article AFL grand final Lachie Neale is used to being the villain. He stepped up in ‘go time’ of a heist for the ages “I feel like we’ve got all the pieces in place, but you never want to assume you’ll be back,” he said. “My brother [Angus] played in one grand final [Melbourne, 2021] and thought he’d be back every year, but it ended up being his only one. “We don’t want to get complacent at all. This will light the fire in the belly, for sure. “We’ll fight, we’ll scrap and we’ll earn our way back in.



“It will make it even more sweet when we get back and get it done.” Freo skipper’s game-ending injury likely to cut into 2027 AAP

Fremantle are shattered for captain Alex Pearce, whose devastating game-ending Achilles injury in the Dockers’ heartbreaking grand final defeat will likely also eat into his 2027 campaign. Alex Pearce was on crutches after the game. AFL Photos With Fremantle leading by nine points in Saturday’s decider at the MCG, Pearce was racing Brisbane opponent Logan Morris to collect a loose ball on the wing when he dramatically fell to the ground without any contact.



The star defender suffered a right Achilles injury, was assisted off the field and watched from the bench as Fremantle capitulated and Morris kicked the winning goal. The Dockers confirmed the dreaded Achilles injury, which will likely also sideline Pearce for a large chunk of 2027 if it is fully ruptured. “He’s putting on a brave face,” coach Justin Longmuir said. “Everyone’s devastated. I’m sure he’s devastated, not only for today’s result, but it looks like it might cost him a bit of time on the sidelines and another stint in rehab. “But he can hold his head up high. Like he’s led us so well across the course of the year, and stood up in really key moments to allow us to get here.



Related Article Updated

AFL grand final Honoured, but surprised: Why Shai Bolton took off his medal right after winning the Norm Smith “Unfortunately it didn’t go his way today and I feel for him on that front.” Longmuir said Pearce was “sore” coming into the game but adamant that didn’t contribute to his injury. Pearce, 31, was heartbreakingly close to becoming Fremantle’s first premiership captain while the Dockers will wonder what might have been if they had their best key defender out there late. “[We had to] reshuffle the deck chairs a little bit,” Longmuir said.

World.title: Lachie Neale is used to being the villain. He stepped up in ‘go time’ of a heist for the ages
World.content:
SportAFLAFL grand final Lachie Neale is used to being the villain. He stepped up in ‘go time’ of a heist for the ages Peter Ryan September 26, 2026 — 8:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories . Loading

An outsized focus on Lachie Neale had become the new norm at the Brisbane Lions in 2026. Not only was he in the centre circle when the heat was on, as he had been ever since starting with the Dockers in 2013, he was suddenly the central character in a sporting drama – attracting tabloid headlines to gossip columns to trade speculation. Lachie Neale was swamped by his Lions teammates after the grand final. AFL Photos So, when the news came through he had been suspended for the grand final for punching Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the guts, there was surprise, but no panic. Football boss Danny Daly went to work to try to clear him, while also arranging contingency plans to send the dual Brownlow medallist to Naracoorte in South Australia to be with his dad Robbie if Thursday’s appeal failed.



But Neale didn’t need to implement those plans after all – the appeals board overturning the suspension, allowing him to play in his fifth grand final. Neale copped an initial one-game ban for this gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. Getty Images, Fox Footy The lead-up, plus his status as a former Docker, meant Neale was always going to be the villain on grand final day. For the sort of people who indulge in booing, it was a matter of picking their reason. Those boos rang out loud and clear as soon as Neale entered the arena at the nine-minute mark after starting the third of his five grand finals on the bench. He didn’t care.



Related Article Updated

AFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented “I don’t give a shit about that, whatever,” he said. “I used to play for them as well, which probably added to it. “It’s part of the game – honestly it doesn’t bother me.” Neale didn’t take over like he did in the second half the previous year, when he came on at half-time as the “super-sub” when the scores were level, finishing the match with 17 touches in a half.



On this occasion, his hands were quick when the ball was in his vicinity, and his mind was willing, but his Dockers opponents were able to find too much space at centre bounces and dominated. Editor's pick Analysis

AFL grand final Wharfie Time and Fagan’s heroes chime Freo’s doom in one of the greatest grand finals Neale was on for short bursts. But the clearances had been few and far between when the Dockers opened up what looked like a matchwinning 17-point lead with less than five minutes remaining and with Neale sitting on the pine. “Wharfie Time” then made the MCG erupt as Neale rose to his 177-centimetre height and took a breath.



He joined Will Ashcroft, Josh Dunkley and Sam Draper in the middle to see if they could pull off the biggest heist in grand final history. He said they had planned for “Wharfie Time” to be “go time”. “The mentality to switch that, and it be ‘go time’ for us, was important,” Neale said. “‘Fages’ once described us as cockroaches – we just don’t die.” Loading



Neale won the first touch and Ashcroft rose with him. It was his career at the Lions writ large as he lifted them off the canvas after joining the club back in 2019. He won’t be there next season, confirming post-match that this was his last game for the Lions. “I’ve loved my time at this club, they are an exceptional club,” he told Seven before his expected move to Collingwood in the coming weeks. “It’s been the best eight years of my life. It’s been an incredible ride. I love this group, [and] I’m going to miss them every much.” Neale’s teammates knew what he had given them, with Ashcroft saying, “I love him so much”, while Jarrod Berry admitted so much attention being on Neale wasn’t a bad thing for his teammates. Neale is used to it by now.



“Unfortunately, I have had experience in compartmentalising things and getting on with the job,” Neale said. Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Lion who scored a perfect 10 – and the Docker who scored just one: AFL grand final player ratings With 20 touches and a third consecutive premiership medal, his job was done. He hugged his dad and kissed his new girlfriend, Emma Field, and stood with a can of beer in his hand. “In a weird way, it’s a strength of mine – my resilience on the field and off the field,” Neale explained. “There are people doing it a lot worse than me. I have won my third premiership at an amazing organisation, so I can’t really complain.



“I have just got to get on with the job and try to be better as a human, and as a footballer.” There was no room for pride, he said, but he had kept at it as the Lions asked him to when all was exploding around him. Club president Andrew Wellington could only praise Neale, and the rest of the club, for how they prevailed in such circumstances. “There is always risk, when you have got a bit of turmoil, that it can affect [you] ... but credit to all the leaders, including Lachie, that they did not let that disturb what they were trying to do,” Wellington said. “Everyone just asked him, [that] as long as he is with us, he gives us everything, and he has done that.”

World.title: Australian senators summon OpenAI boss as hack expands beyond Medicare
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaOpenAI Australian senators summon OpenAI boss as hack expands beyond Medicare Brittany Busch September 27, 2026 — 12:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian senators are demanding OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman appear before a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence as the tech giant reveals its rogue agents have hacked dozens more organisations around the globe. OpenAI confirmed on Friday (US time) its bots had infiltrated United States government websites and leaked more than 50 ChatGPT user photos just days after Anthony Albanese revealed to the world the company had hacked Medicare. The prime minister on Saturday pointed to the broadening security breaches as more evidence humans risked losing control of the technology without a co-ordinated international response, while insisting the AI rollout was inevitable and Australia must get on board. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addressed the US hack fresh off his flight from New York. ABC News Albanese has been walking a tightrope between muscling up to tech giants – with the teen social media ban, a digital duty of care and now the OpenAI hack – and racing to shore up data centre investment worth billions of dollars to the Australian economy.



But the rollout is facing backlash from communities, which have last week railed against the expansion of the towering facilities in Australia’s suburbs in a Greens-led Senate inquiry. The inquiry is now summoning Altman and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to appear on Thursday to answer questions about their companies’ growing footprint in Australia, and the Medicare hack. “This can’t all be done behind closed doors – the public has a right to know what went on here,” committee chair and Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said. The inquiry does not have the power to compel foreigners to appear, but it could turn up the pressure on their Australian representatives if the chief executives refuse to front. Hanson-Young said while the tech leaders warned their agents posed an existential threat to humanity, they were also lobbying the Australian government to water down copyright laws and grant them access to domestic resources.



“If they truly believe their own warnings, they must front up, face the Senate’s questions and

have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should

look like,” the Greens communications spokeswoman said. Related Article Opinion

AI Why Australia simply cannot afford to miss this AI wave Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Albanese said on Saturday Australia had acted in its national interest in going public with the Medicare breach, and he was unsurprised the autonomous agents had struck again. He called on OpenAI to explain the burgeoning number of security incidents. “We now know that it wasn’t just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation, but that there are dozens of cases, including US government sites,” the prime minister said, speaking on his return to Sydney from the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “You can’t stop it happening. It’s here now and the revelations this week just confirmed this.”



Albanese said international collaboration would be essential to ensuring human control was maintained as AI technology rapidly developed. “The key risk is humans not being in charge of the rollout,” he said. In a lengthy blog post on Friday (US time), OpenAI said it had notified dozens of organisations that its agents may have bypassed security controls, impaired availability or “negatively impacted” websites. Sam Altman, addressing the UN Security Council in New York earlier this week, is in the spotlight as his company comes under intense scrutiny. Bloomberg The tech giant also disclosed agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. The company did not clarify if the images were AI-generated or identified real people, or when the images were posted.





Altman dodged questions from this masthead about the Medicare hack earlier this week, refusing to apologise or explain why it took months for OpenAI to detect and report the intrusion. However, in a social media post on Friday (US time), Altman admitted that OpenAI had not been prompt enough in keeping affected organisations informed. “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organisations,” he said in the post. View post on X Albanese announced earlier this week that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to a Medicare portal in June, using the hack to highlight at the UN the urgent need for countries to develop standards to ensure that AI worked for people, not the other way around.



While the agent broke into a defunct database and did not access any personal information, it still marked one of the first publicly disclosed cases of an AI agent breaking into a government website. Loading The prime minister is increasingly at odds with Donald Trump over the issue, with the US president remaining a staunch believer AI companies should continue developing their technology without the fetters of excessive regulation. The Coalition has argued Labor needs to urgently obtain the most advanced US frontier AI models to bolster Australia’s cybersecurity defences. Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said on Saturday morning the breach was more likely a “cock-up” than a conspiracy, but Australia could not bank on the next hack being as benign.



Related Article Exclusive

AI ChatGPT’s evil twin: How criminals and extremists are using AI to lay traps “I’m a little bit worried that the government’s using this as an opportunity to finger-wag at the big tech companies, or try and gazump Donald Trump on the world stage,” she told 2GB. “This is the wake-up call that we need. We’ve got to make sure that we get those AI companies working with Australia, not imposing ridiculous rules upon them that they simply will not abide by, which means that they go and set up elsewhere.” The New York Times reported OpenAI’s agents gained unauthorised access to the US Department of Education, the Department of Commerce and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). OpenAI confirmed the Commerce Department and SEC incidents, while saying the investigation into the Department of Education breach was ongoing.

World.title: Roosters book third consecutive grand final spot with victory against Raiders
World.content:
SportNRLNRLW 2026 Roosters book third consecutive grand final spot with victory against Raiders Billie Eder September 26, 2026 — 9:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Roosters will have two teams come grand final, with John Strange’s NRLW side booking their October 4 spot less than 24 hours after Trent Robinson’s men did the same up in Brisbane. The Tricolours prevailed 20-10 in a dramatic preliminary final against Canberra at Allianz Stadium on Saturday night, that included hair pulls and bloodied faces. It will be the Tricolours’ third consecutive NRLW grand final, after their 2024 premiership and 2025 heartbreak, where they will meet the winner on Sunday’s clash between the Gold Coast and Brisbane. It took the 2026 minor premiers just two minutes to score their first try on Saturday, but they were in real jeopardy of losing their first game of the season until the final moments of the match, when halfback Tarryn Aiken sealed the deal, scoring with two minutes to spare.



“It was good, it’s what we needed,” Roosters coach John Strange said after the match. “Haven’t played a game in 16 days, and the girls were definitely feeling that – the match fitness, sort of not having it. But that’s definitely what we needed going into the grand final next Sunday.” Tarryn Aiken scores the try that seals the deal for the Roosters. Getty Images Their narrow victory means the Roosters remain undefeated this year, with their only loss in the past two years coming in the 2025 grand final against Brisbane. When Canberra’s Chante Temara put Hollie-Mae Dodd across in the second half, there were 10 minutes left in the match with just one converted try the difference, but an epic from Jess Sergis and Aiken’s late try quashed any concerns of an upset.



When Roosters winger Jayme Fressard scored in the second minute of the match, it was entirely possible for a finely-tuned Roosters side to deal some heavy damage ahead of the grand final. But after teammate Rima Butler barged across in the 19th minute, the Raiders fought back while the Roosters attack fell to pieces. Five-eighth Krystal Blackwell scored the Raiders’ opening try – an impressive feat given she was left bloodied enough by a head clash with Rima Butler that she had to change her jersey mid-way through the first half. Krystal Blackwell scores after getting banged up in a head clash. NRL Images



After the Raiders played a set a woman down, as Blackwell changed into the No.25 jersey, she returned to score a beauty that kept her team in the game. Fressard was left banged up trying to make the tackle on Blackwell and did not return for the second half with a shoulder injury. It’s a worry for the Roosters on grand final day, with Fressard – a NSW representative – only just making her return from a hand injury. “She’ll go for scans tomorrow on the shoulder,” Strange said. “Just had a quick chat to her there, she’s pretty positive, but we’ll see what it comes back with. Looks like an AC joint injury at the moment.” The Roosters celebrate Rima Butler’s try. Getty Images Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly was on her way to a long-range try earlier in the half, before she was brought to ground by her hair by Canberra fullback Sheridan Gallagher.



Related Article NRLW 2026 Corban and her son started playing league in the same year. Now they’ve both called time Gallagher was lucky enough to avoid the sin bin despite it appearing to be an act of foul play. “I don’t think it should have been a penalty try, I think it should have been 10 in the bin as a professional foul,” Strange said. “I’ve got no idea what a professional foul is then, if that’s not one.” Canberra’s Lili Boyle was controversially denied an equaliser with 24 minutes left in the match because Roosters winger Brydie Parker had her foot under the ball, which Canberra coach Darryn Borthwick said could have swung momentum in the Raiders’ favour had it been awarded.



“Every day of the week [that’s a try]. Our game is going crazy,” said Borthwick. “We looked at it 10 times, and she got the ball down. I find that hard to believe it wasn’t awarded a try.” Sergis gave the team some breathing room with a try from an impressive kick chase after Canberra winger Isabella Waterman let the ball bounce. And, despite a quiet night from Aiken and halves partner Jocelyn Kelleher, the Roosters No.7 made it count when they needed her most, scoring to seal her team’s spot in the final. World.title: ‘Time is of the essence’: Melbourne hiker, 30, missing for days in remote Peru mountains
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMissing person ‘Time is of the essence’: Melbourne hiker, 30, missing for days in remote Peru mountains Eleanor Campbell September 26, 2026 — 9:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Peruvian rescue team is scouring a remote part of the mountains for a Melbourne man who set out on a solo hike 13 days ago and has not been heard from since. Jordan Yap (right) with his partner Anita. Jordan Yap, 30, embarked on a hiking trip through the remote Huayhuash mountain range on September 14. He told friends and family he was going to be off the grid for 10 days to complete the high-altitude trek, but failed to check in back at his hotel and missed a scheduled flight several days later. Family reported him missing after he failed to check in with his partner, Anita. Private rescuers later told them that other hikers last reported seeing him on day three of his hike.



“It is extremely out of character for him to be out of contact, and if he could manage to, he would know how worried we all are and make every effort to get a message across,” Anita said. “So that’s why we’re very, very worried right now.” Jordan (right) pictured with a friend. Supplied The Huayhuash circuit is known for its steep, rugged terrain and is considered one of Peru’s most challenging mountain routes. According to his family, Jordan is an experienced traveller and previously solo hiked across Australia, China, Turkey and Jordan. “He’s an avid outdoor person. In winter time, he will spend most weekends on the snow field, even though he didn’t have a lot of luck with the weather, he loves hiking,” Jordan’s father, Vinh Dao, said.



Before leaving for Peru, Jordan attempted to find other people to join him on the trek, but decided to go on his own when no one was available. Jordan Yap (left) works as a food regulation specialist for a dairy company. After struggling to get in contact with Peruvian authorities to help search for their son, the family hired local mountain rescue organisation, Socorro Andino Peruano. The family said a rescue team was deployed Friday at 3am Melbourne time. Vinh said he and his wife were preparing to fly to Peru and are urging the Australian government and the Department of Foreign Affairs to liaise with local authorities to assist with search efforts.



“We’re very concerned. While we’ve had some progress we’d really like it for DFAT to apply pressure on the local police and the government because time is of the essence, and it’s really critical now,” Vinh said. A DFAT spokesperson said they were providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Peru.
