World.title: This Lion pulled off the tackle of the grand final, but he barely remembers it
World.content:
The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories .

In the grand final briefing, your wrap of footy news Brisbane Lions defender Ryan Lester says his goal-saving tackle on Josh Treacy is little more than a blur.

The Brisbane Lions can thank Charlie Cameron for making “Wharfie Time” a grand final flop.

Retiring Fremantle forward Sam Switkowski prefers a titanic, heartbreaking defeat to Brisbane to being on the wrong end of a one-sided drubbing.

Fremantle are shattered for captain Alex Pearce, whose devastating game-ending Achilles injury in the Dockers’ heartbreaking grand final defeat will likely also eat into his 2027 campaign. The desperate tackle that halted Freo’s premiership momentum Hannah Kennelly

Brisbane’s Ryan Lester was desperate. With less than seven minutes to go in the final quarter, Fremantle’s Josh Treacy sprinted towards goal and looked certain to extend the Dockers’ lead and help them clinch their maiden premiership.



But Lester was right behind him. The 34-year-old launched himself towards Treacy’s legs, performing a tackle that left the Docker flat on his back and sent his kick wayward, preventing what would have been a crucial goal. Standing wide-eyed in the beer-soaked change rooms after the Lions’ extraordinary seven-point win on Saturday afternoon, Lester was lost for words when asked about the tackle. “Oh God, I don’t even know what happened,” he told this masthead. “I got him and the rest is a bit of a blur.” With his daughter Georgie clutching his leg, Lester said he found it difficult to articulate the magnitude of what the Lions had just achieved. In the early 2000s, the Lions achieved a historic hat-trick under Leigh Matthews. Fast-forward 23 years, and Chris Fagan’s team have repeated history, clinching a third straight premiership and cementing themselves in AFL history.



The significance was not lost on Lester. “Growing up, I looked at the Brisbane Lions and Hawthorn and those teams were just immortal … like unbelievable, and for us to join them is pretty cool,” he said. “Particularly for me, like in 2022, I only played three games in the senior team ... so I feel really lucky the way my career has turned out and so lucky to be a part of this special team.” When the bells from AC/DC’s Hells Bells blared, and with huge waves crashing on the big screen, Fremantle fans in the crowd rose to mark “Wharfie Time”. But Lester said the Lions were ready.



“We spoke about that [Wharfie Time] and then we tried to obviously use that for their motivation,” he said. Related Article Updated

AFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented Bomber turned Lion Sam Draper said the team had rehearsed for Wharfie Time and they were prepared for a hostile crowd. “We thought when they hit that trigger, that’s when we go up a notch,” Draper confirmed. “I think the boys responded well. I think like last week we handled that well [against Hawthorn]. That was a hostile environment, and today the same.



“So, yeah, the boys went crazy at the end of there.” Just 12 months ago, Draper was preparing to leave Essendon and enter the trade period as an unrestricted free agent, after another injury-plagued year at the Hangar including a devastating Achilles rupture in mid-April that ended his season. On Sunday, he stood with a premiership medal around his neck and was overcome with emotion. “It doesn’t feel real,” he said.“I got really emotional towards the end when I saw the high-performance team,” he said referencing his bought of injuries. “I just thanked them for believing in me.”



Charlie seizes his moment and history Marc McGowan

The Brisbane Lions can thank Charlie Cameron for making “Wharfie Time” a grand final flop. The evergreen small forward kicked the opening goal of the match – before unleashing his engine-revving celebration as Take Me Home, Country Roads blared across the MCG – but it was his third that turned the game. Charlie Cameron of the Lions celebrates kicking a goal. AFL Photos via Getty Images Eighty-one seconds after Fremantle cult hero Patrick Voss thought he had blasted through the sealer, Cameron swooped and snapped truly. It provided a swift end to Wharfie Time, the Dockers’ trademark fan-driven activation, which the AFL approved them to use just once in the match.



“As a forward, your job is about creating opportunities and moments,” Cameron told this masthead. “I was like, ‘If I get an opportunity here, I’m going to back myself in’. That’s the good thing about playing finals footy – you get the spotlight to showcase yourself, and when I had that snap, I was like, ‘I’m ready to go again, give me another one’.” Charlie Cameron takes his opportunity. Joe Armao Cameron needn’t have worried. Zac Bailey kicked another shortly after before Logan Morris became the match-winner with the last two goals to transform what had largely been a dirty day for him until then. These Lions now join Leigh Matthews’ and Michael Voss’ 2001-03 immortal teams as three-peat premiers.



Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Lion who scored a perfect 10 – and the Docker who scored just one: AFL grand final player ratings Cameron has played a major role in Brisbane becoming a juggernaut under Chris Fagan, including 410 goals – 64 in finals – in 208 matches for the club. “We spoke about it at the start of the year – do we want to go for a three-peat?” he said. “We said, ‘We have the opportunity here [to create history], with the list we have’, and it just came down to a lot of hard work. It’s pretty crazy to be a three-time, back-to-back-to-back premiership player. It’s unbelievable.” Retiring Docker proud despite devastating grand final loss



Steve Barrett

Retiring Fremantle forward Sam Switkowski accepted how cruel football can be, but would still prefer Saturday’s titanic, heartbreaking defeat to Brisbane to being on the wrong end of a one-sided drubbing. Despite the harrowing result and narrow margin, Switkowski can walk off with his head held high one last time. Retiring Docker Sam Switkowski. AFL Photos “I think we all know footy can be cruel like that,” he said after his 131st and last game. “But I’d still rather the way the game played out than have lost by 10 goals.



“It’s a bit hard to get over the disappointment and devastation of it, but I’m just so proud of everyone gave it their all. “I haven’t been in this position before, clearly – grand final loss, career’s at an end. “But I’m just so proud to have played nine years at this club.” Switkowski spoke with emotion, before walking over to Fremantle great Nat Fyfe – who he now joins in the retired footballers club – for a warm embrace. “I said to the guys in the rooms, after ‘JL’ [coach Justin Longmuir] spoke, that I’m so proud of each and every one of them.



Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Dockers had one hand on the premiership cup. Then came four minutes that turned the grand final “I thanked them for their efforts this season and giving it everything today. “I feel like we gave that our best shot. “I thought we played a Freo brand of footy. We would accept whatever the result is if we did that. “I’m trying to get a bit of perspective and know you’d rather be here today and hurt than not be here at all.”



Wingman Corey Wagner could almost touch and feel the club’s maiden flag – as Patrick Voss’ goal deep into the fourth quarter stretched the Dockers’ lead to 17 points – before it was brutally snatched out of the Dockers’ grasp. “It’s a hard pill to swallow,” Wagner said. “It was that close you could almost grab it and feel it. “The crowd was going nuts and you could almost believe it was going to happen. “We were thinking ‘we’re going to bring it home to Freo’.”



Wagner conceded the Lions played those crunch-time final stages better than the Dockers. “I don’t think we handled the last three minutes as good as we should have,” he said. “Credit to Brisbane – they’ve been here, they’ve done it and they’ve seen these moments before. “Brisbane had to come through this situation [2023 grand final loss to Collingwood] before having their three-peat.” Star midfielder Andrew Brayshaw was confident his team would learn and burn from this, but knows – from his own family’s experience – that contesting multiple grand finals isn’t guaranteed.



Related Article AFL grand final Lachie Neale is used to being the villain. He stepped up in ‘go time’ of a heist for the ages “I feel like we’ve got all the pieces in place, but you never want to assume you’ll be back,” he said. “My brother [Angus] played in one grand final [Melbourne, 2021] and thought he’d be back every year, but it ended up being his only one. “We don’t want to get complacent at all. This will light the fire in the belly, for sure. “We’ll fight, we’ll scrap and we’ll earn our way back in.



“It will make it even more sweet when we get back and get it done.” Freo skipper’s game-ending injury likely to cut into 2027 AAP

Fremantle are shattered for captain Alex Pearce, whose devastating game-ending Achilles injury in the Dockers’ heartbreaking grand final defeat will likely also eat into his 2027 campaign. Alex Pearce was on crutches after the game. AFL Photos With Fremantle leading by nine points in Saturday’s decider at the MCG, Pearce was racing Brisbane opponent Logan Morris to collect a loose ball on the wing when he dramatically fell to the ground without any contact.



The star defender suffered a right Achilles injury, was assisted off the field and watched from the bench as Fremantle capitulated and Morris kicked the winning goal. The Dockers confirmed the dreaded Achilles injury, which will likely also sideline Pearce for a large chunk of 2027 if it is fully ruptured. “He’s putting on a brave face,” coach Justin Longmuir said. “Everyone’s devastated. I’m sure he’s devastated, not only for today’s result, but it looks like it might cost him a bit of time on the sidelines and another stint in rehab. “But he can hold his head up high. Like he’s led us so well across the course of the year, and stood up in really key moments to allow us to get here.



Related Article Updated

AFL grand final Honoured, but surprised: Why Shai Bolton took off his medal right after winning the Norm Smith “Unfortunately it didn’t go his way today and I feel for him on that front.” Longmuir said Pearce was “sore” coming into the game but adamant that didn’t contribute to his injury. Pearce, 31, was heartbreakingly close to becoming Fremantle’s first premiership captain while the Dockers will wonder what might have been if they had their best key defender out there late. “[We had to] reshuffle the deck chairs a little bit,” Longmuir said.

World.title: Lachie Neale is used to being the villain. He stepped up in ‘go time’ of a heist for the ages
World.content:
SportAFLAFL grand final Lachie Neale is used to being the villain. He stepped up in ‘go time’ of a heist for the ages Peter Ryan September 26, 2026 — 8:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The big moments, the celebrations, the heartbreak and all the news and analysis from the MCG. See all stories . Loading

An outsized focus on Lachie Neale had become the new norm at the Brisbane Lions in 2026. Not only was he in the centre circle when the heat was on, as he had been ever since starting with the Dockers in 2013, he was suddenly the central character in a sporting drama – attracting tabloid headlines to gossip columns to trade speculation. Lachie Neale was swamped by his Lions teammates after the grand final. AFL Photos So, when the news came through he had been suspended for the grand final for punching Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the guts, there was surprise, but no panic. Football boss Danny Daly went to work to try to clear him, while also arranging contingency plans to send the dual Brownlow medallist to Naracoorte in South Australia to be with his dad Robbie if Thursday’s appeal failed.



But Neale didn’t need to implement those plans after all – the appeals board overturning the suspension, allowing him to play in his fifth grand final. Neale copped an initial one-game ban for this gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. Getty Images, Fox Footy The lead-up, plus his status as a former Docker, meant Neale was always going to be the villain on grand final day. For the sort of people who indulge in booing, it was a matter of picking their reason. Those boos rang out loud and clear as soon as Neale entered the arena at the nine-minute mark after starting the third of his five grand finals on the bench. He didn’t care.



Related Article Updated

AFL grand final ‘There’s a little bit inside me that would rather walk away’: Fagan’s admission after dynasty cemented “I don’t give a shit about that, whatever,” he said. “I used to play for them as well, which probably added to it. “It’s part of the game – honestly it doesn’t bother me.” Neale didn’t take over like he did in the second half the previous year, when he came on at half-time as the “super-sub” when the scores were level, finishing the match with 17 touches in a half.



On this occasion, his hands were quick when the ball was in his vicinity, and his mind was willing, but his Dockers opponents were able to find too much space at centre bounces and dominated. Editor's pick Analysis

AFL grand final Wharfie Time and Fagan’s heroes chime Freo’s doom in one of the greatest grand finals Neale was on for short bursts. But the clearances had been few and far between when the Dockers opened up what looked like a matchwinning 17-point lead with less than five minutes remaining and with Neale sitting on the pine. “Wharfie Time” then made the MCG erupt as Neale rose to his 177-centimetre height and took a breath.



He joined Will Ashcroft, Josh Dunkley and Sam Draper in the middle to see if they could pull off the biggest heist in grand final history. He said they had planned for “Wharfie Time” to be “go time”. “The mentality to switch that, and it be ‘go time’ for us, was important,” Neale said. “‘Fages’ once described us as cockroaches – we just don’t die.” Loading



Neale won the first touch and Ashcroft rose with him. It was his career at the Lions writ large as he lifted them off the canvas after joining the club back in 2019. He won’t be there next season, confirming post-match that this was his last game for the Lions. “I’ve loved my time at this club, they are an exceptional club,” he told Seven before his expected move to Collingwood in the coming weeks. “It’s been the best eight years of my life. It’s been an incredible ride. I love this group, [and] I’m going to miss them every much.” Neale’s teammates knew what he had given them, with Ashcroft saying, “I love him so much”, while Jarrod Berry admitted so much attention being on Neale wasn’t a bad thing for his teammates. Neale is used to it by now.



“Unfortunately, I have had experience in compartmentalising things and getting on with the job,” Neale said. Related Article Analysis

AFL grand final The Lion who scored a perfect 10 – and the Docker who scored just one: AFL grand final player ratings With 20 touches and a third consecutive premiership medal, his job was done. He hugged his dad and kissed his new girlfriend, Emma Field, and stood with a can of beer in his hand. “In a weird way, it’s a strength of mine – my resilience on the field and off the field,” Neale explained. “There are people doing it a lot worse than me. I have won my third premiership at an amazing organisation, so I can’t really complain.



“I have just got to get on with the job and try to be better as a human, and as a footballer.” There was no room for pride, he said, but he had kept at it as the Lions asked him to when all was exploding around him. Club president Andrew Wellington could only praise Neale, and the rest of the club, for how they prevailed in such circumstances. “There is always risk, when you have got a bit of turmoil, that it can affect [you] ... but credit to all the leaders, including Lachie, that they did not let that disturb what they were trying to do,” Wellington said. “Everyone just asked him, [that] as long as he is with us, he gives us everything, and he has done that.”

World.title: Native bird hospital short on funds despite government cash injection
World.content:
The country's largest native bird hospital says financial pressures are limiting its ability to operate seven days a week, as it prepares for the potential arrival of bird flu.

General manager of BirdCare Aotearoa Dr Rashi Parker said the wildlife hospital was one of the six facilities involved in the Government's bird flu surveillance.

She said staff with clinical skills were a major operational cost, and the organisation relied on grants and donations to maintain a fully staffed seven-day operation.

"At the moment, because of the wages pressures, the financial pressures of wages, we are only open to the public for five days of the week," she said.

The hospital said birds continued to receive care year-round despite the concerns.

BirdCare would receive $25,000 as part of a $150,000 government funding package for facilities involved in bird flu surveillance and response.

World.title: What is the Christchurch NRL club state of play?
World.content:
Explainer: As the NZ Warriors make a premature and deflating exit from the NRL playoffs after a supreme regular season run, ambitious plans for a second NZ-based club are about to be formally presented to competition bosses.

The NRL's aspirations to expand the competition to 20 teams by 2030, underlined by a record-breaking multibillion-dollar broadcast deal, remain on track with the addition of Perth Bears from next season, followed by PNG Chiefs from 2028.

A decision on the 20th team was next on the agenda for the game's powerbrokers, with a Christchurch-based franchise emerging as one of the frontrunners, as rugby league's cultural currency in New Zealand continues to soar.

Across the Tasman, Ipswich Jets were another strong contender to nab the vacancy, which would cement their place as the fifth Queensland team, alongside Brisbane Broncos, North Queensland Cowboys, Gold Coast Titans and the Dolphins.

Christchurch City Council has implanted itself in planning efforts on behalf of the group leading one of the main bids to ensure a proposal to NRL executives is as compelling as possible.

Here is the state of play.

Who is involved?

Over the past few years, New Zealand consortiums have been working behind the scenes to get a Christchurch-based NRL club off the ground, jostling to get into the frame of the sport's administrators.

Christchurch's Te Kaha Stadium. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The latest iteration of one group fronting a bid, trading as Southern Sporting Limited (SSL), includes former Kiwis and Warriors coach, and Canterbury league stalwart Frank Endacott, former Christchurch East MP Poto Williams and Waikato Rugby Board president Coal Groves.

The collective has received the backing of the city council.

Endacott had been involved in a previous bid by South Island NRL Bid Limited (SINBL), led by former Canterbury Rugby League board chair Tony Kidd, Canterbury Rugby League board director Darren Littlewood and former chief executive Duane Fyfe.

Williams also came on board in a community and wellbeing role, but the consortium had disbanded.

SINBL first approached the city council in 2024 to support a bid, claiming a Christchurch-based professional outfit would result in a $50 million economic injection into the region each year.

The council then began working directly with the NRL, championing the region's assets and suitability for the competition's expansion roll-out.

Talks involving council, its economic development arm, ChristchurchNZ, and the NRL continued last year, although competition executives signaled in September 2025 that "expansion wasn't on the table", after the Perth and PNG deals were greenlit.

The council declined an RNZ interview request, but in a statement, head of recreation, sports and events Nigel Cox said it was working with key stakeholders to explore an "opportunity for the city" alongside ChristchurchNZ.

A working group of established figureheads had been established to drive the process, including former NZ Rugby League chairman and former Canterbury Rugby League president Reon Edwards, ChristchurchNZ chair and former Sky NZ executive Lauren Quaintance, and sports industry executive Michael Goldstein. Quaintance also serves as a director on the Crusaders board.

Documents released under the Official Information Act showed Mayor Phil Mauger, Quaintance and Cox met NRL bosses in Christchurch for the Warriors-Cowboys game in June, as part of a charm offensive by local authorities.

Christchurch Mayor Phil Mauger. RNZ/ Anna Sargant

Southern Orcas, a separate proposal led by long-standing administrator and former coach Sir Graham Lowe, and millionaire businessman Andrew Chalmers was previously rejected by the NRL.

Its bid was bankrolled by an ambitious commercial investment, via private equity investors.

The Orcas made a curious play by attempting to secure the services of former All Blacks coach Scott Robertson, who was axed from the coaching role in January.

In August, Lowe told RNZ that its bid had been officially submitted, with the franchise waiting for a decision from Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) chairman Peter V'landys.

"All we know is we've had to put our best foot forward, which I'm confident that we have done," Lowe said. "We're just, sitting and waiting with our fingers crossed."

A separate South Island Kea bid, led by former New Zealand Rugby and NRL chief David Moffett, was also rejected by the NRL in favour of the Perth and Papua New Guinea proposals.

The project has since been scrapped, with Moffett publicly endorsing council-led efforts, while speaking frankly on the Orcas, describing the consortium's push as "pissing into the wind".

Do we need a second NZ NRL club?

The regular sight of boisterous sold-out crowds at Go Media Stadium for Warriors home games, coupled with generous support for New Zealand's sole club across the Tasman, would have given competition chiefs, for better or worse, food for thought.

Endacott told RNZ that the bumper Eden Park crowd at Sunday's Warriors-Knights semi-final clash revealed rugby league's current popularity.

"That tells you something, doesn't it," he said.

Rugby league's ratings were also going through the roof. The latest ARLC annual report said, by last year, the NRL was watched by more than 224 million cumulative viewers in Australia and New Zealand, an increase of 64 percent in six years.

V'landys referenced gaining traction, when announcing Auckland's Eden Park as the venue for a State of Origin game in 2027 earlier this year.

"Rugby league is the No.1 sport in Australia and the Pacific, and the growth we have seen in New Zealand over recent years has been nothing short of extraordinary," he said.

ARL Commission chairman Peter V'landys. NRL Photos 2020

A major piece of essential infrastructure a new club would require is already open. Christchurch's 25,000-seat central city venue One New Zealand Stadium has been met with enthusiastic fanfare, since its April opening.

"The crowds they get down here, every time a league game is played down here, now you pack it out," Endacott said.

"We've got so much going for it to have it in Christchurch. As a number of Australians have said, 'It's a no-brainer'."

Mauger expressed a similar sentiment in a letter to the NRL's executive general manager of corporate affairs in August 2024.

"Our fans turn up with passion and pride to support their national team, but having one team based in Auckland makes it difficult... for the southern part of the country to get behind their players, leaving fans and revenue on the table," he said.

The origins of some of the NRL's fiercest rivalries date back more than a century. Without the same historical lore, could the introduction of Christchurch-based club ignite the NRL's first all-New Zealand grudge match - a classic North-versus-South faceoff for league fans?

There are concerns over whether a second New Zealand club could dilute the player pool and stifle the momentum of the Warriors.

The Penrose-based club has only made two grand finals since its competition debut in 1995 and a maiden premiership remains elusive.

Significant recent gains had seen the team emerge, for some pundits, as genuine contenders.

Putting its anti-climactic post-season showing of recent weeks to one side, the club had made the playoffs three times in the last four years, two of them inside the all-important top four.

Panthers and former Warriors head coach Ivan Cleary warned the game's administrators against fast-tracking a second New Zealand-based club, fearing the addition of a new club in the country could "cannibalise the progress of the Warriors". The four-time-premiership-winning coach led the Warriors to their last grand final appearance in 2011.

Warriors CEO Cameron George. Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz / Photosport Ltd 2025

In July, Warriors chief executive Cameron George told Sport Nation that New Zealand remained a great option for NRL expansion plans, but more investment from competition chiefs was needed.

"Right now, there are no domestic competitions that are at the level we need to to sustain, not only for one team, because we fly all of ours to Sydney each week and vice-versa," he said.

"To underpin two teams, that would mean you're flying 12 teams to Australia every week."

Threat to rugby union?

In a letter to then-NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in August 2024, released under the Official Information Act, Endacott argued that New Zealand's national game was in danger.

"Rugby union is vulnerable," he said. "If we get the second [NRL] club right, rugby league will become the preferred winter sport in New Zealand."

The NRL said it had appointed a new New Zealand general manager based in Auckland who would be "managing rugby league growth in the country and expanding participation programmes".

This did not mean union was floundering, especially not in red-and-black country.

Canterbury Rugby board member and former city councillor James Gough said broadcast audiences of Canterbury NPC games last season had tripled since 2023.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) hosted a summit with the country's key stakeholders this week, tackling financial and structural problems facing the sport in the face of tens of millions of dollars of projected losses, largely at provincial level.

NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster downplayed the threat of rugby league, when talking to Newstalk ZB's Jason Pine in September.

"It's not a binary proposition for us," he said. "For one code to be strong doesn't mean the other has to suffer, there's plenty of space in the market for more than one code to be thriving."

Former Kiwis and Warriors coach Frank Endacott. Photosport

How much will it cost?

A fair bit. V'landys has signaled an entry fee for new licensees would cost AU$100 million (NZ$124.3m).

There was also some serious coin behind the NRL's recently inked broadcast deal.

In July, Nine, Fox and Sky NZ signed a new broadcast rights agreement worth an astronomical $5.3 billion until 2034, underlining just how lucrative the sport had become in this part of the world.

Mauger did point out in correspondence to V'landys in September 2024 that the city council had invested more than $1.25b into rebuilding and developing the city's sports infrastructure, including almost $700m on its crown jewel, Te Kaha (One New Zealand Stadium).

Government supportive, but staying away

As has been shown with the deals struck with Perth Bears and PNG Chiefs, the NRL has an affinity for leveraging public, rather than private, funding models as part of its expansion plans.

Perth Bears are backed by a seven-year, AU$66m investment from the WA government, including A$35m ringfenced for the grassroots game.

PNG is supported by A$600 million of Australian government funding over 10 years.

The deal runs deep and has links within a broader geopolitical partnership between both countries, aimed at growing diplomacy and limiting China's influence in the region.

Christchurch City Council and the mayor have been keen to understand the key mechanics of the Perth bid, as outlined in emails to the NRL.

The New Zealand government had been kept in the loop on plans, with SSL meeting with South Island Minister James Meager last November.

In briefing documents, the group said Christchurch's best chance of securing a license was through a similar approach to that seen with Perth and PNG.

Unsurprisingly, any funding commitments or deal-making involvement from central government were off the table.

Sport and Recreation Minister Mark Mitchell. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Sport and Recreation Minister Mark Mitchell said he supported any plans to advance New Zealand's sporting interests.

"To be clear, the government is not involved in Christchurch's bid for a new NRL team," he said. "At no point has government funding been discussed or requested - nor would I expect it to be."

Next steps

The city council has outlined several workstreams in preparing a formal proposal to the NRL. They include governance and ownership, financial, football high performance, community participation and pathways, infrastructure for elite pathways, fan acquisition strategy, economic development and community impact.

Endacott told RNZ that the proposal was now ready for presentation to the NRL.

If the case proved viable, the council would then commence formal investment discussions with ChristchurchNZ.

World.title: Call for Sams Creek to be included in Kahurangi National Park
World.content:
Labour and the Greens are backing a call for Sams Creek to be included in the Kahurangi National Park to protect it from future mining proposals at the top of the South Island.

Gold was first discovered at Sams Creek in Upper Tākaka in the 1970s and several companies had undertaken exploration work since then. A recent bid for a mining permit by Australian company Siren Gold was declined in May.

The company faced staunch opposition from people in Golden Bay, with many concerned about the impact on the environment and the nearby Te Waikoropupū Springs, which holds some of the clearest water in the world.

A petition calling on the government to recommend that Sams Creek and adjoining conservation land around the Tākaka River and Cobb Valley be included in the Kahurangi National Park was presented to Green MP Lan Pham at the Parliament on Wednesday.

It had more than 11,000 signatures, including that of former Prime Minister Helen Clark and former Nelson MP and Conservation Minister Philip Woollaston.

Pham said the inclusion of Sams Creek in the park was a "no-brainer" and it should not have been left out to start with.

She would hold onto the petition until the next government was elected, before handing it over to the new conservation minister.

Labour conservation spokesperson Priyanca Radhakrishnan said the party supported Sams Creek being added to Kahurangi National Park and if elected, Labour would start the process.

"The Sams Creek area has outstanding scenic and natural features deserving of national park status, like the land it adjoins. The addition will increase the park's size by some 4500 ha, or about one percent, and permanently protect Sams Creek from mining activity."

Sams Creek. Save Our Springs

A spokesperson for Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said he had not been invited to receive the petition and had not yet had an opportunity to consider it.

Woollaston said Sams Creek was an "obvious hole" in the boundary of the national park, which was gazetted in 1996.

"There was a prospecting licence over the Sams Creek area before it was made a national park and I think the powers that be at the time just said the easiest thing is to exclude that from the park, rather than trying to take away a prospecting licence that had been granted."

Given there was now no mining or exploration permit in place, Woollaston said it was a good time for Sams Creek to be added to the national park, "where it always should have been".

"Apart from the prospecting holes they've put in, it's still pristine up there and I think the effect of mining in that area would be very high risk for the Tākaka catchment and the Waikoropupū Springs which are internationally renowned, they are not just a national treasure, they are an international treasure and anything which threatens them should not be allowed."

Woollaston said the exclusion of Sams Creek from the park had been a running sore for the last 30 years.

"Now is the time when it can just be put to bed and the worry of that can go," he said.

Clark said there was a strong case for revisiting the national park's boundaries.

"This is an obvious time to look again at the boundary and include Sams Creek within the national park," she said.

The petition, started by advocacy group Save Our Springs, was seeking to better protect Sams Creek and the famed Te Waikoropupū Springs.

Co-ordinator Kevin Moran said it was significant to have two political parties campaigning on ensuring Sams Creek would be included in the national park.

He said the group remained concerned about another mining application in the area and wanted to see Sams Creek protected in perpetuity.

World.title: Profits from iwi-led solar project tagged for families experiencing energy hardship
World.content:
A floating solar project has transformed a Dannevirke wastewater treatment pond into a source of clean energy, with profit from the electricity generated going to whānau the Tararua community experiencing energy hardship.

The project is a partnership between Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua and Tararua District Council and features 880 solar panels mounted on a floating structure at the Dannevirke Wastewater Treatment Plant.

Owned and operated by Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua, the project will see 50 eligible households receiving contributions towards their electricity bills.

Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua Charitable Trust trustee Mavis Mullins said it was a local solution, led by locals, for the benefit of locals.

"The key to this project was mahi tahi, working together, reflected in the whakataukī: "Nāku te rourou, nāu te rourou, ka ora ai te iwi" - "With your basket and my basket, we will sustain everyone.

"The floating design makes clever use of an existing asset, turning a wastewater pond into a source of clean energy."

Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua Charitable Trust trustee Mavis Mullins speaks at the opening of the floating solar project. Supplied/Tararua District Council

Council provided Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua with a licence to occupy for the solar panels.

Council also entered a power purchase agreement with the Iwi, whereby Council will buy electricity produced by the solar array at a discounted rate to help power the wastewater treatment plant.

Additional power produced and not utilised at the wastewater treatment plant will be fed back into the grid.

Mayor Scott Gilmore said the project could become a blueprint for other councils.

"With hundreds of wastewater ponds across New Zealand, the model could inspire other communities looking for practical ways to combine renewable energy, infrastructure resilience, lower costs and social benefit.

"As energy prices are rising and environmental pressures mount, it is time to start exploring innovative solutions with resources that are not fully utilised."

Tararua District Mayor Scott Gilmore speaks at the opening of the solar project. Supplied/Tararua District Council

The project has also recently secured funding for battery storage, allowing more of the solar energy generated during the day to be stored and used beyond sunshine hours.

Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua Charitable Trust chairperson Aaron Kārena said the iwi was excited to formally launch this development.

"This kaupapa has been led by our energy company, Tū Mai Rā Energy, and is a partnership with the Tararua District Council. Alongside our other mahi, this kaupapa strengthens our connection with our whenua and taiao here at Mākirikiri, and across our wider rohe of Tamaki-nui-a-Rua".
